One warning before we start, because it is the thing that catches people. Evaluation becomes genuinely hard here. In supervised learning you have a held-out set with known answers and you compute an accuracy. Here there is no ground truth, so there is no accuracy to compute, and it is entirely possible to produce clusters that look beautiful and mean nothing. The honest tests are three: does the structure hold up when you rerun it on new data, does it improve some downstream task you actually care about, and can a domain expert look at the groups and recognize them. If none of those three is true, you have found a pattern in noise, and no amount of silhouette score will save you.

The workhorse clustering algorithm is k-means, and it is two lines of idea. First you decide how many groups you want — that is k, and you must supply it. Scatter k points at random into your data space and call them centroids. Now repeat two steps until nothing changes. Step one, assign: give every data point to whichever centroid is nearest to it. Step two, move: shift each centroid to the mean position of all the points that were just assigned to it. Then reassign, because moving the centroids may have changed who is nearest to what. Then move again. Keep going until the assignments stop changing, and you are done. That is the whole algorithm, and you could implement it in twenty lines. There is a small piece of theory worth knowing, because it explains both why it works and what it cannot promise. Each of those two steps can only decrease the total distance from points to their assigned centroids — assignment decreases it by definition, and moving to the mean is exactly the point that minimizes squared distance. Since the quantity only falls and cannot fall forever, the algorithm always converges. But it converges to a local minimum, and which one you land in depends entirely on where the random centroids started. Two different seeds can give you two genuinely different clusterings of the same data. So the standard practice is to run it ten times with different initializations and keep the result with the lowest total distance. Now the genuinely hard part, which no algorithm solves for you: choosing k. The standard approach is the elbow method. Run k-means for k equals one, two, three, and so on, and plot the total within-cluster distance against k. It drops steeply at first — each new cluster explains a lot — and then flattens out, because you are now just splitting groups that were already coherent. The bend in that curve is a defensible choice of k. Silhouette score, which measures how much closer each point is to its own cluster than to the next nearest, is a useful second opinion. Neither is a verdict; k is ultimately a decision about what granularity is useful to you. Finally, initialization is important enough that it has its own algorithm. K-means-plus-plus chooses the starting centroids to be spread far apart rather than uniformly at random, which dramatically reduces bad local minima. It is the default in every serious library, and you should leave it that way.

K-means is fast, simple and everywhere, and it has strong opinions about what a cluster looks like. Knowing those opinions is what stops you from misusing it. First, and by now predictably: it works on distances, so you must scale your features. If one column is measured in millions and another in fractions, the clusters will be defined entirely by the first column, and everything else is decoration. Same trap as k-NN, same one-line fix, and it catches people just as often. Second, and this is the deep one: k-means minimizes squared distance to a mean, which means it implicitly assumes clusters are roughly round, roughly the same size, and roughly the same density. When those assumptions hold, it is excellent. When they do not, it fails in ways that look confident. Give it two long curved bands lying side by side, and it will slice straight across them, because a straight-ish boundary is what minimizing distance to two centres produces. Give it one tight little cluster sitting beside one enormous diffuse one, and the big one will swallow the small one's edge. The algorithm is not confused; it is faithfully optimizing the thing you asked it to optimize, and that thing happens to encode roundness. Third, every point must belong to some cluster. There is no option for 'this one is just weird'. So a single genuine outlier does not get ignored, it gets absorbed, and it pulls its centroid away from where the real group sits. If you expect noise in your data — and in real data you should — that alone is a reason to consider something else. So what else? The usual alternative is DBSCAN, and it thinks about clusters in a completely different way: a cluster is a region of high density, and you grow it by walking from point to nearby point wherever the neighbours are dense enough. That gives you three things k-means cannot. It finds clusters of any shape, including those two curved bands. It discovers the number of clusters itself rather than making you supply it. And it explicitly labels sparse points as noise rather than forcing them into a group. Its own weakness is that it assumes a single density threshold, so it struggles when some clusters are much denser than others. That is the real lesson of this slide, and it generalizes far beyond clustering: every algorithm encodes assumptions about the shape of the answer, and your job is to match those assumptions to your data rather than to run the default and believe it.

Now the second half of the lesson: reducing dimensions. Suppose Nami measures each shell a hundred different ways — length, width, thickness, weight, twenty curvature measurements, colour channels, and so on. She now has a hundred numbers per shell, and she cannot look at a hundred-dimensional plot. But those hundred numbers are not a hundred independent facts. Long shells tend to be heavy. Wide shells tend to be thick. Most of those measurements are moving together, which means the true structure in her data lives in far fewer directions than a hundred. PCA finds those directions, in order of importance. The first principal component is the single direction in which the data varies the most — the long axis of the cloud. The second is the direction of maximum remaining variance among directions perpendicular to the first. The third is perpendicular to both, and so on. Then you re-express every data point in these new coordinates, and because the components are ordered by how much variance they capture, you can simply keep the first few and throw away the rest. And here is where lesson four pays for itself. Those directions are not found by search or optimization — they are exactly the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix of your data. Equivalently, and this is how it is actually computed, they are the right singular vectors from the SVD of your centred data matrix. And each eigenvalue is precisely the amount of variance captured along its eigenvector. So the whole method reduces to a decomposition you already know, and the eigenvalues hand you the answer to 'how many components do I keep?' — plot the cumulative proportion of variance explained and keep enough components to reach ninety or ninety-five percent. Two practical requirements. Centre your data, always, by subtracting the mean of each feature; PCA is about directions of variance around the centre, and if you skip this you get the direction of the mean instead. And scale your features unless they genuinely share units, because PCA chases variance and an unscaled column measured in millions will trivially become the first component regardless of whether it means anything. Both of these are one line each and both are skipped constantly.

Let us be concrete about what you actually use this for, and then honest about where it stopped being enough. The first use is visualization, and it is the one you will reach for most often. Project your data down to two components, plot it, and look. You now have a picture of a hundred-dimensional dataset, and you can see immediately whether there are distinct groups, whether one class overlaps another, whether there are outliers sitting far from everything. That is often the single most informative half hour you can spend on a new dataset, and it costs one function call. The second use is speed and noise reduction. Fewer input columns means faster training and less opportunity to overfit, and the directions you discarded were the ones along which your data barely varied — which is very often measurement noise rather than signal. So dropping them can genuinely improve a downstream model, not merely speed it up. A common pipeline is PCA down to fifty dimensions, then k-means on the result, and the clustering is both faster and cleaner than it was on the raw hundred. Now the two real limits. First, interpretability is gone. Your new axes are linear combinations of the originals — nought-point-three times length, minus nought-point-seven times weight, plus a dozen other terms — and there is usually no story you can tell about what that combination means. You traded meaning for compactness, and if somebody needs to understand the model, that trade may not be acceptable. Second, and more fundamentally: PCA can only find straight directions. If your data lies on a curved surface — points arranged along a spiral, say — no linear projection can unroll it, and PCA will simply flatten the spiral and destroy the structure. That second limitation is exactly why embeddings took over for anything involving meaning. A neural network can learn curved structure, so the embedding of a word or a sentence, which we build in lesson twenty-one, captures relationships that no linear method can reach. But do not file PCA under history. It is fast, deterministic, needs no training, and has no hyperparameters to speak of. And it is used constantly in production today, including on embeddings themselves: a fifteen-hundred-dimensional embedding vector squeezed down to two or three hundred dimensions makes a vector database several times cheaper to store and faster to search, at almost no cost in retrieval quality. Old tools that are honest about what they do tend to survive.
cnn-rnn-tour: Everything so far has used a multilayer perceptron: flatten your input into a vector, and let every neuron look at every number. That is a perfectly reasonable thing to do when your input really is an unordered list of features — age, income, blood pressure — because there is no structure to lose. But hand it a photograph and it goes badly wrong in three separate ways, and it is worth seeing all three, because the fixes in this lesson are precisely aimed at them. First, and most fundamentally: flattening destroys the geometry. A two-hundred by two-hundred colour photograph becomes a list of a hundred and twenty thousand numbers, and in that list, the pixel at row seven column seven and the pixel at row seven column eight are just entries five hundred and something apart. They are neighbours in the world. They are strangers to the model. Every fact about the image that depends on things being next to each other — which is every fact about an image — has to be rediscovered from scratch by the network, from data, when it was sitting right there in the input and you threw it away in the first line. Second, the arithmetic. That first hidden layer needs one weight for every input pixel, for every neuron. A hundred and twenty thousand weights per neuron. A modest layer of a thousand neurons is a hundred and twenty million parameters, in layer one, before the network has learned a single thing. That is not just slow — it is statistically hopeless, because each of those parameters is being estimated from your training set, and there are far more parameters than there are meaningful examples of any of them. Third, and this is the one that really stings once you see it: nothing is shared. Suppose the network learns, in the top-left corner, what the edge of a cat's ear looks like. Those weights belong to that position and nowhere else. Move the cat to the bottom-right and the network has to learn the same edge again, from scratch, with different weights, from different examples. Every feature must be re-learned independently at every location in the image. You are paying, over and over, for the same knowledge. Now notice what all three problems have in common. They are not shortages of data or of compute. They are the result of using an architecture that knows nothing about the kind of thing it is being shown. And there are things we know about images that are simply true: nearby pixels are related and distant ones usually are not, and an object is the same object wherever it appears in the frame. Those two facts are called locality and translation invariance, and they are not learned — they are properties of the world. The move in this lesson, and honestly the move behind most good architectures, is to build a known truth into the shape of the model so the model never has to spend data learning it. Images get convolution. Sequences get recurrence. Both are the same idea wearing different clothes.

The fix for images is one of the most elegant ideas in the field, and it is smaller than people expect. Take a tiny grid of weights — three by three is the standard, so nine numbers. Lay that grid over the top-left corner of the image, multiply each weight by the pixel underneath it, add the nine products together, and write down the single number you get. That is a dot product, exactly the one from Part One, computed over a neighbourhood instead of over the whole image. Now slide the grid one pixel to the right and do it again. And again, across the row, then down. When you have covered the image you have produced a new, slightly smaller image. That grid of weights is called a kernel or a filter, and that sliding operation is a convolution. Here is why it fixes everything. It is local: each output looks only at a small patch, which is exactly the fact we said was true about images. And — this is the part to hold on to — the same nine numbers are used at every single position. That is called weight sharing, and it does two things at once. It means a feature learned anywhere is available everywhere: if those nine weights happen to detect a vertical edge, they detect vertical edges in the top-left and the bottom-right and the middle, automatically, with no extra training and no extra parameters. And it collapses the cost. Where the MLP needed a hundred and twenty thousand weights per neuron, this needs nine. Not nine thousand. Nine. One kernel gives you one output image, and that output is called a feature map, because what it really shows you is where in the original image that kernel's pattern occurs — bright where the pattern is present, dark where it is not. One pattern is not much, so a convolutional layer runs many kernels side by side, each with its own nine numbers, each learning to look for something different. Sixty-four kernels give you sixty-four feature maps stacked together, which you can think of as asking sixty-four different questions of every location in the image at once. That stack is what the next layer reads, so channels in and channels out is the shape you have to keep track of. Three more knobs and you have the whole operation. Stride is how far the kernel jumps between positions — a stride of one looks everywhere, a stride of two skips every other position and halves the size of the output. Padding is a ring of zeros around the edge of the input, which stops the image shrinking a little at every layer and stops the border pixels from being under-counted. And pooling, usually max pooling over a two by two square, is a deliberate downsampling step: keep the strongest response in each little region and throw the rest away. That last one is doing something important rather than just saving memory. Halving the resolution means the next layer's three by three kernel is looking at twice as much of the original image through the same small window, and stacking that is how a network built entirely out of three-pixel-wide filters ends up seeing whole objects.

Sequences have the mirror image of the image problem. A sentence has no fixed length, so there is no fixed-size input vector to build an MLP around, and the order of the words is not incidental decoration — it is where a large part of the meaning lives. The recurrent neural network answers both at once with a single idea: read the sequence one element at a time, and carry a memory along with you. That memory is a vector called the hidden state, usually written h, and it holds everything the network has decided is worth remembering so far. At each step you combine two things: the new element that just arrived, and the state you were already carrying. Concretely, h at time t is the tanh of W-h times h at time t minus one, plus W-x times x at time t, plus a bias. Read that slowly, because it is the whole architecture. There is one weight matrix for the incoming element, one for the previous state, one bias, and a bend. And the crucial word is the same: the same weights are used at every single timestep. That is weight sharing again — the identical trick the convolution used, only now shared across time rather than across space. It is why the network can handle a sequence of any length: there is no per-position parameter to run out of. And it is why the architecture is genuinely order-sensitive. Feed it dog bites man, and feed it man bites dog, and the same three words arrive in a different order, so the state evolves differently, and the final state is different. A bag-of-words model cannot tell those apart. This one can, structurally, without being told. The plain version I have just described is called a vanilla RNN, and it works, but it struggles to hold anything for long — we will see exactly why on the next slide. The repair, and it was the repair for about twenty years, is to make the memory update selective instead of automatic. Instead of overwriting the state with a fresh tanh at every step, learn small networks called gates that decide, per element of the state and per timestep, how much of the old value to keep, how much of the new candidate to write in, and how much of the result to expose to the rest of the network. That is the long short-term memory unit, the LSTM, from nineteen ninety-seven. The GRU is a slimmer version with two gates instead of three and roughly the same performance for less compute. Both are the same skeleton — a state carried forward, one shared rule applied at every step — with gates deciding what survives. And it is worth saying plainly: these worked. LSTMs were the state of the art for translation, speech and text generation for years, they are what Google Translate ran on, and they are still a reasonable choice for a short sequence on a small machine. They did not fail because they were bad. They were replaced because of two specific limitations, and those two limitations are the entire reason the next lesson exists.

Both of these architectures already exist on the Going Merry, and I think the picture makes them stick better than the equations do. Start with the crow's nest. When Zoro takes the watch, he does not carry a hundred spyglasses up the mast, each one permanently aimed at a different patch of sea. That would be absurd, and it is exactly what the MLP does: a separate set of weights for every position. He takes one spyglass, and he sweeps it across the horizon. The instrument is identical everywhere he points it. What changes is only what happens to be in front of it. That is weight sharing, and it is not an analogy for weight sharing, it is the same idea — one small, expensive-to-build detector, moved over the input, because a sail is a sail regardless of which part of the horizon it is on. Now notice the second half of what he does, because it is the part people miss. He does not describe the whole view. He shouts down a summary: sail, two points off the starboard bow. One small statement about one patch of sea. And down on deck, Nami takes his report and Usopp's report and combines them into something bigger — a fleet, a course, a threat. That is the layer structure exactly. Convolution detects a local pattern, pooling summarizes a region into its strongest signal, and the next layer up combines those summaries into something with more meaning than any of them had alone. Edges become corners become wheels become car, and each level only ever talks to the level below it. Now the other half of the ship, and the other architecture. The log book. Nami writes one entry per watch: wind, heading, weather, anything that happened. And she writes each entry knowing what the last one said — the entry is not written in isolation, it is written on top of the accumulated record. Same hand, same rules, same format, applied to a voyage of any length whatsoever. That is precisely the recurrent state: one shared updating rule, applied step after step, carrying everything forward. And now the honest part of the metaphor, which is also the reason the next lesson exists. A log is a lossy memory. By the time the crew is deep in the Grand Line, what actually happened back in the East Blue survives only in whatever form it has been carried through hundreds of intervening entries, each one summarizing and compressing the last. The detail is gone. And the second problem is worse: if you want to check something specific from day one, you cannot simply look at it. You have to read every page in between, in order, because the state at day four hundred is only reachable by having passed through days one to three hundred and ninety-nine. Hold onto both of those complaints. Fading detail, and no random access. They are exactly the two failures of the recurrent network, and the fix for both of them is to stop copying the log forward and let the reader simply look directly at any page they want.

So, the indictment. It really is two sentences, and everything in the next part of this course follows from them. The first is fading memory. Look again at the update rule: the state is multiplied by a weight matrix at every single timestep. To find out how something at step one influences the output at step three hundred, you multiply through three hundred matrices. We have seen exactly this before, in the vanishing gradient lesson — repeated multiplication by numbers below one drives a signal to zero, and repeated multiplication by numbers above one blows it up. Here the same thing happens along the time axis instead of along the depth of the network. In practice, a vanilla RNN struggles to connect information more than about ten steps apart. LSTM gates were built precisely to fight this, and they genuinely help — the gate can choose to leave a value alone rather than re-multiplying it — but they push the limit out to maybe a few hundred steps rather than removing it. For a paragraph that is fine. For a document, or a long conversation, or a codebase, it is not. The second sentence is about hardware, and it is the one that actually killed the architecture. The state at time t depends on the state at time t minus one. That dependency is unavoidable — it is the definition of recurrence. So a sequence of five hundred tokens is five hundred strictly sequential steps, each one waiting for the last. Meanwhile you are running this on a graphics card with thousands of cores designed to do thousands of things simultaneously, and almost all of them are idle, because the architecture forbids you from using them. Convolution does not have this problem: every patch of an image is independent, so a CNN saturates a GPU beautifully. An RNN cannot. And in a field where progress has been driven by scale — more data, bigger models, more compute — an architecture that structurally cannot be parallelized is an architecture that cannot ride the hardware curve, no matter how good it is. Now put the two complaints side by side, because the solution is a single idea that answers both. If the problem is that information degrades while being copied forward, and that you are forced to walk through every intermediate step to get anywhere, then stop copying it forward and stop walking. Let every position look directly at every other position, weight those looks by how relevant each one is, and read what you need in a single step. Nothing is passed hand to hand, so nothing fades. There is no dependency chain, so the entire sequence computes at once and the GPU is finally busy. That is attention, that is the whole content of the twenty-seventeen paper called Attention Is All You Need, and the title is a fair description. One last note so the lesson is honest. CNNs did not lose in the way RNNs did. Convolution is still what runs in your phone camera, in medical scanners, in real-time detection on small devices — it is efficient and it is right about images, and even the vision transformers that beat it borrowed its patch-based structure. It is sequences where the story ends here. The next lesson opens that door.
eigen-svd: Entering the Grand Line, the Going Merry is caught in a monstrous whirlpool, and every heading the crew tries gets bent — sail north, the current drags you northeast; sail west, you are swept southwest. The whirlpool is a transformation: it takes your intended course, a vector, and outputs a twisted one. Panic on deck. Then Nami studies the spiral and finds it: one line through the maelstrom, the surge axis, where the current does not bend your course at all. Sail exactly along it and the whirlpool only accelerates you — you come out pointing the same way, three times faster. Course unchanged, magnitude times three. Nami found the eigenvector, and the times-three is its eigenvalue. That is the whole definition: apply a matrix to lots of vectors and most come out pointing somewhere new, but almost every matrix has a few special directions where the output is just the input scaled, same line, no rotation — A times v equals lambda times v, where v, not zero, is an eigenvector, and the stretch factor lambda is its eigenvalue. Verify one by hand, always do this once. Let A be bracket bracket two one, bracket one two, and v be bracket one one; then A-v is two plus one, one plus two, which is bracket three three, exactly three times v, so bracket one one is an eigenvector with eigenvalue three. Try v equals bracket one minus one: A-v is two minus one, one minus two, which is bracket one minus one, exactly one times v — a second eigenvector with eigenvalue one. This matrix stretches the one-one diagonal by three and leaves the one-minus-one diagonal completely alone, and now you know everything it does, because any input vector is a mix of those two directions. That last clause is the whole point: eigenvectors are the transformation's natural axes. Written in those axes, a scary matrix becomes just a list of per-axis stretch factors, a diagonal matrix, and diagonalization is simply changing to the coordinate system where the machine is simple. Nami did not fight the whirlpool; she found the axis where it becomes plain multiplication.

Here is the single most consequential fact about eigenvalues: multiply by A over and over, and each eigen-direction gets scaled by its lambda each time, so after k steps it is scaled by lambda-to-the-k. The direction with the largest absolute lambda grows fastest and eventually dominates everything, which means any starting vector, transformed repeatedly, swings toward the dominant eigenvector. At the Knock Up Stream the Going Merry rides exactly this: along the dominant axis, every second multiplies the ship's speed again — lambda, lambda-squared, lambda-cubed — until the ship is launched into the sky toward Skypiea. Glorious when you want to reach the sky island, catastrophic when it is your gradients doing the multiplying through fifty layers. This one fact explains three things you will meet again. First, power iteration, which is your lab: to find the dominant eigenvector, just multiply a random vector by A repeatedly and re-normalize each step, and it converges to the top axis. That algorithm, plus a sparsity trick, is how Google's original PageRank ranked the entire web — the ranking literally is the dominant eigenvector of the web's link matrix. Second, exploding and vanishing gradients, which is Part Three: backpropagation multiplies the gradient by roughly the same weight matrices layer after layer, so a largest eigenvalue-ish factor above one makes gradients blow up exponentially, and below one makes them die exponentially. Deep recurrent nets failed on long sequences for exactly this reason, and the fix — attention and transformers — is Part Five's whole origin story. Third, the stability of any iterative system: if the largest absolute eigenvalue is below one, the loop settles; above one, it diverges. Same math, three faces — a search algorithm, a training pathology, and a stability criterion, all just lambda-to-the-k deciding who wins.

The whirlpool's axis was one matrix's natural direction; PCA finds the natural axes of a data cloud, and it is the same eigenvector idea pointed at data instead of a transformation. Take a cloud of data points, rows are samples, and form its covariance matrix C, where entry i-j is the average of feature-i-minus-its-mean times feature-j-minus-its-mean. That matrix summarizes how the features co-vary, and here is the beautiful part: C's eigenvectors point along the cloud's natural axes, the directions of most spread, and each eigenvalue is the variance along its direction. So principal component analysis is simply: pick the top-k eigenvectors, project your data onto them, and throw the rest away. You keep the k directions carrying the most variance, which is usually the most signal, and you compress — seven-hundred-eighty-four pixel dimensions down to fifty while keeping ninety-five percent of the variance. And this is not a heuristic that happens to work; it is an exact optimization solved exactly. The variance of your data projected onto a unit direction v is v-transpose-C-v, so find the direction of maximum variance means maximize v-transpose-C-v subject to v having length one, and the maximizer of that constrained problem is precisely C's top eigenvector, with the achieved variance being its eigenvalue — that is the Rayleigh-quotient argument, and each next component repeats it in the subspace orthogonal to the ones already chosen. The uses you will actually meet: visualizing seven-hundred-sixty-eight-dimensional embeddings down in two dimensions, decorrelating features for classical models, whitening, and building the intuition that real data lives on a much lower-dimensional manifold than its raw dimension suggests. One warning that is the number-one PCA bug: always center the data first, subtract the feature means, because without centering your top component mostly points at the data's mean rather than its spread. Center, covary, take the top eigenvectors — Nami mapping the surge axes of a whole fleet of data points.

Eigendecomposition needs a square, nicely-behaved matrix, but the singular value decomposition works for any matrix at all, even a rectangular one, and it is the tool you will reach for most. It says A equals U-Sigma-V-transpose, where U and V are rotations, matrices with orthonormal columns, and Sigma is a diagonal of non-negative singular values, sigma-one greater than or equal to sigma-two and so on. Read it as a sentence: every linear machine, however messy, is secretly rotate the input axes, then stretch along each axis by sigma-i, then rotate to the output axes. The singular values tell you how much each independent channel of the machine actually matters. And here is the payoff, the reason SVD is everywhere: low-rank approximation. Keep only the top-k singular values and their vectors and you get the best possible rank-k approximation of A — that is the Eckart-Young theorem, best is a proved guarantee, not a hope. Real-data matrices almost always have singular values that decay fast, so a thousand-by-thousand matrix is approximately a rank-twenty product of two thin matrices: forty thousand numbers standing in for a million. That single deal is image compression, it is latent semantic analysis, which is SVD on the TF-IDF matrix and was early embeddings before the word existed, it is recommender systems, the Netflix Prize was won on it, and it is the philosophical core of LoRA in Part Six. LoRA assumes the fine-tuning update, delta-W, is low-rank, and instead of learning the whole update it learns just two thin matrices whose product is the update — and Eckart-Young is exactly why that bet is sensible: if the best low-rank approximation of the true update captures most of it, you lose almost nothing by never leaving the low-rank family. There is also a clean bridge worth knowing for interviews: the singular values of A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of A-transpose-A, which is always square, symmetric, and non-negative, so SVD is eigendecomposition made safe for any matrix. That is why np-dot-linalg-dot-svd is often the most numerically trustworthy tool in the drawer, and why PCA is usually implemented as the SVD of the centered data rather than the eigendecomposition of the covariance.

Step back and the whirlpool gave you all three core facts in one scene: special directions exist, the surge axis; the eigenvalue is the stretch, times three; and repetition amplifies the dominant one, the Knock Up Stream launching the ship into the sky exactly the way exploding gradients launch a loss to infinity. And Sheldon's spot pins the definition itself — guests come, furniture drifts, game night reshuffles the whole apartment, but one point is fixed by every rearrangement, transformed yet unmoved, eigenvalue one. That is Sheldon: that is my spot. Carry forward that one fact wears three faces, all the same lambda-to-the-k math. Power iteration and PageRank find the dominant axis by repeated multiplication. Exploding and vanishing gradients are lambda-to-the-k running through deep layers, the reason initialization schemes, gradient clipping, residual connections, and ultimately attention all exist. And PCA is the top eigenvectors of the covariance, the maximal-variance directions. SVD then generalizes the whole idea to any matrix and hands you low-rank approximation, the compression deal behind LoRA, latent semantic analysis, recommender systems, and image compression alike. Three pitfalls to retire now. First, NumPy returns eigenvectors as columns, not rows — vecs-bracket-colon-comma-i pairs with vals-bracket-i — a classic silent bug. Second, always center your data before PCA, or the top component points at the mean instead of the spread. And third, only symmetric matrices, like every covariance matrix, are guaranteed real eigenvalues; a rotation matrix has complex eigenvalues because it turns every direction in the plane, with no real invariant axis at all — which is geometrically obvious the moment you think in transformations rather than symbols. Eigenvectors are natural axes, eigenvalues are stretch factors, repetition compounds the biggest one, and SVD extends all of it to any matrix — that is the spectral toolkit powering PCA, gradient stability, and LoRA for the rest of the course.
embeddings-rag: Everything in Part Six was about the model itself. This part is about the gap between what the model knows and what your application needs, and that gap is where most real systems live. Start with the shape of the problem. A model knows what was in its training data, up to a cutoff date, and that is the entirety of it. It cannot tell you what your company's refund policy says. It cannot tell you what happened last week. It cannot tell you anything about a private document, a customer record, an internal wiki, or a codebase it never saw. And this is not a limitation that goes away with a bigger model — a frontier model has exactly the same blind spot about your documents as a small one, because the issue is not capability, it is that the information was never present. Now the dangerous part, and it is why this matters more than it sounds. If you ask anyway, you do not get an error. You get a fluent, well-structured, confident answer that is invented. The model has no internal signal separating I have read this from this is the kind of thing that would be true, because both produce the same kind of high-probability text. Confabulation and recall are the same operation from the inside. So the failure is silent and it looks exactly like success, which is the worst property a failure can have. We already ruled out one fix. In the LoRA lesson I said: fine-tune behaviour, retrieve knowledge, and here is the reasoning in full. Facts baked into weights are undated — there is no way to know when they were true. They are unattributable — you cannot show a user the source, which for anything regulated or consequential is disqualifying on its own. They are unchangeable without retraining, so correcting a single sentence of a policy document is a training run. And they are unverifiable, because you cannot inspect what the model absorbed. Every one of those is fatal for a system that has to be trusted. The right answer is retrieval-augmented generation, and I want to state it plainly because people expect something more elaborate. Find the documents relevant to the question. Paste them into the prompt. Ask the question about them. That is RAG. The division of labour is clean and it is the whole insight: the model provides language understanding and reasoning, which is what it is extraordinarily good at, and you provide the facts, which is what you actually control. Nothing is baked in, everything is current, and every answer can point at the passage it came from.

Finding the relevant documents is the hard half, and keyword search is not good enough for a reason you can see immediately. A user types how do I get my money back. Your policy document says refund eligibility criteria. Those two strings share no words at all, and they are about exactly the same thing. Keyword search returns nothing, or worse, returns something irrelevant that happened to share a common word. This is not an edge case; it is the ordinary case, because people ask questions in their own words and documents are written in the organization's words. Which is where this course pays off, because you already have the tool. In Part One you learned that direction in a vector space can carry meaning and that cosine similarity measures it. In Part Five you learned that a BERT-family encoder produces a contextual representation of a whole passage. Put those together: run an embedding model over every chunk of your documents, store the resulting vectors, then embed the user's question the same way and find the stored vectors closest to it by cosine similarity. Get my money back and refund eligibility land near each other in that space, because they appear in similar contexts, which is the distributional hypothesis doing exactly what it promised. Nothing new is required — this is the machinery from Parts One and Five, applied. A vector database is the infrastructure around that. FAISS if you want a library, Chroma for something simple, pgvector if you already run Postgres and would rather not add a system, Pinecone or similar if you want it managed. What they all do is store millions of vectors and answer nearest-neighbour queries in milliseconds. And they do it approximately, by design — exact nearest-neighbour search over ten million vectors is slow, so these systems use index structures like HNSW that find almost-certainly-the-nearest results a hundred times faster. That is a deliberate accuracy-for-speed trade and it is essentially always correct here, because you are going to retrieve five candidates and let the model sort them out. Now the decision that determines your system's quality more than the database choice does, and that people spend the least time on: chunking. You cannot embed a fifty-page document as one vector — a single vector cannot represent fifty pages, and what you get is a blurred average of everything in it that matches nothing specifically. So you split. Chunk too large and the embedding mixes several topics and retrieval becomes vague. Chunk too small and you get a sentence with no context, and the model cannot use it. The practical advice: split on structural boundaries first — sections, headings, paragraphs — rather than on a fixed character count, because a chunk that ends mid-argument is a chunk that cannot answer anything. Aim for a few hundred tokens, overlap neighbouring chunks by ten or twenty percent so a fact spanning a boundary is not lost, and keep the source and section with every chunk so you can cite it later.

The system has two halves that run at completely different times, and keeping them separate in your head makes everything simpler. The offline half is indexing, and you run it once and then again whenever your documents change. Load the documents, whatever they are — PDFs, wiki pages, a repository, a database export. Chunk them, using the structural approach from the last slide. Run each chunk through your embedding model to get a vector. Store the vector alongside two things that people forget and then need: the chunk's original text, because you are going to put the text in the prompt, not the vector; and the metadata, meaning the source document, the section, the date, the access permissions. That metadata is what lets you cite the answer and what lets you filter by user later, and retrofitting it is painful. The online half runs on every question. Embed the question with the same model you used for the chunks — the same model, this matters, because two different embedding models produce incompatible spaces and the similarity numbers become meaningless. Query the vector store for the k nearest chunks, typically three to ten. Assemble a prompt containing those chunks and the question. Send it. Return the answer with its sources. The whole thing is perhaps forty lines of code, and every framework you will meet is a wrapper around exactly these steps. Now the prompt itself, which is where grounding is either enforced or lost. You must tell the model explicitly to answer using only the provided context, and you must tell it explicitly what to do when the context does not contain the answer — which is to say so, rather than to help. If you omit that instruction the model will do what it always does, which is produce the most plausible continuation, and the most plausible continuation of a question it half-knows is an answer from its training data blended seamlessly with your documents. You will not be able to tell which part came from where, and neither will your users. One line of prompt is the difference between a grounded system and a very convincing unreliable one. And finally the property that is usually the actual reason a team chooses RAG over fine-tuning: citations. Because every chunk carried its source through the pipeline, the answer can say which document and which section it came from, and a user can go and check. That changes what the system can be used for. An answer you can verify is usable in a regulated context, in a support workflow where being wrong has consequences, and anywhere a human is accountable for the outcome. An answer you cannot verify is not, no matter how good it is. Fine-tuning cannot give you this at any price, and it is worth being explicit that this — not accuracy — is often the deciding argument.

Nami is famous for knowing the sea, and the interesting thing is that she does not know it in the way people assume. She has not memorised every island, current and reef on the Grand Line — nobody could, and if she had, the knowledge would be frozen on the day she learned it. What she has is a chart room, and her real skill is a filing skill: keeping things in an order such that the right one can be found in seconds when it is needed. That distinction — between holding knowledge and being able to find it — is exactly the distinction between fine-tuning and retrieval, and once you see it in the chart room the rest of the lesson is obvious. Now look at how the charts are actually organized, because this is the part that maps to embeddings and it is not how a library works. They are not filed alphabetically by island name, because that would only help if you already knew the name of what you were looking for. They are organized by what the waters are like. Nami can say: I need whatever we have on a shallow reef approach with a strong easterly in the wet season — and the right two or three charts come out, even though not one of them has that sentence written anywhere on it. She is retrieving by a description of the situation rather than by a title. That is semantic search, precisely, and it is why get my money back finds refund eligibility. Notice what she does next, because it constrains the whole system. She does not carry the chart room to the wheel. She takes three or four charts for the current leg and spreads them on the table. Not because the rest are irrelevant in principle, but because the table is a fixed size and because looking at four hundred charts while navigating a reef is worse than looking at three. That is top-k retrieval and the context window together, and it is why the retrieval step matters so much: what gets onto the table determines what can be reasoned about, and everything left in the room may as well not exist. And then the property that decides whether the crew can trust her, which is the one to carry out of this lesson. She can point at the chart. Here, this sounding, drawn in this year, by this surveyor. If the depth turns out wrong, the crew can see whether the chart was wrong or whether Nami misread it, and either way they know something. Compare a navigator who says only that she remembers this water being deep enough. She may well be right, and she is asking to be trusted rather than checked, and there is no way to tell the difference in advance. That is exactly a fine-tuned model against a retrieval system. Same answer, possibly. Completely different thing to build a ship's course on.

Naive RAG is a weekend project, and the first version usually underwhelms. The good news is that the ways it fails are well understood and mostly have specific fixes. The most important diagnostic first, and it will save you weeks. When answers are bad, almost everyone starts editing the prompt. Do not. Print the chunks that were retrieved and read them. The overwhelming majority of the time you will find that the passage containing the answer was never fetched at all, and in that case there is no prompt in the world that helps — the model was asked to answer from material that did not contain the answer, and it did the best it could, which is either to say it does not know or to invent something. Retrieval is the bottleneck, not the model, and the whole debugging discipline follows from taking that seriously. Now the specific failures. Pure vector search has a real blind spot: it is bad at exact matches. Product codes, error numbers, function names, unusual proper nouns, version strings. Embeddings capture meaning, and an error code has no meaning to capture — it is a token that either appears or does not. So run keyword search, BM25, alongside the vector search, and fuse the two ranked lists. That is hybrid search, it takes an afternoon, and on most corpora it is the single largest quality improvement available. Second, reranking, which is the highest-value thing most people have not done. Embedding similarity is a fast approximation: the question and the chunk were embedded separately, so nothing ever compared them directly. A cross-encoder does compare them directly — it reads the query and the chunk together and scores the pair — and it is far more accurate and far too slow to run over a million documents. So do both: retrieve fifty candidates cheaply with vector search, then rerank those fifty with the cross-encoder and keep the best five. You pay for fifty comparisons instead of a million, and the five chunks that reach the prompt are much better chosen. Third, the queries themselves. Users write short, vague, context-dependent questions, and a follow-up like what about for annual plans is meaningless as a standalone search. So rewrite the query before searching: have a small model expand it using the conversation history, or generate two or three phrasings and retrieve for all of them. Cheap, and it fixes the multi-turn case that otherwise falls apart. And finally, evaluate the two stages separately, because a single end-to-end score tells you nothing actionable. Measure retrieval by whether the correct chunk appears in the top-k, on a set of questions where you know the answer's location. Measure generation by faithfulness: given the chunks that were retrieved, is the answer actually supported by them, or did the model add something. Those are different failures with different fixes, and a team that reports one blended quality number will spend its time guessing. Build the evaluation set first — fifty questions with known source passages — and the rest of the work becomes measurable instead of anecdotal.
finetuning-lora: Fine-tuning is not a new idea in this course — BERT gave it to us in Part Five, and the recipe was clean: take a pretrained model, replace the head, update every weight on your labelled examples, and get a specialist for a fraction of the cost of training from scratch. That works beautifully at a hundred million parameters. It stops working, for boring and completely decisive reasons, at seven billion. The reason is the memory arithmetic we did two lessons ago, and it is worth saying out loud because people are surprised by how bad it is. To train a model you need the weights, one gradient per weight, and — with Adam — two moment estimates per weight. Roughly four copies of the model. A seven-billion-parameter model in sixteen-bit floats is fourteen gigabytes of weights, and by the time you have gradients and optimizer state in the mix you are somewhere between sixty and eighty gigabytes before storing a single activation. That is several data-centre accelerators, rented by the hour, for a task you had hoped to run on the one GPU in your machine. And for a seventy-billion model, multiply by ten. The second cost is one people notice later and resent more. Full fine-tuning produces an entire new model per task. If you fine-tune a seven-billion model for ten different jobs, you now own a hundred and forty gigabytes of weights that are, in truth, almost identical to each other and to the original — and each one has to be stored, versioned, shipped and loaded into memory separately to serve. There is no way to have one server hold ten specialists, because each specialist is a whole model. That is an operational problem long before it is a research one. The third cost is catastrophic forgetting, and it is the subtlest. When you update every weight on a narrow dataset, you are optimizing only for that dataset, and nothing in the process is protecting the abilities the model had before. Train hard enough on your support tickets and the model gets better at support tickets and measurably worse at everything else — reasoning, general knowledge, following instructions in a different format. You did not intend to trade those away, and nothing warned you. Now, all three of these problems come from the same source, which is that you are moving every weight. So the obvious question is whether you have to, and the answer — which is the subject of this lesson — turns out to be no, not remotely. You can freeze the entire pretrained model, train something tiny alongside it, and get most of the benefit for about one percent of the cost.

Here is the idea, and it is one line of linear algebra with enormous consequences. When you fine-tune, what you end up with is the original weight matrix plus a change: W plus delta-W. The change is the only thing that is task-specific — W was already there. So the question is not how to store a new model; it is how to store delta-W cheaply. And the observation behind LoRA is that delta-W has low intrinsic rank. Adapting a model to a task does not move the weights in all sixteen million directions available to them; it moves them in a small number of directions, and the rest of the matrix is essentially unchanged. If that is true, then delta-W can be factored: instead of one d-by-d matrix, write it as B times A, where A is r by d and B is d by r, and r is small — eight, or sixteen, or sixty-four. The product is still d by d, so it slots into the model unchanged, but you only ever store and train A and B. Put numbers on it, because the numbers are the argument. For a model dimension of four thousand and ninety-six, the original matrix has about sixteen point seven million entries. With r equal to eight, A and B together have sixty-five thousand. That is about four tenths of one percent of the parameters, trainable, and the other ninety-nine point six percent is frozen. Frozen means no gradient, which means no optimizer state, and remember that optimizer state was three of the four copies in our memory calculation. So the saving is much larger than the parameter count alone suggests: a seven-billion fine-tune goes from something needing eighty gigabytes and multiple accelerators to something that fits comfortably on a single consumer graphics card. Two practical consequences that matter as much as the memory. First, what you save at the end is not a model — it is the adapter, A and B, a file of a few megabytes. The base model is unchanged and shared. So you can hold one copy of a seven-billion-parameter model in memory and serve twenty different specializations from it by swapping which adapter is applied, per request. Ten fine-tunes now cost you fourteen gigabytes plus a few tens of megabytes, instead of a hundred and forty gigabytes. That single property is why LoRA took over. Second, a small design detail that is doing real work: B is initialized to zeros while A is initialized randomly. So at the very start of training, B times A is exactly zero, the adapted model is bit-for-bit the original model, and training begins from a known-good state and departs from it gradually. Without that, you would start by injecting random noise into a carefully pretrained model, which is a bad way to begin. And because the change is additive and separate, it is completely reversible — you delete the adapter and you have the original back, which you cannot say for a full fine-tune.

LoRA solved the optimizer-state problem, and then QLoRA solved what was left, which was that you still had to hold the frozen base model in memory at full precision. The insight is simple once stated: the base model is never updated. Gradients flow through it but nothing is written to it. So its precision only has to be good enough to compute a forward pass and pass a gradient along — it does not need the precision required to accumulate tiny optimizer updates, because it never accumulates anything. So quantize it to four bits. Keep the adapter in sixteen bits, because that is the part that is actually learning. The result is that fine-tuning a seventy-billion-parameter model fits on a single forty-eight-gigabyte card, which two years earlier would have been an absurd claim. There are a few clever details in the paper — a four-bit format designed for the way neural network weights are actually distributed, quantizing the quantization constants, and paging optimizer state to CPU memory when a spike would otherwise crash the run — but the load-bearing idea is the one sentence: a frozen weight needs less precision than a trained one. Now the settings, because there are only four that matter and people waste a lot of time on them. Rank, r, is the size of the bottleneck and the main dial. Eight to sixteen is enough for almost everything people actually want — adopting a tone, following a specific output format, learning a domain vocabulary. Go to sixty-four or higher only when you are teaching genuinely new behaviour rather than adjusting existing behaviour. And resist the instinct that a bigger rank is a safer default: more capacity mostly buys you a faster route to overfitting on the small dataset you are fine-tuning with. Which matrices to adapt. The original paper applied LoRA only to the query and value projections in attention, and that was mostly a demonstration that a very small intervention suffices. Current practice targets every linear layer, including the feedforward — remember that the feedforward holds about two thirds of the model's weights, so leaving it out means leaving most of the model unreachable. Adapting everything at a low rank generally beats adapting a little at a high rank. Alpha, which confuses everyone, is a scaling factor: the adapter's contribution is multiplied by alpha over r. Its purpose is to let you change r without also changing the effective size of the update. The practical advice is to fix alpha at twice r and then treat r as your only dial. People who tune alpha and r independently are usually tuning the same underlying quantity from two directions and getting confused about which one did what. And the last one, briefly: learning rate. LoRA adapters want a much higher learning rate than full fine-tuning — one e minus four rather than two e minus five is a reasonable starting point — because you are training a small number of freshly initialized parameters rather than nudging a large number of already-good ones. Using a full fine-tuning learning rate is the most common reason a LoRA run appears to do nothing.

Wado Ichimonji is one of the twenty-one Great Grade swords. Somebody spent years forging it, and the properties that make it what it is — the steel, the temper, the geometry of the edge — are settled and are not up for discussion. Now suppose Zoro is facing a specific opponent and wants the blade to behave slightly differently. What he does not do is take it to a forge and melt it down. That would be enormously expensive, it would take a very long time, and the overwhelmingly likely outcome is that he destroys the thing that made the sword worth having in the first place. Nobody reforges a masterwork to suit a Tuesday. What a swordsman actually adjusts is everything around the steel. The wrap on the hilt, for grip in the wet. The balance. The guard. The angle at which it sits at his side. These are small changes, they cost almost nothing, they take an evening, and they genuinely change how the blade performs in this hand for this fight. The steel is untouched. And here is the part that maps most precisely: he can keep several wraps for one blade and swap between them. One sword, several configurations, a few grams each, chosen per opponent. That is LoRA, and I do not think the analogy strains anywhere. The pretrained model is the blade — millions of dollars and months of compute, and its core capabilities are settled. Full fine-tuning is reforging: ruinously expensive at scale, and it risks the general ability that made the model worth using, which is exactly what catastrophic forgetting is. The adapter is the wrap: a few megabytes, an afternoon on one GPU, entirely reversible, and it changes how the model behaves on your task without touching a single pretrained weight. And keeping many adapters for one base model is keeping many wraps for one sword — which is, in production, the whole reason this technique won. But the analogy also tells you the limit, and this is the part to carry into the next slide. A rewrap changes how a sword is wielded. It cannot turn a sword into a spear, and it cannot put a keen edge on steel that was never properly hardened. If the capability is not in the blade, no amount of work on the hilt will produce it. Fine-tuning adjusts how a model's existing capability is delivered — its format, its register, its defaults, its vocabulary. It does not install a capability the base model does not have. People routinely expect otherwise, and it is the most common reason a fine-tuning project disappoints.

Let us finish with judgement, because the technique is easy now and knowing when not to use it is the valuable part. Fine-tune when you want to change form. If you need output in a specific structure every single time — a particular JSON shape, a report template, a fixed set of fields — fine-tuning is much more reliable than asking politely in a prompt, and it is cheaper per call because you are not spending tokens on instructions. If you need a consistent house tone or persona, fine-tuning gives you that in a way prompting only approximates. If you have a domain with vocabulary and conventions the model handles awkwardly, a few thousand examples fix it. And distillation is a genuinely good use: have a large model produce high-quality outputs, then fine-tune a small fast model to imitate them, and deploy the small one. All of these are adjustments to how existing capability is expressed, which is exactly what the hilt can change. Do not fine-tune to add facts. This is the mistake, and it is made constantly. Knowledge baked into weights is undated, unattributable and unchangeable — to correct a single sentence of a policy document you would have to retrain, and you cannot show a user where an answer came from. Facts that change, facts you need cited, and any corpus you might have to update belong in retrieval, which is the whole of Part Seven. The rule of thumb is: fine-tune behaviour, retrieve knowledge. The escalation order is worth memorizing because it saves real money. Start with a better prompt — it costs an hour and no infrastructure. Then few-shot examples in the prompt, which handle a surprising amount of format specification. Then retrieval, if the gap is knowledge rather than behaviour. Only then fine-tune. Every step up that ladder costs more, takes longer, and is harder to undo, and in my experience most projects that reached step four had a problem that step two or three solves. Fine-tuning is not the sophisticated answer; it is the expensive one, and it is correct only when the cheaper ones have actually been tried and actually failed. And when you do fine-tune, the thing that determines your result is the data, not the hyperparameters. A thousand examples you have personally read, in a consistent format, with the failure cases you care about deliberately represented, will beat fifty thousand scraped ones every time. Garbage examples teach garbage very efficiently. Hold out a test split before you start, look at the model's actual outputs on it rather than just the loss curve, and compare against the base model with a good prompt — because if the base model with a good prompt is close, you have just spent a week to move a number that did not need moving.
how-ai-fits-together: When the Straw Hats enter the Grand Line, Nami's trusted compass spins uselessly — the islands' magnetic fields make ordinary navigation impossible, and she needs a Log Pose, an instrument that locks onto one island, adapts, and only then points to the next. That is the map you need before anything else. Start at the top: artificial intelligence is the umbrella, any technique that makes a computer do something that looks intelligent — a nineteen-ninety-seven chess engine counts, and so does a hand-coded if-else expert system from the eighties. Machine learning is the subset of AI where the behavior is learned from data instead of hand-coded: you do not write rules for recognizing spam, you show the machine ten thousand spam emails and ten thousand real ones and it finds the rules itself, and those rules it finds are just numbers, called parameters or weights. All of machine learning is adjust numbers to fit data — that one sentence carries the whole field. Deep learning is the subset of machine learning where the model is a neural network with many layers, the same idea but with millions or billions of numbers arranged in layers, which turns out to let the model learn its own features instead of you engineering them by hand. NLP, natural language processing, is not a subset of any of these — it is a problem domain, making computers deal with human language, done with classical machine learning for decades before deep learning took over. Large language models sit at the intersection: very large deep-learning transformers trained on the NLP task of predict the next token at internet scale — GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, all the same species. And agents are not models at all: an agent is a program you write that calls an LLM in a loop, lets it use tools like search and code, and feeds results back until a task is done. The LLM is the engine; the agent is the car you build around it.

Strip away the mystique and a model is a function with tunable numbers inside — nothing more mystical than that. Linear regression is f-of-x equals w times x plus b: two tunable numbers. A GPT-four-class model is the exact same idea with roughly ten-to-the-twelfth tunable numbers and a much fancier function shape, but the category is identical. Training means one thing at every scale: measure how wrong the function's outputs are — that gap has a name, the loss — then compute which direction to nudge each number to make the loss smaller, which is the gradient, and that is exactly the calculus of Part One. Nudge every number a little in that direction; that single nudge is one training step. Repeat it millions of times, and what is left when you stop is the model. So when someone says download the model, they mean download the saved values of those numbers — that is what the multi-gigabyte dot-safetensors or dot-gguf files on Hugging Face are, just the learned numbers — plus a small amount of code describing the function's shape, which is called the architecture. This matters for a reason that trips up a lot of people: a weights file is numbers, not a database. There is no lookup table of facts inside a model; knowledge is smeared, lossily, across billions of weight values, which is precisely why models can hallucinate — they reconstruct a plausible answer from compressed statistical patterns rather than reading a stored fact. Hold onto the five-step loop, because it is the entire course in one shape: start with data and a model, measure the loss, compute the gradient, update the numbers, repeat until you have a weights file. Linear regression in Part Two runs this loop with two numbers; a mini-GPT in Part Five runs the identical loop with millions. Same story, more numbers.

A library is nothing exotic: it is a folder of Python files someone else wrote, tested, and published so you do not have to rewrite it. Pip install numpy contacts PyPI, the public package index, downloads that folder, and unpacks it into your environment's site-packages, which is on Python's import path — which is why import numpy finds it afterward. Import numpy as np loads it into your program and gives it the nickname np, and from then on np-dot-dot of a and b runs their dot-product code, written in C and roughly a hundred times faster than the Python loop you would write by hand. This is the pattern behind every single tool in this course. NumPy is fast math on arrays. PyTorch is NumPy plus automatic derivatives plus GPU support — which is exactly what training needs, since training is derivatives at scale. Scikit-learn is the classical machine-learning algorithms pre-implemented with a uniform interface, dot-fit to train and dot-predict to use. Hugging Face transformers puts thousands of pretrained models one function call away. Ollama runs open-weight LLMs locally with one command. And LangChain or Google's ADK are scaffolding for agent loops. The reason this all works is that Python is the steering wheel, not the engine: when you call torch-dot-matmul, the heavy lifting runs as compiled machine code on the CPU or GPU, and Python only orchestrates, so you get C-speed math from a five-line script. The slowness only bites if you write raw Python loops over millions of numbers, which is exactly why the ecosystem pushes you to express math as whole-array, vectorized operations. And here is the rule for this whole course: every time we call a library function, we first learn what it computes, usually by implementing a small version ourselves in the code lab. Library calls should be a convenience, never a mystery — so when you see model-dot-fit of X and y in Part Two, you will already have written the gradient-descent loop it hides.

There are three jobs this course prepares you for, and it helps to see which parts feed each. The ML engineer builds and ships classical and deep models: data pipelines, training, evaluation, deployment. Their interviews test Parts One through Three hard — the math, the bias-variance trade-off, backpropagation — plus the system-design material near the end. The AI or LLM engineer builds products on top of LLMs: prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, fine-tuning, agents, evaluations, serving. Their interviews test Parts Five through Seven — attention math, LoRA, RAG architecture, agent design — and, increasingly, still test Parts One and Two fundamentals specifically to filter out API-only candidates who can call an endpoint but cannot explain why the retrieval returns garbage. The researcher reads papers, forms hypotheses, runs experiments, and writes papers; they need everything the other two need plus the ability to derive things from scratch, which is why the Part One math is non-negotiable, and the ability to implement a paper from nothing, which is exactly what the mini-GPT you build in Part Five is training you for. This course deliberately teaches to the hardest of the three, the researcher-level why, and that is a deliberate strategy, not showing off: that depth is precisely what distinguishes candidates in the other two interviews. The engineer who can explain why cosine similarity ignores magnitude, or why the loss uses cross-entropy rather than raw accuracy, is the one who gets the offer over the one who only knows which function to call. Depth is the differentiator, so we aim for it from the first lesson.

Nami's route through the Grand Line is a dependency chain — you cannot sail to Alabasta before your Log Pose has adapted at Whiskey Peak, and skipping an island does not make you faster, it makes you lost. This course is your Log Pose route through AI, and it is a real dependency chain, not an arbitrary ordering. Cosine similarity in Part One is the island your instrument must adapt to before attention in Part Five is even reachable, because attention literally is scaled dot products — the exact math of Part One, at scale. Gradient descent in Part One must be visited before fine-tuning in Part Six means anything, because fine-tuning is gradient descent on a subset of weights, nothing more. Every flashy destination — LLMs, agents — sits at the end of a chain of unflashy islands, and the crews that try to skip ahead, like every rookie crew that ignored the Log Pose rules, end up circling in fog, copy-pasting LangChain code they cannot debug when the retrieval returns garbage. So treat each lesson's skill the way Luffy treats each nakama he gains on an early island: it joins your crew, and it will be called on again. The dot product you learn next lesson returns inside every transformer's attention. The gradient returns in fine-tuning. The evaluation habit returns in every part. And two dangerous misreadings are worth retiring right now, before they cost you an interview or a product decision. First, the model did not look it up — there is no database inside a weights file, knowledge is smeared lossily across billions of numbers, which is exactly the mechanism behind hallucination. Second, library calls are not incantations — if you cannot say what dot-backward or dot-fit computes, stop and find out, because this course always tells you. Take the islands in order, keep every nakama, and the flashy destinations arrive on schedule.
inference-sampling: Everything up to now has been about producing a probability distribution over the vocabulary. This lesson is about the step after that, and it is worth separating cleanly in your head, because it is a different kind of decision. The model gives you fifty thousand probabilities. Which token do you actually emit? That is decoding, and here is the important property: it happens at runtime, it involves no training, and changing it changes the character of your output completely. Two systems using the identical model with different decoding settings will feel like different products. The simplest strategy is greedy: take the highest-probability token, every time. It is deterministic and reproducible, which is genuinely useful, and for open-ended text it is bad in a specific and recognizable way. It produces flat, repetitive, lifeless prose, and it can lock into outright loops — the same phrase repeating until you cut it off. The reason is worth understanding rather than memorizing. Once you have emitted a slightly bland sentence, the most likely continuation of a bland sentence is another bland sentence, and there is no mechanism to escape, because greedy never takes a step that is not locally optimal. Blandness is an attractor. Temperature is the first fix. Before the softmax, divide the logits by a number T. Below one, the differences between logits get amplified, the distribution sharpens, and you approach greedy. Above one, differences shrink, the distribution flattens, and rare tokens get a real chance. In practice about zero point seven is a good default for prose — enough variation to sound alive, not enough to wander — and zero, which is just greedy, is what you want for anything that must be reproducible or extracted programmatically. But temperature alone has a flaw: it rescales the whole tail, so even at a modest temperature there is always some chance of sampling something absurd, and one absurd token early in a sentence derails everything after it, because the model then conditions on it. So you truncate. Top-k keeps the k most likely tokens, renormalizes over them, and samples from that. It works, and it has one weakness: k is fixed. Sometimes the model is genuinely certain and only two tokens are sensible, and a k of fifty admits forty-eight bad ones. Sometimes it is genuinely open — the middle of a creative sentence — and fifty is too restrictive. Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, fixes that by defining the cut by probability mass instead of by count: sort the tokens, and keep the smallest set whose probabilities sum to p, typically zero point nine. Now the candidate set adapts automatically — three tokens where the model is confident, two hundred where it is not. That adaptivity is why top-p is the default nearly everywhere, usually with a temperature applied alongside it.

Beam search deserves its own slide because it is the strategy that sounds most obviously correct and is most obviously wrong here, and understanding why teaches you something about the whole enterprise. The method is sensible. Greedy is myopic: it commits to the best token now even if that forecloses a much better sentence later. So keep several options alive. At each step, maintain the b most probable partial sequences — b is the beam width, usually four or five — extend all of them, keep the best b of the extensions, and at the end return the complete sequence with the highest total probability. It is a principled search for the most likely output, and for tasks where a single correct output exists it genuinely helps. Translation and summarization both use it, and it beats sampling there. Now point it at open-ended generation — a story, an explanation, a chat reply — and the output is noticeably bad. Bland, short, repetitive, and strangely lifeless. And here is the part I want you to sit with: that is not a failure of the search. The search is working perfectly. It is finding a very high probability sequence, which is exactly what you asked it for. The problem is that the request was wrong. The most probable sequence is not the best sequence, and once you say that out loud it is obvious. Look at how humans actually write. Real text is full of choices that were not the single likeliest continuation — a specific example instead of a generic one, an unexpected verb, a turn the reader did not see coming. That surprisingness is not noise on top of good writing; it is a large part of what makes writing good. A model maximizing total sequence probability is explicitly avoiding all of it. What you get is the average of everything the model has ever read, which is the most predictable text it is capable of producing. There is a well-known measurement of this: human-written text sits at a fairly consistent level of per-token surprise, and beam search output sits far below it. It is too likely to be human. There is a second, more mechanical problem. Every token you add multiplies the sequence probability by a number less than one, so longer sequences are always less probable than shorter ones. Beam search therefore has a systematic bias toward stopping early, and implementations patch this with a length normalization or a length penalty. That patch works, and notice that it is a patch — you are hand-correcting an objective that does not match what you want. So the rule is simple, and the reasoning behind it generalizes. Use beam search when there is one right answer and you want the most likely one: translation, summarization, structured extraction, anything with a reference output. Use sampling with top-p when there are many acceptable answers and you want a good one rather than the modal one. And carry the deeper point out of this lesson: likelihood was the training objective because it was trainable, not because high likelihood is what makes text good. Those are different things, and every generation strategy is a way of negotiating the gap.

You met this problem when you wrote generate in the Mini-GPT lesson, and now here is the fix. Recall the waste. At every step, the naive loop feeds the entire sequence through the model again, which recomputes the keys and values for every token already processed. Now ask whether any of those could have changed. They could not — and the reason is precise. The causal mask guarantees that a token attends only to itself and to earlier positions, so a token's representation, and therefore its key and its value, depends on nothing that comes after it. Once computed, they are fixed for the rest of the generation. Recomputing them is not merely inefficient; it is provably recomputing an identical number. So cache them. Keep, for each layer and each head, the keys and values you have already produced. At each new step, you run the model on exactly one token: compute its query, key and value, attend that single query against the whole cached set of keys and values, and append the new key and value to the cache. The complexity of generating n tokens drops from order n cubed to order n squared, and — the thing you feel — the cost per token stops growing with the length of what you have already written. This changes the shape of inference in a way you need to know about, because it explains the latency behaviour of every system you will build on. There are now two distinct phases. Prefill processes the whole prompt at once, in parallel, in a single forward pass. It is compute-bound, it uses the hardware efficiently, and it is what determines your time to first token.
