Then decode runs one token at a time. Each step does very little arithmetic but must read the entire model's weights and the entire cache from memory, so it is memory-bandwidth-bound, and it is what determines your tokens per second. These two phases want different optimizations and are measured separately, which is why serving benchmarks always report both numbers. Now the cost, because there is one and it is the binding constraint in production. The cache holds two tensors — keys and values — per layer, per head, per position. Multiply it out: two, times the number of layers, times the number of heads, times the head dimension, times the sequence length, times the batch size. For a large model at long context this reaches many gigabytes per sequence. And that is per user: every concurrent conversation needs its own cache. So on a served endpoint, it is not the model weights that limit how many people you can handle at once — the weights are loaded once and shared. It is the cache. This is why long context is expensive in a way that surprises people, and it is the direct motivation for multi-query and grouped-query attention, where several attention heads share one set of keys and values specifically to shrink this number.

Nami's job is exactly the decoding problem, one leg at a time, and I think it makes all four ideas sit in the right place. Start with what she does not do. She does not ask, at each moment, what is the single safest bearing right now, and take it. That sounds prudent and it is a trap, and any sailor could tell you why. Always steering for calm water walks you straight into a calm belt, and then there is no wind, and you sit with slack sails going nowhere while the crew eats through the provisions. The locally safest choice, taken every single time, produces a voyage that goes in circles. That is greedy decoding, and the repetitive loop a greedy model falls into is the same failure with the same cause: there is no mechanism for leaving a comfortable local situation, because leaving it always looks worse for one step. What she actually does is a two-part move, and it is precisely top-p. First she narrows: given the sky, the current, the season and the state of the ship, most of the compass is not a real option, and she discards it without a thought. Then she chooses among what is left, and there is genuine choice there — sometimes three plausible bearings, sometimes twenty, depending on how much the conditions constrain her. Notice that the size of the shortlist is not fixed. In a storm there may be exactly one workable heading; in open water on a clear day there are many. That is the whole argument for nucleus sampling over top-k: the number of reasonable options is a property of the situation, not a constant you set in advance. And crucially, the bearing that ends on the rocks is never on the list, no matter how the die falls. Now beam search. Imagine planning the entire voyage in advance, enumerating routes, and picking the one with the highest total probability of arriving safely. For a delivery to a known port, that is exactly right and it is what you should do. But for a voyage whose whole purpose is to find something nobody has charted, the highest-probability plan is to stay in port, and the second highest is a short hop to a well-known island. The optimizer is not malfunctioning; it is answering the question you asked, and the question was wrong. The most probable voyage and the voyage worth making are different things, and the Grand Line is the case where they diverge completely. And finally the log book, which we met two lessons ago in a different role and which does one more job here. Nami does not re-survey water she has already sailed. Yesterday's depth soundings, currents and bearings are written in the log, they cannot change — the sea behind you does not rearrange itself — so she reads the log rather than sailing back to measure again. That is the KV cache. And notice the honest cost sitting inside the metaphor: on a long voyage the log gets thick, and it has to be carried, and consulted, and kept dry. Every additional day of sailing adds pages you must keep. That is exactly the memory bill for long context, and it is why a system serving many long conversations at once is carrying a great many heavy books.

Three pieces of engineering and then a practical table. Quantization first, and note that this is different from the QLoRA case: there you quantized a base model so you could train an adapter on top, here you are shrinking a finished model purely to serve it. Store the weights in eight bits or four instead of sixteen. Eight-bit is essentially free — the quality difference is not measurable on most tasks. Four-bit, using GPTQ or AWQ or the GGUF formats that run on consumer hardware, costs a little quality and quarters your memory, which is often the difference between a model fitting on your card and not. And there is a second benefit that people miss: it makes generation faster, and understanding why matters. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, which means the accelerator spends most of its time waiting to read weights, not computing with them. Four-bit weights are a quarter of the bytes to move, so you wait a quarter as long. Fewer bytes is the speedup. Second, continuous batching, which is the single largest throughput win in serving and is purely a scheduling idea. Naive batching groups requests, runs them together, and waits for all of them to finish before starting the next batch — so one long generation holds up a batch full of short ones, and the accelerator idles on the slots that finished early. Continuous batching, sometimes called in-flight batching, operates at the level of a single decoding step: after each step, any sequence that has finished is retired and a waiting request takes its slot immediately. The hardware stays full. This routinely multiplies throughput several times over with no effect on output quality at all, which is a rare kind of improvement. Third, PagedAttention, from vLLM. The problem it solves: because you do not know how long a generation will be, the naive implementation reserves a contiguous block of cache memory for the maximum possible length of every request, and most of it is never used. That is severe fragmentation. PagedAttention borrows the idea of virtual memory: store the cache in fixed-size blocks that need not be contiguous, and allocate them on demand. Much higher memory utilization, therefore many more concurrent requests on the same hardware, and it makes sharing a common prompt prefix across requests almost free as a side effect. Finally, the practical table, which is the thing to actually take away. For deterministic extraction — pulling fields out of a document, classification, anything you will parse — use temperature zero and check that your provider honours it. For code, around zero point two: code needs to be correct more than it needs to be interesting. For prose, explanation and chat, zero point seven to zero point eight with top-p at zero point nine. For brainstorming, where you want range and will filter afterwards, one point zero or above. And add a repetition penalty around one point one when you see loops, though if you need much more than that the real problem is usually your prompt. One last piece of advice that will save you an afternoon: log your decoding settings alongside your outputs. When somebody reports that the model gave a different answer yesterday, the cause is almost never the model. It is a temperature that nobody wrote down.
information-theory: Long voyages need ship-to-ship signals, and waving flags is slow, so Nami designs a codebook — and to design it well she first has to measure something slippery: how much information does a message carry? That was Claude Shannon's starting question in nineteen forty-eight, and his answer is that rare equals informative. The message the sun rose carries essentially nothing, because you already knew it; the message snow in the Sahara carries a lot, precisely because it is surprising. The measure is I of x equals minus log-base-two of the probability of x, in bits. A certain event, probability one, carries zero bits — no surprise. A fifty-fifty event carries one bit. An event with probability one-over-one-thousand-twenty-four carries ten bits. Now, why the logarithm, of all functions? Because we want independent surprises to add. Two independent events with probabilities p and q have joint probability p-times-q, and minus the log of p-times-q equals minus log-p minus log-q — so the log is the unique choice that turns multiplication of probabilities into addition of information, which is exactly the additive behavior we want from a measure of surprise. And the word bit here is not a metaphor: an event with probability one-eighth carries three bits because identifying it takes exactly three optimal yes-or-no questions, each halving the possibilities — eight to four to two to one. Information is surprise, measured in the number of yes-or-no questions the answer is worth.

Nami's design rule is simple: the commoner the message, the shorter its flag sequence. All-clear happens hourly, so it gets one white flag; Sea-King-attack is rare, so it gets a five-flag sequence. When she balances it perfectly, the average flags-per-message drops to a theoretical floor, and that floor has a name: the entropy of the message distribution. Entropy is the expected surprise of a distribution — H of p equals minus the sum over i of p-i times log-base-two of p-i, which is just the average of the per-outcome surprises, weighted by how often each outcome happens. A fair coin has entropy one bit. A fair eight-sided die has three bits. A biased coin that comes up heads ninety-nine percent of the time has entropy of only about zero-point-zero-eight bits, because there is almost no uncertainty to resolve. Two endpoints anchor it: entropy is maximized by the uniform distribution, where every outcome is equally likely and your ignorance about the next one is total, and it drops to exactly zero when one outcome is certain. And Shannon proved something remarkable: this same number is the compression limit. No code can transmit samples from p using fewer than H-of-p bits each, on average, and an optimal code — short codewords for frequent symbols, exactly like Morse code giving the letter E a single dot — actually achieves it. So entropy is the irreducible average message length, the floor of communication that Nami's clever flags approach but can never beat. In machine learning you will meet entropy in three places: as a measure of a model's uncertainty over its classes; as the impurity that decision trees minimize when they choose where to split, in Part Two; and as a bonus term in reinforcement learning that keeps a policy exploratory instead of prematurely certain. One number — average surprise — with a compression theorem attached.

Now the star of the lesson. Suppose reality generates symbols from a distribution p, but you built your code — your beliefs — for a different distribution q. Your average message length is the cross-entropy: H of p-comma-q equals minus the sum over i of p-i times log-q-i, and it is always at least the true entropy H-of-p, with equality only when q exactly equals p. Read it as a division of labor: reality, p, picks the symbols, and your codebook, q, prices them. If you bet short codes on things that rarely happen and long codes on things that happen constantly, it costs you, and the excess cost is exactly your model's wrongness. This is precisely the Buggy disaster. Crossing into Buggy's territory, the crew lazily captures and uses Buggy's codebook, which is optimized for circus emergencies, so his shortest flags mean juggling accident, and all-clear, which the Straw Hats need constantly, now takes seven flags. Every message costs extra waving, and that average cost of using Buggy's beliefs on Straw-Hat reality is the cross-entropy. Now watch cross-entropy become the training loss. For one classification example, the true distribution is one-hot — the label, held with certainty — so the whole sum collapses to a single term: minus log q of the true class. The loss is simply how surprised the model was by the correct answer. Confident and right means loss near zero. Confident and wrong means minus log of nought-point-zero-zero-one, about ten — a catastrophic penalty and a huge gradient. That asymmetric punishment of confident errors is exactly why cross-entropy, and not accuracy or MSE, trains classifiers: it makes hubris expensive. And note the connection straight back to last lesson: minimizing cross-entropy over a dataset is identical to maximizing the sum of log q of the true labels, which is maximum likelihood — the same formula arriving from two different lineages, information theory and statistics. An LLM's pretraining loss is exactly this, per token: minus log q of the actual next token given its context, averaged over trillions of tokens.

Take cross-entropy and subtract off its irreducible part, the true entropy, and what remains is the pure penalty for wrong beliefs — the Kullback-Leibler divergence. KL of p-against-q equals H of p-comma-q minus H of p, which works out to the sum over i of p-i times log of p-i-over-q-i. In Nami's story, the cross-entropy was the total average waving under Buggy's codebook, and the KL divergence is specifically the extra waving compared to Nami's perfect code — the exact, quantified price of believing the wrong world. Three properties matter: KL is always greater than or equal to zero, it is zero if and only if p equals q exactly, and crucially it is not symmetric — KL of p-against-q is not KL of q-against-p, so it is not a distance despite feeling like one. Where will you meet it? In RLHF fine-tuning, a KL penalty keeps the tuned model close to the base model, so reward optimization cannot drag it into degenerate high-reward gibberish — a leash on how far it may drift from the pretrained distribution. In knowledge distillation, you train a small student model to match a big teacher's output distribution by minimizing KL, transferring the soft-probability knowledge that hard labels throw away. And variational autoencoders regularize their latent codes toward a Gaussian with a KL term. That asymmetry — mode-seeking versus mean-covering — is a legitimately deep interview topic worth knowing. Finally, perplexity, which is just cross-entropy made human-readable: PPL equals two-to-the-H for bit-based losses, or e-to-the-loss for the natural-log losses PyTorch reports. The interpretation is lovely: the model is as uncertain as if it were choosing uniformly among PPL options. A perplexity of eight means the model's average next-token uncertainty equals a fair eight-way choice. GPT-two scored about twenty-nine on WikiText-one-oh-three; modern LLMs are under five on similar text. So when a paper says our model reaches three-point-two perplexity, you can now decode it completely: that is an average per-token cross-entropy of log-base-two of three-point-two, about one-point-seven bits, meaning the model finds real human text only slightly surprising. Every gradient step in training is Nami revising the codebook — shortening the flags for whatever text actually does — and perplexity is the scoreboard.

Step back and Nami's codebook has chained all four concepts into one story. Entropy is her optimal flag lengths, the floor no code beats. Cross-entropy is the cost of waving Buggy's flags on Straw-Hat seas. KL divergence is the extra waving on top of the floor, the pure price of wrong beliefs. And training a language model is Nami's job at scale — the model's predicted distribution is a codebook for real text, cross-entropy loss measures the average code length it assigns to what humans actually wrote, and every gradient step is a codebook revision, shortening the flags for what actually happens. Sheldon supplies the two poles: Rock-Paper-Scissors-Lizard-Spock deliberately pushes the choice distribution back toward uniform, log-base-two of five, about two-point-three bits of genuine surprise per throw, a high-entropy game engineered to be unpredictable; while his triple knock, knock-knock-knock-Penny three times, has probability essentially one, zero bits, no information — which is exactly why it works as a signature, because total predictability identifies. Carry forward four things. First and most practical: do not apply a softmax before nn-dot-CrossEntropyLoss. It takes raw logits by design and fuses log-softmax internally for numerical stability, so a manual softmax gives you a double-softmax that still trains, quietly underperforms, and hides for weeks — one of the most common real PyTorch bugs, and the same story for BCE-with-logits versus sigmoid-plus-BCE. Second, why cross-entropy beats MSE for classification, mathematically: its gradient through softmax is the beautifully clean predicted-minus-true, q minus p, which is large exactly when the model is wrong with no saturation, whereas MSE's gradient through a sigmoid vanishes precisely when the model is confidently wrong — the worst possible time to stop learning. Third, perplexity is tokenizer-dependent: it is per-token, so a model with a coarser tokenizer faces fewer, harder tokens and its perplexity is not comparable across vocabularies — use bits-per-byte when you need to compare. And fourth, KL is not a distance: it is asymmetric and violates the triangle inequality, so if you truly need a metric, reach for the square root of the Jensen-Shannon divergence, not KL. Information as surprise, entropy as the floor, cross-entropy as the training loss, KL as the penalty, perplexity as the scoreboard — that is Shannon's toolkit, and it is the language every LLM paper is written in.
knn-trees-forests: We now switch from models that fit an equation to models that reason by resemblance, and the first one is so simple it barely looks like machine learning. Here is k-nearest-neighbours in full. To classify a new example, measure the distance from it to every example in your training set, take the k closest ones, and let them vote. For regression, average their values instead. That is the entire algorithm. Notice what is missing: there is no training phase, no loss function, no gradient descent, no parameters at all. The training set is the model. You just store it. This is Chopper with a field guide — he does not have a theory of mushrooms, he has a memory of mushrooms, and when he meets a new one he asks which of the ones he has seen it most resembles. The word 'closest' is doing the real work, and it points straight back to lesson one. For physical measurements you use Euclidean distance. For text vectors or embeddings you use cosine, for exactly the length-invariance reasons we discussed last lesson. Changing the metric changes the model completely, so this is a modelling decision, not a detail. Now the parameter k, which is the bias-variance trade-off made visible in a way you can literally draw. With k equal to one, every single training point gets its own little territory, and the decision boundary is jagged and honours every mislabelled outlier. That is high variance — resample your data and the boundary moves everywhere. With k very large, you are averaging over a huge neighbourhood, the boundary becomes smooth and lazy, and in the limit you simply predict the global majority for everything. That is high bias. The useful k sits between, and you find it on the validation set, exactly as always. Small practical note: prefer an odd k for two-class problems, so the vote cannot tie. And finally, the property that makes k-NN feel strange: its costs are inverted relative to every other model in this course. Training is instantaneous because there is nothing to do. Prediction is expensive, because every single query has to be compared against the entire dataset. That is why it is called a lazy learner — it defers all of its work until someone actually asks a question.

k-NN's simplicity comes with two failure modes, and both are severe enough that people abandon the model without understanding why it failed. The first is scaling, and here it is not a nicety, it is the entire model. Suppose one feature is salary in rupees, running from zero to ten million, and another is age in years, from zero to a hundred. Compute a Euclidean distance across those two and the salary term is around ten to the tenth times larger than the age term. Age contributes nothing. You believe you built a two-feature model; you actually built a salary-only model, silently, and no error will tell you. Standardize every feature to comparable scale before you compute a single distance. This applies to every distance-based method, and it is the most common reason a k-NN result is inexplicably bad. The second failure is deeper and stranger, and it is called the curse of dimensionality. As you add dimensions, all pairwise distances start converging toward one another. In two dimensions, some points are genuinely close and some genuinely far. In five hundred dimensions, the distance from your query to its nearest neighbour and the distance to its farthest neighbour become nearly the same number. And once that happens, the phrase 'the nearest neighbour' has stopped meaning anything — you are taking a majority vote among points that are all equally unrelated to you. There is a second-order consequence worth naming. In this model, irrelevant features are not merely useless, they are actively harmful. Each one adds its own noise to every distance calculation, drowning the features that mattered. Compare that to logistic regression or a decision tree, which simply assign an unhelpful feature a small weight or never split on it. k-NN has no mechanism to down-weight a column, so feature selection is not optional here either. Finally, the practical fixes for speed, which lead somewhere important. In low dimensions, KD-trees and ball trees prune the search so you do not compare against everything. Above roughly twenty dimensions those structures stop helping, and you switch to approximate nearest neighbour indexes such as HNSW, which trade a little exactness for enormous speed. Remember that name — that is exactly the machinery inside the vector databases we build for RAG in lesson thirty-four. Semantic search is k-NN, wearing a much better index.

The second family reasons by asking questions, and it is the most human-looking model in this course. A decision tree repeatedly splits the data on one feature at one threshold. Is the cap red? Yes goes left, no goes right. Within the left branch, is the stem longer than four centimetres? And so on, until each group at the bottom — each leaf — is nearly pure, containing almost entirely one class. To predict, you walk a new example down the questions and read off the majority class of the leaf it lands in. The whole art is in one question: which split do you make first? And the answer comes straight from the information theory lesson. You want the question that reduces your uncertainty the most. So you compute the entropy of the labels before the split, then the weighted average entropy of the two groups after the split, and take the difference. That difference is called the information gain, and the tree simply tries every feature at every threshold and takes the split with the highest gain. Then it recurses. That is the entire training algorithm — no gradients, no learning rate, no iterations. Gini impurity is a common alternative to entropy here and behaves almost identically; do not spend time agonizing over which. Now, why practitioners genuinely love trees. They need no feature scaling at all, because a threshold does not care what units you measured in — this alone removes the most common source of bugs from the previous slide. They handle categorical features directly without one-hot encoding. They cope with missing values. They capture interactions automatically, because a split deeper in the tree is by construction conditional on the splits above it. And, most valuable of all in a real organization, the fitted model is a flowchart. You can print it, hand it to a doctor or a loan officer or a mechanic, and they can read it and tell you it is wrong — which is a form of validation no neural network offers. But a single tree has a fatal weakness, and it follows from the same recursion. Left to grow to full depth, the tree will keep splitting until every training row sits in its own leaf. Training accuracy hits one hundred percent, and the tree has memorized the noise exactly as Usopp memorized Syrup Village. So you must constrain it: limit the maximum depth, require a minimum number of samples in a leaf, or grow it fully and then prune branches back by validation performance.

Now the fix, and it is one of the most elegant ideas in classical machine learning. A single deep tree is a high-variance model: it fits its particular sample too closely. But recall from the bias-variance lesson that when you average many high-variance models whose errors are independent, the errors cancel while the signal survives. So: do not build one tree. Build five hundred, and have them vote. But five hundred trees trained on the same data with the same algorithm would be five hundred identical trees, and averaging identical things achieves nothing. So you inject randomness twice. First, bootstrap sampling: each tree is trained on a sample of n rows drawn with replacement from your n rows, so each tree sees a slightly different world — some rows twice, some not at all. Second, and this is the ingredient that makes it a random forest rather than just bagging: at every single split, each tree is only allowed to consider a random subset of the features, typically around the square root of their number. This second ingredient sounds arbitrary and is essential. Suppose one feature is strongly predictive. Without feature subsetting, every one of your five hundred trees picks it as the very first split, and from there they all look nearly the same. Their errors are then correlated, and correlated errors do not cancel when you average. Forcing each split to choose from a random handful means the other features get their turn, the trees become genuinely diverse, and the averaging actually does its work. Bias stays roughly where a single tree had it; variance falls dramatically. Two free gifts come with the construction. First, out-of-bag error: because each bootstrap sample leaves out about thirty-seven percent of the rows, every row is unseen by roughly a third of the trees, so you can evaluate each row using only the trees that never saw it. That is a validation estimate for free, with no separate split. Second, feature importance: add up how much each feature reduced impurity across all the splits in the whole forest, and you get a ranking of what mattered. Treat that ranking as a hint rather than truth — it is biased toward high-cardinality features — but it is a genuinely useful starting point for a conversation with a domain expert.

One more ensemble, and then the practical conclusion that I most want you to carry into an interview. Random forests build their trees in parallel and independently. Boosting does the opposite: it builds them in sequence, where each new tree is fitted specifically to the errors the ensemble has made so far. Train a shallow tree, see where it is wrong, train the next shallow tree to predict those residuals, add it in with a small weight, repeat hundreds of times. The distinction is worth memorizing because it is a standard question: bagging, meaning random forests, reduces variance by averaging independent models. Boosting reduces bias by iteratively correcting a weak model. That makes boosting more powerful and correspondingly more delicate. Because each round deliberately chases the remaining errors, running too many rounds will eventually chase the noise, so boosting genuinely can overfit in a way that a random forest largely does not. It therefore needs a learning rate, needs early stopping, and needs a validation set watched carefully. A random forest is far more forgiving: throw more trees at it and it does not get worse, just slower. If you have one afternoon and no time to tune, use a forest. If you have a week and a leaderboard, use boosting. And now the conclusion. On tabular data — rows and columns, the kind of data that most companies actually have — gradient-boosted trees are still state of the art. XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost win competitions and production deployments today, in a world of trillion-parameter models. Deep learning has genuinely not displaced them here, and being able to say that calmly in an interview signals experience rather than fashion. The reason is worth understanding. Neural networks win where the data has structure they can exploit — spatial locality in images, sequence in text — and tables have neither. Table columns are heterogeneous and unordered; swapping two columns changes nothing about the meaning, which is exactly the invariance a convolution cannot use. Trees are naturally invariant to feature scale and naturally piecewise-constant, and real tabular relationships tend to be full of thresholds and interactions rather than smooth surfaces. Add that most tabular datasets are thousands of rows rather than millions, and the deep model never gets the data it needs. Use the tool that matches the shape of the problem.
langchain-langgraph: Now that you have written a RAG pipeline and an agent loop by hand, we can have the framework conversation honestly, which is difficult to do in the other order. Start with what a framework actually gives you, because the useful part is not the part that gets advertised. It is the boring surface area. Document loaders for forty different formats, so you are not writing a PDF parser this afternoon. Text splitters that respect structure. A uniform interface across model providers so switching is a config change — which, as we said last part, is something you would have built anyway. Adapters for a dozen vector stores. Streaming, retries, callbacks, token accounting, tracing. Individually each of these is a small piece of work; collectively they are several weeks, and none of them is the interesting part of your product. That is a real offer and it deserves to be taken seriously. Now the cost, which is indirection, and it is also real. When a chain misbehaves, you are no longer debugging your own control flow — you are debugging somebody else's, through documentation, and the prompt that was actually sent to the model is assembled three classes away from anything you wrote. Frameworks in this space have also moved quickly and broken things, so code written a year ago may not run today. And there is a subtler cost: an abstraction that hides the mechanism will also hide your understanding of it, which is fine until the day you need to reason about why something is expensive or slow or wrong. The rule that resolves this cleanly is about ordering, not about whether frameworks are good. Learn the mechanics first, adopt the abstraction second. You have done that. You know what a chunk is, what an embedding is, what the prompt looks like, and what the agent loop does, because you wrote them. So when a framework does those things for you, it is saving you labour rather than hiding a mystery, and when it does something surprising you can open it up and read it, because you know what it is supposed to be doing. Somebody who started with the framework has no such recourse. And one thing worth flagging because teams discover it late: the strongest argument for adopting a framework is often the observability rather than the abstractions. A tracing tool that shows you every prompt, every tool call, every intermediate result and the token cost of each, laid out in one timeline for a single request, is genuinely hard to build yourself and enormously useful once your system has more than two steps in it. Several teams end up using very little of a framework's chain machinery and all of its tracing, and that is a perfectly sensible outcome.

LangChain's central idea is composition, and it is a good idea. Everything is a runnable — a prompt template, a model, an output parser, a retriever — and runnables compose with a pipe operator. Prompt pipe model pipe parser. Read left to right, data flows through, and the whole thing has one interface so you can swap any piece. For a linear pipeline it is genuinely pleasant, and it removes a real amount of boilerplate around formatting, invoking, streaming and parsing. This design was a good fit for its moment, and the reason is worth noticing. Almost every early LLM application was linear. Take the user's question. Retrieve some documents. Stuff them into a prompt. Call the model. Parse the output. Return it. That is a straight line with five stations on it, and a chain is exactly the right abstraction for a straight line. Nobody was wrong to build it. Then applications got more ambitious, and the requirements that arrive are exactly the ones a straight line cannot express. If the first retrieval finds nothing useful, try a different query strategy — that is a retry with state. Classify the request first, and send it down one of three different paths — that is a branch. Generate an answer, check it against the sources, and if the check fails, generate again with the criticism included — that is a loop, and a line has no loops. Pause here, wait for a human to approve the action, and resume tomorrow from where you stopped — that is durable state, and a function call has none. You can express all of these in a chain, with conditional runnables and callbacks and branch objects, and people did. What you end up with is a control-flow graph written sideways in a composition syntax that was designed for pipelines. It works and it is hard to read, hard to test, and hard to reason about, because the actual structure of the computation is scattered across nested runnables instead of being written down anywhere. That experience — a whole community discovering that their applications were graphs and their tool was a pipe — is the direct reason the next slide exists. LangGraph is not a competitor to LangChain; it is the same team saying that the primitive was wrong once applications stopped being linear, and that the honest thing to do is make the graph explicit.

LangGraph's model is a state machine, and if that phrase sounds unfashionable it is because state machines are old, well understood and correct for this problem. Three concepts and you have it. First, state: you declare a typed object, usually a dictionary with a schema, that represents everything the run knows. Messages so far, retrieved documents, the current draft, a retry counter, whatever your application needs. Every step reads it and returns updates to it. Second, nodes: a node is a function that takes the state and returns a partial update. One node retrieves. One node calls the model. One node validates. They are ordinary functions and you can unit test them, which chains made awkward. Third, edges: an edge says which node runs after which. And the important variant is the conditional edge — a function that looks at the current state and returns the name of the next node. That is your branching, and notice that it is a plain Python function you can read and test, not a configuration object. Now the feature that justifies the whole redesign: cycles are first class. An edge can point backwards. The agent loop from the last lesson — call the model, run a tool, go back to the model — is two nodes and an edge returning to the first, and you write it exactly like that. Compare hiding a while-loop inside a chain abstraction that was designed for pipelines. The graph makes the loop visible in the structure, which means you can see it, draw it, and put a step counter on it in the obvious place. Then checkpointing, which is the feature teams end up depending on most and rarely anticipate. Because the state is an explicit object, LangGraph can persist it after every node. That makes a run durable, and durability unlocks a set of things that are painful otherwise. You can interrupt a run and resume it hours later. You can inspect the exact state at step four when something went wrong at step seven. You can rewind to an earlier checkpoint, change something, and replay from there. And human-in-the-loop stops being an architectural problem: pausing for approval before a destructive action is a node that interrupts, and resuming is a call with the approval in the state. In a chain, adding that means restructuring; in a graph it is an edge. The trade is verbosity, and it is a genuine trade. A LangGraph agent is more setup code than the equivalent chain — the state schema, the nodes, the edges, the compile step. What you get for it is a structure you can draw on a whiteboard and that matches the code exactly, nodes you can test individually, and a run you can stop and inspect. For a demo that is overhead. For a system that runs for months and that somebody other than you has to debug, it is the difference between maintainable and not.

The Log Pose is one of the best abstractions in the whole story, and it is a chain. Think about what it does. It locks onto the magnetic field of the next island and points at it. You do not calculate anything, you do not plot a course, you do not need to know the geography. You follow the needle and you arrive. For the first half of the Grand Line that is genuinely sufficient, and it is why most crews get that far — the abstraction is doing real work and hiding real complexity, which is what a good abstraction does. Now notice its shape, because the shape is the argument. A Log Pose is a straight line with one next step on it. It has no opinion about where you actually want to go — it points where it points, and the route is chosen for you. It cannot take you back to an island you have left. And when the needle is wrong, or the island it locked onto is not the one you needed, you have nothing to check it against, because you never had a chart. You have been navigating by following, and following gives you no way to reason. That is exactly a chain: a good abstraction for a linear journey, and no help at all the moment the journey stops being linear. Then the New World, where the Log Pose grows three needles and gives you no rule for choosing between them. This is the moment the abstraction runs out, and notice that it does not fail loudly — it simply stops answering the question. Three needles is not a route. What you need now is a chart you drew yourself: where you are, which of the three you took, what you found there, which route you rejected and why, and what you will do if this one turns out badly. That is state, nodes and edges, and the reason you need them written down is that the situation is no longer a line — it is a set of choices with consequences that you may have to revisit. And a chart gives you one more thing the needle never could, which is the ability to stop. You can drop anchor, mark your position, and take up the voyage next week from exactly where you left it. You can go back to a fork you passed and take the other branch. You can hand the chart to somebody else and they can see what you were doing and why. That is checkpointing, and it is the difference between a voyage that can survive an interruption and one that has to be started again from the beginning. It is not an accident that in the New World the crews that do well are the ones that write things down. The needle is faster while the route is simple. The chart is the only thing that works once it is not.

Let us finish with a decision procedure, because this is a question every team argues about and it has a reasonably clean answer. Write it yourself when the flow is simple and you want to understand it. A single RAG pipeline is about forty lines. A small agent loop is about sixty. If that is what your application is, writing it directly gives you no dependency, no version churn, complete visibility into every prompt, and a codebase that a new engineer can read in one sitting. This is not purism — it is often the correct engineering answer, and the fact that a framework exists does not create an obligation to use it. Reach for a framework in three situations. First, when you need the boring surface area: you have to ingest twelve document formats, or support four model providers, or you are evaluating three vector stores. That is exactly the work a framework has already done, and reimplementing it is a poor use of a month. Second, when your control flow is genuinely a complex graph — several branches, retries with different strategies, sub-agents, and a real state object that many steps read and update. At that point you are going to build a state machine whether you like it or not, and using one that already has checkpointing and tracing is better than growing your own accidentally. Third, and this one is decisive on its own: when you need durability. If a run must survive a process restart, or pause for a human and resume tomorrow, or be rewound and replayed, then persisted state is the requirement and you should use something that has it rather than building a checkpointing layer as a side project. Third piece of advice, independent of the framework question: adopt tracing early. Whatever you build, you need to be able to look at one request and see every prompt that was sent, every tool that was called, every intermediate result and the cost of each, on one timeline. Debugging a multi-step LLM system without that is guessing, and every team I have seen adds it late and wishes they had added it first. It is also the part of these frameworks that stands on its own — you can use a tracing tool with hand-written code perfectly well. And the last one, which ties back to Part Six: keep the model boundary yours either way. Whether you adopt a framework or not, your provider calls should sit behind your own thin interface. Frameworks in this space move fast, some of them will not exist in three years, and a codebase where the framework's abstractions have reached every file is a codebase that cannot leave. If the framework sits on your side of a boundary you control, then adopting it is a reversible decision — and reversible decisions are the ones you are allowed to make quickly.
linear-regression: We start the modelling half of this course with the simplest model that exists, and I want to be honest about why. It is not a warm-up. Linear regression is the skeleton that every later model is built on, and each of its parts — the dot product, the loss, the gradient — reappears completely unchanged inside a transformer. Learn it properly once and you have learned a piece of everything that follows. The model is this: y-hat equals w dot x plus b. That is all of it. Each feature gets a weight, you multiply each feature by its weight, sum them, and add an intercept b that shifts the whole thing up or down. Notice what is doing the work: the dot product from the first lesson. You already know how to compute this, and you already know it is a similarity — the prediction is high when the input points along the weight vector. Now the property that makes this model worth keeping around in the age of billion-parameter networks: the weights are readable. Weight i tells you how much the prediction moves when feature i rises by one unit, while every other feature is held fixed. That last clause carries enormous weight, and it is the entire reason multiple regression exists rather than just looking at one variable at a time. Suppose ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together. Look at ice cream alone and it seems lethal. Put temperature into the same regression, and the ice cream coefficient collapses toward zero, because now it means 'the effect of ice cream at a fixed temperature'. The geometry is equally simple and never changes. With one feature you are fitting a line. With two, a plane tilted over the data cloud. With three hundred, a hyperplane in three hundred dimensions — which you cannot draw, but nothing about the maths cares. And here is the payoff to keep in mind. This slide is exactly one neuron with no activation function. Every network in Part 3 is stacked copies of this, with a bend inserted between them. So the effort you spend here is not spent on an old model. It is spent on the atom.

Having a model is only half of it; we need a definition of wrong. The standard choice is mean squared error: average, over all examples, of the squared difference between the true value and the prediction. Three things justify the square. It makes every error positive, so overshooting by five and undershooting by five do not cancel out into a false sense of accuracy. It punishes one large miss much more than several small ones, because five squared is twenty-five while five errors of one are five in total — so this loss actively prefers a model that is consistently slightly off to one that is usually perfect and occasionally catastrophic. And it is smooth everywhere, meaning it has a well-defined gradient at every point, which the absolute value does not have at zero. Now the deeper reason, which we already earned in the statistics lesson. Squared error is not an arbitrary aesthetic choice. If you assume the noise around the true line is Gaussian, then maximum likelihood estimation derives squared error for you as the answer. So choosing MSE is not a neutral act — it is quietly asserting a belief about the shape of your noise. And that belief has a price. Squaring makes MSE violently sensitive to outliers. A single mislabelled row, sitting a hundred times further away than it should, contributes ten thousand times the error of a typical point, and it will drag your entire line toward itself. If your data has heavy tails — incomes, file sizes, damages — consider mean absolute error, which does not square and therefore does not panic, or Huber loss, which is squared near zero and linear far out, giving you smoothness where you need it and robustness where you need that. Finally, the geometric picture, because it makes the whole thing click. Minimizing squared error is projecting the vector of true answers onto the space your features are able to span. The residual — what is left over — comes out exactly perpendicular to every one of your features. And that perpendicularity is precisely what it means to say the model has extracted every scrap of linear signal available: there is nothing left in the leftovers that correlates with anything you gave it.

So we have a model and a loss. How do we actually find the weights? There are two routes, and knowing when each wins is a genuine interview question. The first is the closed form, called the normal equation: w equals X-transpose-X inverted, times X-transpose y. Set the derivative to zero, solve, done. It is exact, it happens in one shot, and there is no learning rate to tune and no convergence to babysit. The catch is cost. Inverting that matrix is roughly cubic in the number of features, so with a hundred features it is instant, with ten thousand it is painful, and with a hundred thousand it is simply not happening. The second route is gradient descent, which you already know from the calculus lesson. Start the weights anywhere, compute the gradient, take a step downhill, repeat. And the gradient here is worth memorizing because it is so clean: two over n, times X-transpose, times the vector of prediction errors. Read that in words — it is the error of each prediction, weighted by the inputs that caused it. Features that were large when you got it wrong get blamed proportionally. That exact expression, unchanged, is what backpropagation will hand you at the last layer of a neural network. Now the good news that makes linear regression special. Mean squared error over a linear model is convex. There is one bowl, one bottom, and no local minima anywhere. Gradient descent literally cannot get stuck in the wrong place here — a luxury that disappears permanently the moment you insert a single hidden layer. One practical note to close on. Even when your problem is small enough for the closed form, you often should not use it. When two features are strongly correlated, X-transpose-X becomes nearly singular, inverting it amplifies tiny numerical noise into enormous swings in the coefficients, and you get a model whose weights are unstable nonsense. Adding lambda times the identity before inverting — which is exactly ridge regression from the previous lesson — makes the matrix well-behaved again. That is a lovely moment: regularization arriving not as a statistical idea about overfitting, but as a numerical rescue.

Here is something that surprises people coming from software: in classical machine learning, the model is the easy part. The work — the part that decides whether your project succeeds — is in the features. Four things to internalize. First, scale your features. Suppose one column is distance in metres, ranging up to fifty thousand, and another is a ratio between zero and one. The loss surface becomes a long narrow valley instead of a round bowl, and gradient descent crawls painfully along one axis while bouncing back and forth across the other. Standardize each feature to mean zero and standard deviation one, and the valley becomes a bowl, and everything converges faster. Note also that with regularization, scaling is not optional but mandatory: an unscaled feature gets penalized purely for the units it happens to be measured in. Second, categories are not numbers. If you encode ship names Sunny, Merry and Baratie as one, two and three, you have just told the model that Baratie is three times Sunny and that Merry sits exactly halfway between them. You did not mean that. Use one-hot encoding — one column per category, holding one or zero — and drop one of them, because keeping all of them plus an intercept makes the columns perfectly collinear and the matrix un-invertible. Third, and this is the one that unlocks real power: linear regression is linear in the weights, not in the features. Nothing stops you from adding x-squared, or log-x, or the product of two features, as new columns. The machinery does not change at all, but now you are fitting curves and interactions. This is the cheapest capacity upgrade available in machine learning, and it is also the fastest way to overfit, so pair it with the validation discipline from the last lesson. And fourth, keep the intercept. Without b, your line is forced to pass through the origin, which is almost never where real data lives. A model that is required to predict zero output for zero input has an untested assumption welded into it, and it will pay for that assumption with bias everywhere else.

You have fitted a model. Now read it honestly, which is a separate skill and a rarer one. Start with R-squared, the fraction of the variance in y that your model explains. Zero means you did no better than always predicting the mean; one means perfect prediction. It is a useful summary, and it has a trap that catches people constantly: R-squared always goes up when you add a feature. Always. Even if the feature is a column of random numbers, it will find some accidental scrap of correlation to exploit, and your R-squared will improve. So never use raw R-squared to compare models with different numbers of features. Use adjusted R-squared, which charges you for each parameter, or better, forget both and compare the models on validation data as we did last lesson. Next, and this is the habit that separates practitioners from people who just call fit: plot the residuals. Take the errors and plot them against the predictions. If the model is right, you get a shapeless cloud centred on zero with no pattern in it. If you see a U-shape, the true relationship was curved and your straight line is systematically wrong at both ends and in the middle — add a squared term. If you see a widening funnel, the variance of the error grows with the size of the prediction, which means your model is most confident exactly where it is least reliable. These pictures tell you things that no single summary number can. Third, multicollinearity. When two of your features move together closely, the model can trade weight between them freely without changing predictions much, so the individual coefficients become unstable — refit on a slightly different sample and they can swing wildly or even flip sign. The predictions survive this perfectly well; the explanations do not. If you only need forecasts, ignore it. If somebody is going to act on the coefficients, deal with it. And finally the warning that matters most outside the classroom. Correlation is not causation, and a regression coefficient is a correlation. The phrase 'holding the others fixed' is only true for the features you actually put in the model. Any cause you left out is still there in the world, hiding inside the coefficient of everything it touches.
llm-pretraining: Start from where the last lesson left you, because the continuity is the point. The model you assembled is the model. There is no second, secret architecture that the large labs use; a hundred-billion-parameter model is your file with wider layers and more of them. If you understood the two hundred lines, you understand what is being trained. What changes at scale is not the model. It is three problems that simply do not exist at small size and that dominate everything once you cross a threshold. The first is data. At small scale, data is a download — you fetch a corpus, you tokenize it, you move on. At trillion-token scale, data becomes the single largest engineering effort in the project, and it is also, by most people's reckoning, the largest determinant of how good the resulting model is. You are assembling something no human will ever read, from sources of wildly varying quality, and every decision about what to include, what to throw out, and in what proportion, is baked irreversibly into the result. The second is sizing. When your model trains in twenty minutes you can simply try three sizes. When one run costs several million dollars and takes months, you get one attempt, and you need to know in advance what shape of model your compute budget deserves. It turns out there is a real answer to that question, it is empirical, and for several years the whole field had it wrong in a specific and expensive way. The third is fitting. A model with a hundred billion parameters needs four hundred gigabytes just for the weights in thirty-two-bit floats, and with gradients and Adam's two moment estimates you are at one point six terabytes before a single activation is stored. No accelerator has that. So the computation itself has to be cut into pieces and spread across many machines that then have to agree with each other, constantly, over a network, without falling out of step. None of these three is deep learning in the sense of the previous lessons. There is no new mathematics here. They are data engineering, empirical economics, and distributed systems, and that is genuinely what pretraining a large model consists of. I want to be honest that you are not going to do this yourself — the entry price is thousands of accelerators for months. But you will use the artifacts constantly, you will read model cards that describe these choices, and understanding what was decided during pretraining explains an enormous amount about why a given model behaves the way it does.

If you take one thing from this lesson, take this: at scale, data work is not preparation for the real project. It is the real project. Teams that report the largest quality gains almost always got them from the corpus rather than from the architecture, and the architecture has barely changed in years. Four stages. Collection. The bulk of the text comes from Common Crawl, an open snapshot of a large fraction of the public web, or from cleaned derivatives of it. But raw web text alone makes a noticeably worse model than a mixture, so labs add books, source code, Wikipedia, academic papers, and selected forums and discussion sites. The reason mixture helps is that these sources fail in different ways: the web is broad and shallow and full of junk, books are long-form and coherent but old and narrow, code is precisely structured, papers are dense and correct. Together they cover things none of them covers alone. Filtering. Most of what you collect is not text you want a model to imitate. Navigation menus, cookie banners, SEO word salad, auto-generated listings, low-quality machine translation, and pages that are almost entirely markup. The standard approach layers cheap heuristics — document length, punctuation ratios, fraction of lines ending in a full stop, presence of banned tokens — with a small learned classifier trained to recognize text that looks like a reference corpus. The proportion discarded is startling to people who have not seen it: over ninety percent of raw Common Crawl typically does not survive. Deduplication, and this is the step that is both the most valuable and the most often skipped in smaller efforts. The web is enormously redundant — the same article appears on hundreds of sites, the same licence text on millions of pages, the same boilerplate in every template. If a passage appears five thousand times, the model does not learn the general pattern behind it, it memorizes the passage. Exact deduplication is easy; near-duplicate detection, usually with MinHash, is what actually matters. Removing near-duplicates improves quality and shortens training, which is a rare combination and the reason it is the first thing to do. Then mixing, which is a set of deliberate proportion choices rather than a default. One finding worth knowing because it is counter-intuitive: including a substantial fraction of source code improves performance on reasoning tasks that have nothing to do with programming, apparently because code is text with rigorous, checkable structure. And finally contamination, which is a discipline rather than a stage. If your benchmark's test questions are somewhere in your training data — and on a web-scale corpus they very likely are, because benchmarks get posted and discussed — then your evaluation is measuring recall rather than ability. Decontamination means actively searching the corpus for your evaluation sets and removing them, and a model card that does not mention doing it has told you something about how much to trust its numbers.

This is one of the few places in deep learning with a genuinely predictive quantitative theory, and it is worth understanding because it drove billions of dollars of decisions, including one large mistake. The empirical finding is this: test loss decreases as a smooth power law in three quantities — the number of parameters, the number of training tokens, and the total compute. Plot loss against any of them on log axes and you get a remarkably straight line, over many orders of magnitude, with no bumps and no plateau in the range anyone has measured. That smoothness is the useful part. It means you can run a series of small, cheap experiments, fit the curve, and extrapolate to predict what a run a thousand times larger will achieve — before you spend the money. Very little else in this field lets you do that. Now the mistake, because it is instructive. In twenty twenty, the Kaplan scaling laws were read as saying that when you get more compute, you should spend most of it on making the model bigger, and comparatively little on more data. The industry took that seriously, and it is why GPT-3 has a hundred and seventy-five billion parameters and was trained on only three hundred billion tokens. That is under two tokens per parameter. In twenty twenty-two, DeepMind redid the experiment more carefully — over four hundred training runs, sweeping model size and token count against a fixed compute budget — and found the earlier conclusion was wrong. The optimal allocation is to scale parameters and tokens roughly together, at about twenty tokens per parameter. They demonstrated it directly: Chinchilla, at seventy billion parameters trained on one point four trillion tokens, using the same compute as the much larger Gopher, beat it on essentially every benchmark. Most of the models trained in the preceding two years were substantially undertrained for their size. Now the twist that makes this more than a historical correction, and it is the part that actually shapes what you can run today. Compute-optimal means optimal for the training run. But a model is trained once and then serves inference for years, and inference cost is set by the number of parameters — not by how many tokens it was trained on. Training a smaller model for much longer costs more up front and then is cheaper on every single call, forever. So once you account for deployment, the right thing to do is deliberately overshoot Chinchilla: take a seven-billion or seventy-billion parameter model and train it on far more tokens than compute-optimality would suggest. That is precisely what Llama and the open-weight families that followed did — trained well past the optimal point on purpose — and it is the direct reason you can run a genuinely capable model on one consumer GPU. The scaling law told the field what was efficient to train. Economics told it what was worth deploying, and the two answers are different.

The Grand Fleet is the right picture for this, because a fleet is not just more ships — it is a coordination problem, and coordination is what distributed training actually is. Start with the simple arrangement. Seven crews sail under one flag, and for most of the voyage each ship is doing the same kind of work on a different share of it. Every captain has the full plan. Every ship carries its own portion of the cargo to its own set of ports, and then they meet at a rendezvous point, compare notes, agree on what the plan should now be, and sail on with the updated plan. That is data parallelism, and it is the common case. Every accelerator holds a complete copy of the model, each one processes a different slice of the batch, and at the end of every step they exchange gradients and average them so that all copies stay identical. The rendezvous is the all-reduce, and it is where the network cost lives. Now the harder case. Some cargo will not fit in any single hull, no matter which ship you pick. So one load is cut into parts and distributed across several ships that must now arrive at the same place at the same time, because the cargo is only useful reassembled. That is model parallelism, and it changes the character of the fleet completely: no individual ship is carrying anything usable on its own. In practice this comes in two flavours. Splitting a single large matrix across devices is tensor parallelism, and it needs communication inside every layer, so those ships must be lashed together with the fastest links you have. Putting different layers on different devices is pipeline parallelism, and it needs communication only at the handover points, so those ships can be further apart — but now there is a new problem, which is that ship four has nothing to do until ship three passes something along, and keeping the pipeline full is its own discipline. Two properties of fleets, and both are properties of distributed training. First, the fleet moves at the speed of its slowest ship, because everyone waits at the rendezvous. One straggler — a slower accelerator, a congested link, a machine doing something else — sets the pace for thousands of others, and this is why real training runs spend so much effort on load balance. Second, a fleet loses ships. On a run of thousands of machines for months, hardware failure is not a risk, it is a certainty, and it happens repeatedly. That is why checkpointing is not optional: without a recent saved state, one dead node costs you everything since the last one. And finally the provisions, because it is the same lesson as the data slide and worth hearing twice. A voyage is decided as much by what was loaded as by how well the ships sail. Rotten barrels are worse than empty ones, because the crew eats them and gets sick. And loading the same crate five thousand times fills the hold, looks like an enormous supply, and feeds nobody.

Two engineering techniques before the punchline, because they are the ones that decide what is possible on the hardware you have. Mixed precision. Thirty-two-bit floats are more precision than neural network arithmetic needs, and they cost you memory and bandwidth for nothing. So you run the matrix multiplications in sixteen bits while keeping a thirty-two-bit master copy of the weights for the optimizer update, where the small increments genuinely do need the precision. There are two sixteen-bit formats and the difference matters. Standard half precision has a narrow exponent range, so small gradients underflow to zero and you need loss scaling — multiplying the loss by a large constant before the backward pass and dividing it out afterwards — to keep them representable. Brain float sixteen instead keeps the same exponent range as thirty-two-bit and gives up mantissa bits, which for gradients is the right trade, and it removes the loss-scaling machinery entirely. Every modern accelerator supports it and it is the default now. Second, gradient checkpointing. During the forward pass you normally store every activation because backward needs them, and on a deep model those activations are most of your memory. Instead, store only a few, and recompute the rest during the backward pass from the nearest stored point. You pay roughly thirty percent more compute and you get a large fraction of your memory back, which very often is the difference between a batch size that trains and one that does not fit. Now the punchline, and it is the most important sentence in the lesson. What comes out at the end of all of this — the data pipeline, the fleet, the months of compute — is a base model. It is an extraordinarily good next-token predictor and it is not an assistant. It has no notion of being asked a question, no concept of a helpful answer, no idea that there is a user. Ask a base model what the capital of Nepal is and a perfectly reasonable continuation is another question, and then another, because lists of questions are a thing that exists on the web and your text looked like the start of one. Ask it for advice and you may get a plausible forum thread including the replies. It is not being unhelpful. Helpfulness was never in the objective; the objective was to predict what text follows, and it is doing that correctly. So there is a second stage, and the encouraging thing is that it is very much cheaper than the first. Instruction tuning teaches the format of a request and a response, using a comparatively small set of curated examples. Preference alignment then teaches which of two valid responses a person would rather have. Together they cost a tiny fraction of pretraining and they are the entire difference between a text predictor and something you can talk to. Pretraining buys capability. Alignment buys behaviour. They are separate stages, they fail in separate ways, and the next two lessons are about the second one.
logistic-regression: Most of the decisions you actually care about are not numbers, they are questions with two answers. Is this transaction fraud. Will this customer leave. Is this crew member sick. So the obvious thing is to reach for the model we just learned: encode healthy as zero and sick as one, and run linear regression. Let us see exactly how that fails, because the failure teaches the fix. First, the outputs escape. A straight line is unbounded, so your model will cheerfully predict minus nought-point-four for one patient and one-point-eight for another. If those numbers are probabilities, you now have a probability of minus forty percent, which is not a thing. Second, and more damaging, it is unstable in a way that is hard to see coming. Imagine Chopper fitting a line through his patients. Then one crew member turns up who is not merely sick but catastrophically sick, sitting far out along the severity axis. Squared error hates being far from any point, so the fitted line tilts to reach that patient — and in tilting, it moves the decision boundary for everybody else. One extreme case has quietly rewritten the diagnosis of all the ordinary ones. That is not a small numerical annoyance; that is the model doing the wrong thing for a structural reason. The fix is not a better line. The fix is to change what the model outputs. Keep the familiar part — the score z, which is still w dot x plus b, still a dot product, still readable — and then pass z through a function that squashes it into the open interval between zero and one and can never leave. That function is the sigmoid: one over one plus e to the minus z. Look at its behaviour. Very negative z gives you something just above zero. z of exactly zero gives you exactly one half. Very positive z gives you something just below one. It is smooth, it is differentiable everywhere, and it is monotonic, which matters more than it sounds: the ordering of the scores is completely preserved, so the sigmoid changes the scale of your confidence without ever changing who you consider more likely to be sick.

The sigmoid can feel like an arbitrary bit of algebra someone chose because it happened to have the right shape. It is not, and the way to see that is to invert it. Solve the sigmoid for z and you get: z equals the log of p over one minus p. That quantity, p over one minus p, is the odds — familiar from betting. Two-to-one odds means a probability of two thirds. So z, your linear score, is not the probability at all. It is the log of the odds. Logistic regression is a linear model; it simply lives on the log-odds scale rather than the probability scale. And that single realization hands you back the interpretability that we prized in the last lesson. A one-unit increase in feature i adds w-i to the log-odds, which means it multiplies the odds by e to the w-i. So a weight of nought-point-seven means: this feature roughly doubles the odds of the outcome. And crucially, it means that at any starting point — this is a multiplicative statement, so it holds whether you began at long odds or short ones. That is a genuinely useful sentence to be able to say to a doctor or a risk officer. The log-odds view also explains the S-shape, which otherwise looks like a design choice. Near a probability of one half, the curve is steep, so a bit of evidence shifts the probability substantially — which is right, because that is where you are genuinely uncertain and evidence should matter most. Out at ninety-eight percent, the curve is nearly flat, so piling on more evidence barely moves the number. That is also right: once you are almost certain, additional confirmation should be worth very little. The sigmoid is not a squashing hack, it is a model of how belief ought to respond to evidence. And one last thing to hold on to. The decision boundary is still a straight line. The model says yes when z is greater than zero, and w dot x plus b equals zero is a hyperplane, exactly as in linear regression. The sigmoid changed what comes out of the model. It did not change the shape of what the model can separate.

We have a model that outputs probabilities. Now we need a loss. The tempting move is to reuse mean squared error on the probability, and it is a genuine disaster for two separate reasons. First, MSE composed with a sigmoid is not convex, so you lose the guarantee of a single bottom and gradient descent can now stall in a bad place. Second, and more insidiously: when the model is confidently and completely wrong — it said nought-point-zero-one and the answer was yes — the sigmoid is almost flat out there, so its derivative is almost zero, so the gradient is almost zero. The model is maximally wrong and receives almost no correction. That is precisely backwards. The right loss is cross-entropy, also called log loss, and we already derived it in the information theory lesson. Written out it is minus y log y-hat, minus one minus y, times log of one minus y-hat. Because y is either zero or one, only one of those two terms is ever alive, and what remains is simply minus the log of the probability you assigned to the truth. Look at what that does to the incentives. Say the true answer is yes. If you said nought-point-nine, your loss is minus log nought-point-nine, about nought-point-one — barely a scratch. If you said nought-point-zero-zero-one, your loss is about six-point-nine. With squared error the worst possible punishment was one. With cross-entropy there is no ceiling at all: confident wrongness costs unboundedly. That unbounded penalty on hubris is exactly the pressure a classifier needs to be calibrated instead of merely decisive. And now the payoff, which is genuinely one of the most satisfying results in the field. Work through the derivative of cross-entropy composed with the sigmoid, and everything cancels. The messy derivative of the sigmoid is exactly annihilated by the derivative of the logarithm. What survives is: y-hat minus y, times x. Prediction error, times the input that caused it. That is identical in form to the gradient of linear regression with squared error. Two different models, two different losses, one shared gradient. And that expression is not a curiosity — it is literally the formula that backpropagation will hand you at the output layer of every classifier you build for the rest of this course.

Your model now outputs a probability, and probabilities are not decisions. To act, you need a cut-off, and here is the thing almost every beginner gets wrong: nought-point-five is a default, not an answer. It is only the optimal threshold in the special case where a false positive and a false negative cost you exactly the same amount, and that case is almost vanishingly rare in real life. Go back to Chopper. He is screening the crew for an illness that is fatal if missed but straightforward to treat if caught. What does a false negative cost? Someone dies. What does a false positive cost? An afternoon of tests and an embarrassed patient. Those are not remotely equal, so the threshold should not be one half. It should be something like nought-point-one: flag anyone with even a modest probability, accept a pile of false alarms, and catch every real case. Now flip the costs. For denying someone a loan, or accusing a customer of fraud, a false positive does real harm to a real person, so you push the threshold high and demand strong evidence before acting. Same model, same weights, same probabilities — completely different threshold, because the world outside the model is different. Sweeping the threshold across its whole range traces out the ROC curve we will meet in the evaluation lesson, and the area under it summarizes the model's ranking ability independently of any single choice. But do choose the threshold deliberately, choose it on validation data and never on test, and revisit it when the base rate moves, because a threshold tuned when fraud was one in a thousand is wrong when fraud becomes one in a hundred. And one final property worth knowing, because it catches experienced people. Calibration is a separate question from accuracy. A model can rank cases perfectly — every sick patient scored above every healthy one — and still be badly calibrated, saying nought-point-nine for a group of events that actually occur sixty percent of the time. If all you do is threshold, miscalibration may not hurt you. But if a human reads that number, or a downstream rule multiplies it by a cost, then the number itself has to mean something. Check it with a calibration plot: bucket your predictions, and see whether the things you called seventy percent happened about seventy percent of the time.

Three things to finish, and they carry all the way to the end of this course. First, more than two classes. Suppose you are sorting incoming messages into Marine, Pirate, and Civilian. Give each class its own weight vector, so each class gets its own score z. Those scores can be any real numbers, so you normalize them with the softmax: exponentiate each one and divide by the sum of all the exponentials. Exponentiating forces everything positive, and dividing by the sum forces them to add to one — so you get a genuine probability distribution across the classes. The loss stays exactly what it was: minus the log of the probability you assigned to the true class. Notice that softmax with two classes reduces algebraically back to the sigmoid, so this is a strict generalization, not a new idea. And here is why it matters so much: that softmax layer is the output layer of essentially every classifier in Part 3, and it is the output layer of a large language model predicting the next token — where the number of classes is simply the vocabulary, fifty thousand of them. You have just learned the last layer of GPT. Second, regularization applies here unchanged, and it matters more than it did for regression. If your classes happen to be perfectly separable, the likelihood keeps improving as the weights grow without bound — the model can always be more certain — so the weights literally race toward infinity and the probabilities collapse to hard zeros and ones. An L2 penalty stops that dead. Regularization is what keeps a classifier honest rather than fanatical. Third, and this is the practical point I most want you to leave with: logistic regression is still the correct first model for a serious team. It trains in seconds on millions of rows. It gives calibrated probabilities rather than bare labels. Every coefficient can be defended in a meeting, with a direction and a magnitude and a units. It has almost no hyperparameters to get wrong. Build it first, always. Then, when you bring in the gradient-boosted trees or the neural network, you have a real number to beat — and if the deep model cannot beat it, you have learned something extremely valuable about your problem for almost no cost.
matrices: Trafalgar Law raises a hand — ROOM — and a sphere spreads over the battlefield, and inside it he does not fight objects one at a time; he transforms the space itself. Shambles swaps positions, Takt rotates everything skyward, and every coin, cannonball, and marine inside the room is relocated by the same rule at once. That is a matrix: not an operation on one vector, but a rule applied uniformly to all of space. Concretely, an m-by-n matrix is a grid of numbers with m rows and n columns, and its job is to eat an n-dimensional vector and spit out an m-dimensional one. The rule, matrix-vector multiplication, is that output slot i equals the sum over j of A-i-j times x-j — which means each output slot is the dot product of row i of A with the input x. So read a matrix as a stack of dot products: each row is a detector, exactly last lesson's matching score, and the output vector is the list of all the detector scores. This is precisely what a neural layer does when it computes W-x — each row of W is one neuron's weights asking how much does the input match my pattern, and five hundred twelve rows means five hundred twelve pattern detectors run at once. A worked example to fix it: A equals bracket bracket two zero, bracket one three, and x equals bracket four one; A-x is two times four plus zero times one, then one times four plus three times one, which is bracket eight, seven.
