And the geometric view is Law's room made precise: A moves every point in space simultaneously — rotating, stretching, squashing, reflecting — but it always keeps grid lines straight and parallel and the origin fixed, and that is exactly what the word linear means. Law's rules keep straight lines straight, no point torn from its neighbors — the linear in linear transformation. The plus-b in W-x-plus-b then shifts the whole space bodily, which is called affine, and neural nets stack these with nonlinear squashes in between, which is Part Three.

Why is matrix multiplication defined by that strange rows-times-columns dance instead of something simpler? Because it is exactly the definition that makes A-B applied to x equal A applied to B-x — apply B first, then A. Matrix multiplication is composition of transformations, full stop. The formula, entry i-j of A-B equals the sum over k of A-i-k times B-k-j, is not an arbitrary convention; it is derived by asking what single matrix does the combined machine correspond to. Here is the crucial scene: Law and Doflamingo both cast overlapping rooms. Doflamingo's strings drag everything ten meters east; Law's Shambles rotates everything ninety degrees. If Law acts first and Doflamingo second, a marine standing north ends up in a totally different spot than if Doflamingo acts first — the order of transformations changes the outcome. Composition of rooms is matrix multiplication, and A-B not equal to B-A is not algebra trivia, it is two Warlords arguing about who goes first. Sheldon says it plainer with his Saturday laundry: sort, wash, fold, a fixed pipeline, and when Penny folds first and then washes, the same two operations in the opposite order give a basket of wrinkled chaos — wash-then-fold is not fold-then-wash. Three consequences you must own. First, order matters, A-B is generally not B-A. Second, shapes must chain: an m-by-n times an n-by-p gives an m-by-p, the inner dimensions must match because machine B's output size must equal machine A's input size, and every shape error you will ever see in PyTorch, mat-one and mat-two shapes cannot be multiplied, is exactly this sentence. Third, cost: multiplying an m-by-n by an n-by-p takes m times n times p multiply-adds, and that one little formula is where GPU-goes-brrr and every LLM's FLOP budget come from.

Four special matrices you will actually use, each with a plain job. The identity, capital I, has ones on the diagonal and zeros everywhere else, and I-x equals x — it is the do-nothing machine. It shows up in residual connections, where the idea is start from identity and learn only the correction, and in regularization. The inverse, A-to-the-minus-one, is the undo machine: A-inverse of A-x gives back x. When Law wants to undo his chaos he casts Shambles again, swapping everyone back — that is the inverse. But it exists only if A destroyed no information, which means A must be square and full rank, no dimension flattened away. If Law's room had flattened everyone onto one line, losing who-was-where, no counter-spell could unswap them; an information-destroying transformation has no inverse — it is singular, rank-deficient, unrecoverable. In machine learning you rarely compute inverses explicitly, because they are numerically fragile and cost n-cubed; you solve linear systems instead, with np-dot-linalg-dot-solve. The transpose, A-with-a-T, flips rows and columns, and you meet it constantly for two reasons. It re-orients data — the Q-K-transpose inside attention is exactly dot every query row with every key row — and in calculus the gradient flows backward through a layer via W-transpose, which is Part Three's backprop. Finally, rank: the number of dimensions the output really spans. A seven-hundred-sixty-eight by seven-hundred-sixty-eight matrix of rank eight only ever produces outputs inside an eight-dimensional slice — it is secretly a small machine wearing a big costume. Hold that thought, because it is literally the idea behind LoRA fine-tuning in Part Six, where the weight updates are constrained to low rank to save ninety-nine percent of the trainable parameters. Rank is not abstract; it is the compression deal the whole field runs on.

Now put it together: why do neural network layers use matrices at all? Because a layer must turn n input features into m output features where every output can depend on every input with learnable strengths, and the simplest such function is m dot products — that is, one m-by-n matrix. It is differentiable, so gradient descent can train it; hardware-friendly, because GPUs are matrix-multiply machines; and composable, because stacking layers means multiplying matrices. So when you print a model and see Linear, in-features seven-sixty-eight, out-features three-thousand-seventy-two, that is a three-thousand-seventy-two by seven-sixty-eight matrix plus a three-thousand-seventy-two bias: three thousand seventy-two pattern detectors, two-point-three-six million parameters, one at-sign. But there is a catch that explains the entire existence of activation functions: the collapse theorem. Two Linear layers with no nonlinearity between them are equivalent to a single Linear layer, because W-two times W-one x equals the single matrix W-two-W-one times x. Linear composed with linear is linear, so a hundred-layer net with no nonlinearities equals a one-layer net — depth only buys expressiveness when nonlinear squashes separate the layers, and that is the whole reason activations exist, which you will see in Part Three. Two practical habits before we leave. Shape discipline: data is stored as rows, so a batch of thirty-two samples with ten features is thirty-two by ten, and a layer turning ten features into five uses weights ten by five, giving X-at-W equals thirty-two by five. Write the shape comment before you write the line — batch-in at-sign in-out arrow batch-out — inner numbers must match, outer numbers are the answer, and that comment is a senior engineer's habit, not beginner scaffolding. And FLOP counting: a transformer's cost is essentially the sum of its matmul costs, and in a matmul every parameter participates in exactly one multiply and one add per token, which gives the famous two-times-N-parameters rule — a seven-billion-parameter model does roughly fourteen GFLOPs per token, and training costs about six times N per token. One little formula, billions of dollars of GPU consequences.

Step back and keep the mental model, because it will save you every time PyTorch throws a shape error or you cannot remember whether to transpose. A matrix is Law's room: one rule moving all of space at once. Matrix multiplication is casting rooms in sequence, and the order is the two Warlords arguing about who goes first. When something breaks, re-ask the story's three questions: what space does this machine eat, what space does it emit, and which room is cast first? A neural layer, y equals W-x-plus-b, is one room — the rows of W are detectors transforming the input space, b shifts it, and deep nets are simply rooms cast in sequence, with nonlinear squashes inserted between them so the stack does not collapse into a single room. Two traps to retire right now, because both cost real debugging hours. First, do not fix shape errors by sprinkling dot-T until the code runs, because it very often runs while computing the wrong thing — dotting samples with samples instead of features with weights — so write the shape chain first, batch-in at-sign in-out gives batch-out, and let the error message tell you which machine expected which dimension. Second, do not confuse A-star-B, the elementwise Hadamard product, with A-at-B, true matrix multiplication: on two same-shaped square matrices both run with no error at all and produce completely different results, which is exactly the kind of silent bug that survives to production. And one interview classic to bank: to solve A-x equals b, call np-dot-linalg-dot-solve of A and b, never inverse-of-A at-sign b — the explicit inverse is slower, numerically worse, and interviewers notice the difference immediately. Master rooms-and-composition, keep the shape-comment habit, and every matrix you meet for the rest of the course — attention, weight layers, covariance, the SVD next lesson — is just another room, or a room decomposed into simpler ones.
minigpt-code: This lesson has no new ideas in it, and I want to say that first, because it changes how you should approach it. You already derived causal self-attention — twice, once on paper and once as a formula. You already know the transformer block: attention, feedforward, residual around each, layer norm before each. You already know the objective, which is predict the next token and never look right. Every conceptual piece of a GPT is in your hands. What is left is assembly, and assembly is not nothing. There is a real gap between understanding a diagram and having a thing that runs, and that gap is made almost entirely of details that no diagram shows you. Which tensor is what shape at which line. Where the causal mask actually lives and how it gets onto the GPU. Whether the output projection shares weights with the input embedding. What happens at the very first generation step when there is only one token. None of those are deep, all of them will stop your code, and working through them is what converts a picture in your head into something you could debug at three in the morning. The finished artifact is small, and its smallness is the point. Three classes. CausalSelfAttention, which does one multi-head attention with a triangular mask. TransformerBlock, which wraps that and a feedforward in pre-norm residuals. And MiniGPT, which holds the embeddings, stacks N blocks, and projects to the vocabulary. Plus a generate method, which is a loop. That is roughly two hundred lines of PyTorch, and it is the same two hundred lines, structurally, that are inside the model you are talking to when you use a commercial LLM. The difference between your file and theirs is the width of the layers, the number of them, and about ten million dollars of electricity. One expectation to set before you run it, because people are disappointed by this and should not be. Train this on a few megabytes of text on a laptop for twenty minutes and what you get back will look like English — it will have plausible word shapes, roughly correct punctuation, sentences that start and stop in the right places — and it will mean absolutely nothing. That is the correct outcome. It tells you the architecture, the loss, the masking and the optimizer are all wired up properly, because a broken model produces noise rather than fluent nonsense. Fluent nonsense is the signature of a working small model, and it is genuinely more informative than a good result would be, because it shows you exactly which part of a language model comes from architecture and which part comes from scale.

Let us walk the three classes and stop at the four places people get stuck. First, CausalSelfAttention. The obvious implementation makes three separate linear layers for Q, K and V. Do not. Make one Linear from d to three-d and split the output into three chunks. The mathematics is identical — you are computing exactly the same three projections — but it is one matrix multiplication instead of three, and this code runs in every layer on every forward pass, so the difference is real. Then reshape to separate the heads, and here is where you will spend your debugging time: the tensor goes from batch by time by three-d, to batch by time by heads by head-dimension, and then you transpose so that heads sit next to batch and the attention maths operates on the last two dimensions. Write the shape in a comment at every line. Everyone does this and nobody admits it. Second, the mask. You need a lower-triangular matrix of ones, and the important thing is how you attach it to the module. Do not set it as a plain attribute — use register-buffer. A buffer is state that belongs to the module but is not a parameter: it moves to the GPU when you call dot-to on the model, it is saved and loaded with the state dict, and crucially the optimizer never sees it, because it is not something to learn. Setting it as a plain tensor attribute means it silently stays on the CPU while your model moves to the GPU, and you get a device mismatch error several layers deep with no obvious cause. Third, TransformerBlock, and there is one line worth writing exactly. Pre-norm means: x equals x plus attention of layernorm-one of x, then x equals x plus feedforward of layernorm-two of x. Notice the shape of that. The normalization happens inside the sublayer call, on the way in, and the residual addition happens outside it. That leaves the residual path — the plus x — completely unobstructed from the first block to the last, which is exactly the clean corridor we talked about, and it is why this version trains stably without a learning-rate warmup. The original post-norm version puts the normalization outside the addition and needs babysitting. Fourth, MiniGPT itself, and one trick worth knowing. You have a token embedding matrix that maps vocabulary size to d, at the bottom. You have an output projection that maps d back to vocabulary size, at the top. Those are maps between the same two spaces in opposite directions, and it turns out you can and should use the same matrix for both — that is weight tying. In a small model where the vocabulary is large relative to everything else, the embedding table can be most of your parameters, so tying it halves the model. And it usually improves quality rather than hurting it, because the two roles genuinely are related: a token's input representation and the direction you need to point to predict it should not be independent facts.

The generate method is where the model stops being a classifier and starts being the thing people actually use, and it is four lines. Given a starting sequence of token ids, run the model forward. You get logits at every position, but you only want the last one, because that is the model's prediction for what comes next — throw the rest away. Convert those logits into a probability distribution and sample a token from it. Append that token to your sequence. Go back to the top. Do that a hundred times and you have a hundred tokens. That is it. Every chat interface you have ever used is this loop with a network connection wrapped around it, and the fact that you can see the text appearing word by word is not a design flourish, it is the loop running. Two details will bite you. The first: crop the context. Your model has a fixed block size, because the position embeddings are a table with a fixed number of rows. If the generated sequence grows past that, you index off the end of the table and crash — and you crash a hundred tokens in, after a generation that looked like it was going well, which is an annoying way to lose a run. So before each forward pass, take only the last block-size tokens. Notice what that means behaviourally: the model has a hard horizon, and text that scrolls off it is simply gone. The second: no-grad and eval. You are not training, so wrap the whole loop in torch dot no-grad, which stops autograd recording the tape. On a model of any size the tape is most of your memory, and here it is pure waste — memory you would much rather spend on a longer context. And call model dot eval so dropout is off and any normalization uses its running statistics. Now, the hidden cost, and it is the reason a later lesson exists. Look at the loop again. At step one you run the model on the full prefix. At step two you append one token and run the model on the full prefix again. At step three, again. Every step recomputes the keys and values for every token you have already processed, and none of those have changed — they cannot change, because the causal mask means a token's representation never depends on anything after it. So the naive loop does an enormous amount of provably redundant work. Generating n tokens costs on the order of n cubed operations, when it should cost far less. This is not a small constant factor. It is the difference between a model responding in a second and a model responding in a minute, and it is why every serving stack has a KV cache — you store the keys and values you have already computed and only compute the new column each step. You will build one later. The point of meeting the problem here, in your own two-hundred-line file, is that when you meet the fix you will recognize exactly what it is fixing.

Two years before Sabaody, the crew is scattered across the world and every one of them trains alone. Zoro is on Gloom Island learning to cut things he cannot see. Sanji is at Kamabakka learning a leg technique built out of heat. Luffy is on Rusukaina doing the same four moves ten thousand times a day. Nami studies weather she could not previously read. Each of them, separately, becomes good at one specific thing, and none of that training is joint. That is the last three parts of this course. You learned attention in isolation. You learned the block in isolation. You learned the objective, and the optimizer, and the loop, each on its own, and none of it was assembled. Now the reunion, and here is the detail I want you to notice, because it is the entire point of this lesson. Sabaody is not a training arc. Nobody acquires a new technique on the day they meet at the Sunny. There is no lesson, no master, no revelation. They walk up the hill, they get on the ship, and they leave. All that happens is assembly — the parts are put in the same place, wired to each other, and pointed in one direction. And the crew that sails out of Sabaody is not the sum of nine improved individuals; it is a qualitatively different thing that can attempt a sea none of them could have entered alone. That is what you are doing today. Causal self-attention on its own is a weighted average with a triangular mask — mildly interesting. A feedforward network on its own is the most ordinary object in this course. A residual connection is an addition. A sampling loop is four lines. Every one of these parts is unremarkable, and you have understood each of them separately for several lessons now. Put them in the right order, with the right shapes, pointed at one loss, and the thing that comes out generates language. Nothing new was learned. Everything changed. There is one more honest note in the picture, and it keeps the lesson from being triumphalist. The crew that reassembles at Sabaody is still, by New World standards, very small. They have not become Yonko. What they have is the right structure, and what they lack is time and scale, and the next two years of the story is them acquiring those the hard way. Your two-hundred-line file is in exactly that position. It has the correct architecture — genuinely the same one — and it has seen a few megabytes of text on one laptop instead of trillions of tokens on ten thousand accelerators. When you read your model's fluent, meaningless output, you are looking at precisely what architecture gives you and precisely what scale gives you, cleanly separated, in one experiment. Very few things in this field are that legible.

Let us finish with arithmetic, because being able to estimate a model's size in your head is genuinely useful and almost nobody teaches it. Work per block. Attention has four projection matrices — query, key, value, and the output projection after the heads are concatenated — and each is d by d. So attention is four d squared. The feedforward expands from d to four d and comes back, so that is four d squared going up and four d squared coming down: eight d squared. Add them and one block is about twelve d squared parameters, ignoring the biases and layer norms, which are negligible. Multiply by the number of blocks and the transformer stack is twelve N d squared. Then add the embedding table, which is vocabulary size times d. Notice how those two terms behave differently as you scale, because it explains several design decisions you will see. In a small model, d is a few hundred and the vocabulary is fifty thousand, so the embedding table can easily be more than half of all your parameters — which is exactly why weight tying is such a big win at small scale. In a large model, d is twelve thousand and there are ninety-six layers, so the stack is enormous and the embedding table is a rounding error. Same formula, completely different balance, and it is why advice that is correct for a small model is often wrong for a large one. Put numbers through it. A model with d equal to three eighty-four and six layers gives you twelve times six times three eighty-four squared, which is about ten million parameters in the stack — small enough to train on a laptop CPU overnight or a modest GPU in minutes. GPT-2 small is d equal to seven sixty-eight with twelve layers: twelve times twelve times seven sixty-eight squared is about eighty-five million in the stack, plus a large embedding table, giving the one hundred and twenty-four million everyone quotes. The formula holds all the way up, and you can use it on any model card you read. One final number, and it is the one that answers most practical questions. Training memory is not just the parameters. You need the weights, a gradient for every weight, and — if you are using Adam, which you are — two moment estimates for every weight. That is four copies. In thirty-two-bit floats, a one-billion-parameter model needs four gigabytes for the weights and sixteen gigabytes before you have stored a single activation. This one ratio, four times the parameters, explains almost every why does this not fit on my GPU question, and it is why the memory-saving techniques in the next few lessons — mixed precision, gradient checkpointing, and the low-rank adapters that train a tiny fraction of the weights — exist at all.
ml-fundamentals: Let's be precise about what machine learning actually is, because the word 'learning' does a lot of hiding. In classical programming you write the function f yourself: data goes in, answers come out, and every rule inside f is one you typed. Machine learning inverts that arrangement. You do not write f. Instead you supply pairs — an input and the answer that belongs to it — and the machine searches for the f that would have produced those answers. Your job shifts from writing rules to two other decisions: what shape f is allowed to take, and what counts as being wrong. There are always three ingredients. The first is the hypothesis space, which is simply the set of functions you have allowed. Is f a straight line? A polynomial? A decision tree of depth six? A neural network with ten layers? This choice is made before any data is seen, and it bounds everything that follows. The second ingredient is the loss, a single number that says how wrong one prediction was. The third is the optimizer, the search procedure that adjusts f to push that number down — and if you remember the gradient descent island, you already know the main one. Now the vocabulary. Supervised learning means every example arrives with its correct answer attached. Unsupervised means no answers at all: find the structure yourself. Reinforcement learning means no answers either, only a reward that arrives late and vaguely, after a whole sequence of actions. Nearly everything in this course is supervised, and that includes the pretraining of large language models — which surprises people, until you notice that the 'correct answer' there is simply the next token in the text, which the text itself provides for free. And here is the sentence to keep. The goal is never a low training loss. The goal is generalization: low loss on data the model has never seen. Every single technique in this lesson exists to buy generalization, and almost all of them do it by making training deliberately harder.

Now the failure that defines the whole field. Usopp decides to become a great sniper, so he practises for a month in Syrup Village. Same range every day, same three trees, the same steady afternoon wind off the same hill, the same distance paced out from the same fence post. By the end of the month he is flawless — on that range. Then the crew reaches the Grand Line, where the wind reverses direction halfway through the flight of the shot, and he misses everything. Usopp did not learn to shoot. He memorized one island. That is overfitting, and once you have that picture you can diagnose it forever. Concretely, overfitting is a shape you see in two curves. Training loss keeps falling, smoothly, encouragingly. Validation loss falls for a while, reaches a minimum, and then starts climbing while the training loss is still improving. That crossing point is the moment the model stopped learning the signal and started fitting the noise — the accidents of this particular sample, the specific gust on that specific afternoon, which will never repeat. The opposite failure is underfitting: both curves stay high and flat, because the hypothesis space you allowed was too small to contain the truth. Fitting a straight line to a circle, no matter how long you train, leaves you with a straight line. This is why the data split is non-negotiable, and why it has three parts, not two. The training set fits the parameters. The validation set chooses the settings — how deep, how much regularization, when to stop. The test set is measured once, at the very end, and never again. The moment you choose anything by looking at the test score, the test set has quietly become a training set with extra steps, and your reported number is a fiction. And finally, learn to read the gap rather than the level. A model at ninety-nine percent on training and seventy-one on validation is worse than a model at eighty-four and eighty-two. The second one actually learned the task. The first one memorized Syrup Village.

Now we make that intuition exact, because there is a decomposition here that professionals actually use. Take the expected error of your model on new data, averaged over all the training sets you might have drawn. It splits into three separate pieces: bias squared, plus variance, plus irreducible noise. Bias is the error that comes from your assumptions being too rigid to reach the truth. If reality is a curve and you insisted on a straight line, no amount of data fixes that; you are wrong in a systematic, repeatable direction. Variance is the error that comes from your model swinging wildly when the training sample changes. Here is the picture that makes it stick. Imagine retraining your model twenty times, each time on a different sample of the same size, and then laying all twenty predictions on top of one another. In the high-bias case, all twenty models agree with each other beautifully — and all twenty are wrong in the same direction. That is Zoro confidently walking north twenty times in a row when the ship is east. In the high-variance case, the twenty models disagree violently with each other; their average is actually quite good, but no individual one of them is, and you only get to ship one. Now the trade-off itself. Adding capacity — a deeper tree, more features, more parameters — buys you lower bias and costs you variance. Removing capacity does the reverse. That much really is a trade-off. But it is not a law of nature, and here is the escape hatch that matters most in practice: more data lowers variance for free, without raising bias at all. That is precisely why the boring advice — get more data — beats almost every clever architectural fix, and why the last decade of this field looks the way it does. And do not forget the third term. Irreducible noise is the floor. If two genuinely identical inputs sometimes have different answers, then no model on earth reaches zero error, and every step you take toward zero past that floor is a step spent fitting noise. Knowing roughly where the floor sits is what stops you optimizing past it.

So overfitting is the enemy. The counter-attack is called regularization, and the idea behind every variant is the same: deliberately make training harder, so the model cannot afford to memorize. The classic form adds a penalty to the loss. In L2 regularization, also called ridge, you add lambda times the sum of the squared weights. Think about what this changes. Before, a huge weight was free; if it bought even a sliver of training accuracy, the optimizer took it. Now every large weight costs something, so the model will only grow one when the evidence genuinely supports it. The result is a gentler fit that shrinks all the weights toward zero without any of them quite arriving. L1, also called lasso, adds lambda times the sum of the absolute values instead. This looks like a small change and is not. The absolute value has a corner at zero, and that corner does something the smooth square cannot: it drives weights exactly to zero and leaves them there. So L1 performs feature selection as a side effect. It does not just hand you a gentler model, it hands you a shorter one, with the useless inputs switched off entirely — which is worth a great deal when you have to explain the model to somebody. In both cases lambda is the dial, and it is chosen on the validation set, never on training. Lambda of zero is no regularization at all. Lambda approaching infinity crushes every weight to zero, and your model predicts the same mean value for everything. The useful setting is somewhere between, and the only honest way to find it is to sweep a range and look at where the validation curve bottoms out. And finally, do not let the word 'regularization' shrink to mean 'penalty term'. Early stopping is regularization: you halt while the model is still too simple to memorize. Dropout is regularization. Augmenting your data with rotations and crops is regularization. And plain more data is the strongest regularizer of all. They all do one job — restrict what the model is able to express, so that the only thing left worth expressing is the signal.

One last piece, and it is the one that separates people whose numbers hold up from people whose numbers collapse in production. A single train-validation split is itself a random draw. If your dataset is small, the model you crown as best may simply be the one that got lucky about which rows landed in which half. The fix is k-fold cross-validation. Split the data into k parts — five and ten are the usual choices. Train k times, each time holding out a different part as the validation set, and average the k scores you get. Now your estimate rests on all the data instead of one arbitrary slice. But the average is only half the value, and most people stop there. Look at the spread of those k scores. A mean of nought-point-eight-six with a spread of plus or minus nought-point-nought-one is a result you can act on. The same mean with a spread of plus or minus nought-point-nought-nine means you have measured almost nothing, and if you rank two models whose difference is smaller than that spread, you are ranking noise. This is the same lesson as the confidence interval island, arriving in a new costume. Now two traps that ruin real projects. First: never shuffle time. If your data is ordered in time — prices, weather, logs, anything sequential — random folds let the model train on Thursday and validate on Wednesday, which is peeking at the future. Train on the past, validate on the future, always. The same applies to grouped data: all the rows belonging to one patient, one user, one ship must sit in the same fold, or the model recognizes the individual rather than learning the pattern. And second, the rule that survives every framework and every fashion: fit every transformation on the training fold only. Scaling, imputation of missing values, feature selection, vocabulary building — all of it learns from the training fold, and is then applied to the held-out fold. Fitting a scaler on the whole dataset before splitting feels harmless and is the most common silent leak in this entire field. It will not throw an error. It will simply give you a number that is too good, and you will not find out until production.
ml-system-design: This is the last lesson, and it is deliberately the one with the least new technology in it, because the thing that most often decides whether an ML project succeeds is not the model. It is whether anybody wrote down what the system was supposed to do. Every real brief you will receive is underspecified. Build us a recommender. Add AI to search. Make the support queue faster. Those are directions, not specifications, and the first piece of work is not modelling — it is turning that sentence into something with a measurable definition of done. Four questions, and the order matters. Who is this for, and what will they do differently because it exists? If nobody's behaviour changes, the system has no value regardless of its accuracy, and you will find this out after six months rather than after an afternoon. Second, what does success mean as a number? Not better search — click-through on the top three results, or reduction in queries that get abandoned. If you cannot name the metric you cannot tell whether you are finished. Third, what are the constraints? Latency, because a recommendation that takes four seconds is not a recommendation. Cost per request, because a system that works and cannot be afforded has not worked. Volume, because ten requests a day and ten thousand a second are different projects. Fourth, and this is the one people skip: what happens when it is wrong? Notice how much that changes. A wrong film recommendation costs the user a shrug, so you can be aggressive, ship fast and learn from behaviour. A wrong medication interaction alert costs a life, so you need review, explainability, an audit trail and a much higher confidence threshold before the system acts on its own. Same technology, completely different system, and the difference comes from that one question. The cost of an error is what determines how much confidence you need before acting, and it should be settled before anyone picks a model. And then the question that a surprising number of projects should answer differently: does this need machine learning at all? Rules are cheaper to build, faster to run, explainable by construction, testable, and they never drift. If the problem is genuinely covered by twenty rules, write twenty rules — you will ship in a week and everyone will understand the system. Machine learning earns its place when the rules would be too numerous to write down, or when they would change faster than you could maintain them, or when the pattern is real but nobody can articulate it. Choosing a model because a model was expected is the most expensive mistake in this lesson, and the version of it that shows up now is reaching for an LLM when a lookup table would do.

If you take one operational rule from this lesson, take this one: build the dumbest thing that could possibly work, first, before you build anything clever. For a recommender, that is recommending the most popular items to everybody. For search, returning the most recent matching document. For classification, always predicting the majority class, or a handful of keyword rules. It takes an afternoon. And it is the single highest-value afternoon in the project, for four separate reasons. The first is that it tells you whether the problem is hard. If popularity gets you eighty percent of the click-through of a sophisticated system, the problem was not hard, and everything you were planning to build was going to buy you the last twenty percent at a hundred times the cost. That is worth knowing before you plan a quarter around it, not after. The second is that it gives you the only number your later work can be judged against. Without a baseline, a model with seventy-eight percent accuracy is a meaningless statistic — it might be excellent or it might be worse than a coin weighted by class frequency. Every accuracy figure quoted without a baseline is uninterpretable, and this is worth remembering when you read other people's results too. The third is that the answer is frequently uncomfortable and always useful. It is genuinely common for the trivial baseline to reach eighty percent of the achievable gain for two percent of the effort. When that happens, the correct engineering response is to ship the baseline and go and work on something else. That feels like a defeat and it is a result — you found out cheaply that the sophisticated version was not worth building, which is exactly what the exercise was for. Projects that skip the baseline discover this at the end, after the investment, when nobody wants to hear it. And the fourth reason is the one people appreciate only in retrospect: the baseline proves the plumbing. To ship even the dumbest model you have to solve every problem in the system that is not the model. Getting the data out. Cleaning it. Computing a metric on a held-out set. Serving a prediction with acceptable latency. Logging what was served. Measuring the effect on the thing you actually care about. Every one of those is a place where real projects die, and every one of them is easier to fix now, with a trivial model behind it, than later when you are also debugging a transformer. The baseline is not a formality you perform before the real work. It is a load test of everything except the model, and it is the fastest way to find out which of your assumptions about the data were wrong.

The model is the small part. The data pipeline is where projects actually succeed or fail, and there are four things to settle early. First, and it should be the very first question in any design discussion: where do the labels come from? This is more important than the architecture and it is asked far too late. Implicit labels come from behaviour you already collect — clicks, purchases, whether a support ticket was reopened, whether a suggestion was accepted. They are free and plentiful and they are biased, because they only exist for things the user was shown. Explicit labels come from someone deciding: an annotator, a moderator, a domain expert. They are clean, they are slow, and they cost real money. Most systems use both, and every system needs an answer here. A project that cannot say where its labels will come from is not a project yet. Second, split your data by time whenever time exists in it. Train on the earlier period, evaluate on the later one, because that is what production does — the model is always predicting the future from the past. A random split lets examples from next month sit in your training set, the model learns from a world it will not have access to, and your offline number is excellent and your production number is not. This one mistake accounts for an enormous share of models that looked good in the notebook and disappointed in deployment. Third, leakage, which is the same failure in a subtler costume. A feature that is computed after the outcome — an account status field updated when the customer churned. An identifier that happens to encode the answer because of how the records were created. The same user appearing in both training and test. Duplicated rows across the split. In every case the model learns something that will not be available at prediction time, and in every case the symptom is the same: a result that is better than you expected. Treat surprisingly good results as a bug report. Nearly always there is a leak, and finding it after you have promised the number to somebody is much worse than finding it now. Fourth, and this is the one that separates people who have run a system from people who have trained a model: design the feedback loop deliberately. Once deployed, your model changes the behaviour you are learning from. A recommender that shows an item causes the clicks that become tomorrow's training data, so the model reinforces its own choices and the catalogue narrows. A fraud model that blocks transactions never learns whether they were actually fraudulent. This is not avoidable, but it is manageable: log what was shown alongside what was chosen, so the two can be separated later. Reserve a small fraction of traffic for random or exploratory serving, so you keep learning about options the model has stopped suggesting. And monitor the input distribution, not only the accuracy, because the first sign of a decaying system is usually that the data changed rather than that the model got worse.

Watch how Iceburg takes a commission, because everything in this lesson is in it. He does not begin by choosing timber, and he does not begin by talking about construction techniques. He asks what the ship is for. What waters will she sail — the Grand Line is not the East Blue, and a hull built for one is wrong for the other. What is she carrying, and how much of it. How many crew, because that decides the accommodation and therefore the layout. How far between ports, which sets the stores and the water. Who will sail her, because a ship that needs forty trained hands is useless to a crew of nine. And the question he always asks and clients rarely expect: what happens if she is caught in the wrong weather? Notice that not one of those is a question about shipbuilding. They are questions about use, and every one of them constrains the design more tightly than any opinion about timber or rigging could. By the time he has the answers, most of the ship is already determined — the brief decided it, and the craft is what executes the decision. A shipwright who starts from I would like to build a fast ship, and works out what it is for afterwards, builds a beautiful vessel that is wrong for the job. That is exactly the project that starts from we should use a transformer. Then, before the yard commits any serious material, he builds a model of the hull and floats it. It is not the ship. It carries nothing, it has no rigging, and nobody would sail it. What it does is answer the only question worth answering at that stage, which is whether this shape works at all — whether it sits right in the water, whether it heels the way it should. If the model is wrong, he has lost a week. If he had found out from the finished hull, he would have lost the commission. That is the baseline, precisely: the cheapest possible object that tests the assumption everything else rests on, built specifically so that being wrong is affordable. And the last thing, which is the part of shipbuilding that people forget is part of shipbuilding. A ship is not finished at the launch. It is careened and scraped, planks are replaced, rigging is renewed, and it is refitted when it starts sailing different waters. Every shipwright knows the vessel's life is mostly maintenance, and the design accounts for it — you build so that the parts that will wear can be reached. Machine learning systems are the same and are frequently designed as if they were not. The data will drift, the users will change, the upstream feed will silently alter its format, and the model that was excellent in March will be quietly mediocre by September. If nobody owns that, the system is not permanent, it is just not yet obviously broken. A system nobody maintains was designed to be abandoned, and that is a decision somebody made — usually by not making it.

Two practical topics and then how to say all of this out loud, because you will be asked. Deployment first. Do not swap a system over. Start in shadow mode: run the new model on live traffic, log what it would have done, and act on nothing. This is remarkably informative and completely safe — you see the real input distribution, which is never the one in your test set, you find the crashes on inputs nobody thought of, and you can compare its decisions against what actually happened. Then release it to a small percentage of traffic behind a flag, with the ability to turn it off in seconds, and measure the metric you defined in the first slide. Expect the online result to be worse than the offline one. It nearly always is, because offline evaluation uses a fixed dataset and production has feedback, distribution shift and users who behave differently once the system exists. Offline metrics are a filter for what is worth testing online; they are not a prediction. Monitoring second, and the key insight is that you usually cannot monitor accuracy. Labels arrive days later, or only for the cases you acted on, or never. So monitor what you can see immediately: the distribution of inputs, the distribution of predictions, latency, cost per request, and error rates. A shift in the input distribution is the earliest warning you will get that something upstream changed, and it precedes the accuracy drop you cannot yet measure. Alert on the input distribution, and you find out that a data provider changed a field before your users find out that your product got worse. Now the interview, because this exact material is the ML system design round and there is a reliable way to do well in it. Spend the first five minutes on requirements, and do it visibly. Who uses this, what do they do differently, what is the metric, what is the scale, what is the latency budget, what does a wrong answer cost. Interviewers are specifically watching for whether you do this, and a candidate who names an architecture in the first minute has already lost marks that are hard to recover. Then walk the pipeline in order: baseline first, then data and labels, then features, then the model, then evaluation, then deployment, then monitoring, then failure modes. At each step, name a trade-off, say which side you chose, and say why — precision against recall for the metric, latency against accuracy for the model size, cost against freshness for retraining. The trade-offs are the substance. The right answer to almost every question in that round is a defensible choice with a stated reason, not a specific technology, and a candidate who says I would start with logistic regression to get a baseline and here is what would make me move past it is more convincing than one who names the largest model they know. And that is the course. You started with vectors on graph paper, you have derived backpropagation, built a transformer, aligned it, retrieved for it, given it tools, and now designed the system it lives in. The last thing worth saying is the thing this whole part has been circling: the model was never the hard part.
model-evaluation: Nami closes her ledger and says: the model is ninety percent accurate. Usopp is delighted. She is not, and this slide is why. Suppose five out of every hundred ships have a hull breach. Now consider the laziest possible model, one that ignores its input entirely and always answers 'no breach'. What is its accuracy? Ninety-five percent. It beats Nami's model, it took no work to build, and it will sink the fleet, because it has never once identified a hole in a hull. That is the whole problem with accuracy in a sentence. When one class is rare — and in the interesting problems it always is, because fraud, disease, defects and failures are all rare by definition — accuracy is dominated by the majority class and tells you almost nothing about the thing you actually care about. It is a number that flatters you. The fix is to stop collapsing four genuinely different outcomes into a single number. Lay them out in a two-by-two table called the confusion matrix. You predicted breach and there was a breach: true positive. You predicted breach and there was none: false positive, you cried wolf. You predicted no breach and there was one: false negative, you missed it. You predicted no breach and there was none: true negative. Four cells, four different things that happened, and any metric that averages across them has thrown away information. And the reason that matters is not aesthetic. Those two error types are almost never equally expensive. A false positive on hull inspection costs you an afternoon of unnecessary checking. A false negative costs you the ship. A false positive on a spam filter sends a real invoice to junk. A false negative on the same filter shows you one more advertisement. In each case one error is dramatically worse than the other, and any single averaged score has already discarded exactly the distinction you needed to make. So here is the habit I want you to build, and it comes before any modelling at all. On any classification task, ask two questions first. What is the base rate — how common is the positive class? And which of the two errors hurts more, and by roughly what factor? Everything on the next three slides follows mechanically from those two answers, and if you cannot answer them, you are not ready to choose a metric.

So we need metrics built from the confusion matrix that keep the two errors apart, and there are exactly two that matter. The first is precision: of everything I flagged as positive, what fraction was really positive? True positives divided by all your positive predictions. Precision answers the question 'can I trust an alarm from this system?' A low-precision fraud detector floods your team with false alerts until they stop reading them, which is a real failure mode with a name — alert fatigue. The second is recall: of everything that was genuinely positive, what fraction did I catch? True positives divided by all the actual positives. Recall answers a completely different question: 'am I missing anything?' A low-recall cancer screen lets sick patients walk out the door believing they are well. Notice that the numerator is the same for both and only the denominator changes, and that difference in denominator is the entire content of the distinction. Precision is judged against what you said. Recall is judged against what was true. Now the crucial property: they pull against each other. Suppose you want perfect recall. Easy — flag everything as positive. You have now caught every real case, recall is one, and your precision is dreadful. Suppose you want perfect precision. Also easy — flag only the single case you are most confident about. Precision one, recall almost zero. Because both extremes are trivially reachable, a report of one number alone is meaningless. If somebody tells you their model has ninety-five percent recall and does not mention precision, they have told you nothing at all. F1 is the standard way to combine them: the harmonic mean, which is deliberately harsher than the ordinary average. If precision is nought-point-nine and recall is nought-point-one, the arithmetic mean would report a comfortable nought-point-five, and F1 reports nought-point-one-eight. That harshness is the point — it refuses to let a good score on one side hide a catastrophe on the other. Use F1 when the two errors are roughly comparable in cost. When they are not, do not use it. Report precision and recall separately, and say plainly which one you chose to optimize and why. That sentence — 'we tuned for recall because a missed breach costs the ship' — is what a senior engineer sounds like.

Here is a fact that reorganizes the whole topic. Every precision and recall pair you can quote belongs to one particular threshold. Move the threshold and you get a different pair. So a single precision-recall pair does not describe your model — it describes your model at one setting. What describes the model is the whole curve you trace as you sweep the threshold from one down to zero. The classical version of this is the ROC curve, which plots the true positive rate, which is just recall, against the false positive rate, which is the fraction of negatives you wrongly flagged. At a threshold of one you flag nothing and sit at the origin. At a threshold of zero you flag everything and sit at the top right. In between, the curve bulges toward the top-left corner, and the more it bulges the better your model separates the classes. Summarize it by the area underneath, the AUC, and that number has a genuinely beautiful interpretation: AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen positive example receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative one. So nought-point-five is a coin flip — your model has no ranking ability at all — and one is a perfect ranking. That interpretation is worth memorizing, because it makes clear what AUC does and does not measure: it measures ranking quality, entirely independent of any threshold you pick and independent of the prevalence of the classes. That independence is exactly why AUC is excellent for comparing two models to each other, and exactly why it can mislead you about whether either model is useful. Consider a rare class: one positive in a thousand. Your false positive rate can be a comfortable-looking one percent, which puts the ROC curve up in a lovely arc — but one percent of a thousand negatives is ten false alarms for every one real case, so your precision is under ten percent and the system is unusable in practice. ROC did not lie; it answered a question about ranking while you needed an answer about usefulness. So the rule for imbalanced problems: use the precision-recall curve instead. It plots precision against recall across the same threshold sweep, and because precision has false positives in its denominator rather than true negatives, it does not get quietly rewarded for the enormous, trivial mass of correct negatives. On rare-class problems the PR curve degrades honestly and the ROC curve flatters. When the classes are balanced, the two tell the same story and you may use either.

Classification gets most of the attention, so let me be brisk but complete about regression, where you are predicting a number rather than a class. Mean absolute error is the average of the absolute differences, and its great virtue is that it is expressed in the units of the thing you predicted. 'On average we are off by four-point-two metres' is a sentence any stakeholder understands without a statistics lesson, and because it does not square anything, one wild outlier does not dominate it. Root mean squared error squares the errors before averaging and then takes the square root to get back into the original units. Because of the squaring, it punishes large errors much more harshly than MAE does. So the choice between them is not a matter of taste, it is a statement about your problem: if one enormous miss is much worse than several small ones — as with delivery times, or dosage, or anything with a cliff in it — use RMSE. If an error of ten is exactly twice as bad as an error of five, use MAE. Reporting both costs nothing and tells the reader something real: if RMSE is far larger than MAE, you have a few big misses hiding behind an acceptable average, and that is worth knowing. Mean absolute percentage error expresses the error as a percentage of the true value, which makes it comparable across quantities of wildly different size. It has two sharp edges. It explodes when the true value is near zero, so it must never be used on data containing zeros, and it penalizes over-prediction and under-prediction asymmetrically, which quietly biases any model you tune on it. And now the habit that matters more than the choice of metric, and that I want you to take away from this entire lesson. Always compute a trivial baseline. Predict the mean of the training set for everything. Or, for time series, predict that today equals yesterday. Then report your model against it. An RMSE of four-point-two means absolutely nothing in isolation — it might be superb or it might be worse than a constant. 'RMSE four-point-two, against a baseline of eleven-point-zero' is a result. And this single habit catches more broken pipelines than any unit test you will write, because a model that has silently lost its features, or been trained on shuffled labels, will land right on the baseline and stay there — and without the baseline in front of you, you will not notice.

Finally, the discipline that makes all of these numbers mean something. A single train-test split gives you one number with no error bar, and if your test set is small, that number moves by several points depending on which rows happened to land in it. K-fold cross-validation gives you k numbers instead. Report their mean, and report their spread, and adopt this rule: never declare one model better than another when the gap between them is smaller than the spread across folds. That rule alone will save you from a great deal of confident nonsense. Two details on how you build folds. Stratify them, so that each fold preserves the overall class balance — with a two percent positive class and ten folds, an unstratified split can easily hand you a fold containing almost no positives, and the metric on that fold is noise. And respect structure: never shuffle time-ordered data, and keep all the rows belonging to one patient, one customer, one ship inside a single fold. Now leakage, which is the silent killer of this entire field. Leakage is when information about the answer reaches your features by a route that will not exist at prediction time. A column computed after the outcome was known. A record ID that happens to be assigned in outcome order. A scaler or a vocabulary fitted on the full dataset before splitting. In every case the model learns something real that it will never have access to in production. The symptom is always the same: a suspiciously excellent score. So build this reflex — when your AUC comes back at nought-point-nine-nine, do not celebrate, investigate. Treat it as a bug report. Ask what your model could possibly be seeing, and check whether each feature would genuinely have been available at the moment of prediction. And last: even a perfectly measured number decays. You trained on last year and you deployed this year, and the world moved underneath the model — customers changed, fraudsters adapted, a supplier changed their format. That is drift, and it is not a failure of your modelling, it is the normal condition of deployed systems. So monitor the live metric, monitor the distribution of the inputs, which usually shifts before the metric visibly does, and plan the retraining schedule before you launch rather than after the complaint arrives. Evaluation is not a milestone you pass on the way to shipping. It is a process that starts at shipping and does not stop.
multi-framework-agents: There are a lot of agent frameworks and the marketing makes them sound more different than they are. Underneath, every one of them is the loop you wrote two lessons ago: a model, a set of tools, a dispatch step, an observation, and a termination condition. None of them can express something the others cannot. What they genuinely differ on is which decisions they force you to make explicitly and which they make for you, and if you evaluate them on that axis the choice becomes straightforward. LangGraph you already know: an explicit state graph, nodes and edges you declare, durable checkpointing. It gives you the most control and asks for the most setup, and it is the right answer when the control flow is complex, when runs are long, or when you need to pause and resume. Its abstraction is a state machine, which is a very general shape, and generality is why it is verbose. CrewAI takes a different bet: the abstraction is a team. You define agents as roles — a researcher, a writer, an editor — each with a goal and a backstory, and a manager coordinates them. It is remarkably fast to a working demo, and the reason is that the abstraction does a lot for you. That is also the risk: if your problem genuinely looks like a team of specialists producing a document, it fits beautifully; if it does not, you will find yourself describing your problem as a team of specialists in order to use the tool, which is the abstraction leading rather than serving. AutoGen models agents as participants in a conversation, and it includes an agent that executes code, which makes it strong for research and analysis workflows where the task really is a dialogue that produces and runs programs. Microsoft's rewrite is more production-oriented than the original research release, so check which generation you are reading about. And then the thin provider-aligned ones — the OpenAI Agents SDK, Google's ADK. Few concepts, close to the underlying API, less magic, correspondingly less help when your flow gets complicated. If you are already committed to one provider and your agent is simple, these are often the least-overhead choice. So the honest summary of the landscape: they all wrap the same loop. Choose by how much structure you want imposed and how much you want to write yourself, and by whether their central metaphor — a graph, a team, a conversation — matches the shape of your actual problem. If none of them does, that is a signal to write the loop yourself, not to pick the closest one and bend your problem to fit it.

Multi-agent means several model instances with different prompts and different tools, cooperating on one task. Three patterns cover almost everything people actually build, and it is worth being precise about why they help, because the usual explanation is wrong. The supervisor pattern is the most useful one. A router agent receives the task, works out which specialist should handle it, and delegates — with each specialist having its own focused prompt and its own small set of tools. A support system might route to a billing agent, a technical agent and an account agent. This is the pattern that most often earns its complexity, and the reason is not that the agents collaborate cleverly. It is scoping. Each specialist has a short prompt about one domain and four tools instead of a long prompt about six domains and twenty tools, and a shorter prompt with fewer available wrong choices is measurably more reliable. Sequential pipelines are the second pattern: agent A researches, agent B drafts from the research, agent C edits the draft. Each step is specialised and the handoffs are explicit. This is predictable, testable, and easy to debug because you can inspect the artifact between any two stages. It is also, honestly, a workflow with model calls in it — and I mean that as praise rather than criticism, because that is exactly what you should prefer when the sequence is knowable. Debate and critique is the third. One agent produces something, a second attacks it, and either the first revises or a third adjudicates. This genuinely improves quality on open-ended work — arguments get stronger when something looks for holes in them, and the effect is real and measurable on writing and analysis. It also costs three or more times as much and takes three times as long, so it belongs on work where quality matters more than latency and where a human would otherwise be doing the reviewing. Now the sentence to take away, because it corrects the most common misconception in this area. The benefit of multi-agent systems is scoping, not emergent intelligence. Five agents do not think better together than one agent thinks alone — they are the same model, and nothing about running it five times creates a capability that was not there. What multi-agent buys you is that each instance has a narrower job, a shorter prompt, a smaller tool set, and therefore fewer ways to go wrong. Every real benefit you will measure traces back to that. Which is a useful thing to know, because it tells you when the pattern will not help: if your task cannot be cleanly divided into narrower jobs, adding agents adds coordination cost and buys you nothing.

Multi-agent systems demo extremely well, and the demo omits four costs that decide whether one is a good idea. Cost, first, and it multiplies faster than people expect. Each agent has its own system prompt, its own tool schemas, and its own conversation history, and every one of those is tokens on every call that agent makes. A five-agent system working on one task frequently uses five to ten times the tokens of a single well-scoped agent doing the same job, and the supervisor pattern adds another layer because the router is itself a model call. If your justification for the architecture is quality, measure whether you got quality proportional to a tenfold bill. Reliability, second, and it is the same arithmetic that limited long agent loops, now applied sideways. If each agent in a chain is ninety percent reliable, five of them in sequence give you fifty-nine percent. Adding agents adds steps, and steps multiply. So a multi-agent system is not more robust than a single agent by virtue of having more parts — it is usually less robust, and each additional specialist has to earn its place by removing more error than it introduces. Debugging, third, and this is the one that hurts in practice. With a single agent, something goes wrong and you read the trace: here is what it thought, here is what it called, here is what came back. With five agents you first have to work out which agent produced the bad output, then what it was actually handed by the agent before it, then whether the fault was in that agent's reasoning or in the handoff. The trace is now several interleaved traces, and reproducing the failure requires reproducing the whole choreography. This is why good tracing is not optional for multi-agent work — it is the only thing standing between you and guessing. Fourth, and it is the subtlest: information loss at the handoffs. Agent A finished its research and wrote a summary for agent B. Somewhere in the material A read was a caveat it did not think worth including. B never sees it, produces a confident answer that the caveat would have changed, and nothing in the system reports that anything was lost — because from B's perspective nothing was. Every handoff is a lossy compression step performed by a model that does not know what the next agent will need. Adding agents adds handoffs, and each one is a place where something quietly falls out of the system. So the discipline is: start with one agent, and add a second only when you can name the specific failure it fixes and measure that the fix worked. Growing a multi-agent system by intuition produces something expensive, fragile and unexplainable, and it usually performs worse than the single agent it replaced.

Enies Lobby is a multi-agent system, and it is a useful one to think with because it shows both halves — why the pattern works and how it nearly comes apart. Watch the structure. The crew arrives at the gate and immediately splits, and they do not regroup until the objective is achieved. Zoro takes the swordsman. Sanji takes the one he can reach fastest. Chopper handles what needs a doctor's knowledge, Nami takes the one who fights with weather, Usopp takes the one nobody expected him to take. Nine people, one objective, and after the first minute almost no communication between them. That is exactly what a multi-agent system is, and stating it that plainly already tells you where the risks are. Now, why does it work? Not because they coordinate brilliantly, because they do not coordinate at all. It works because the division of labour is clean. Nobody has to hold a meeting about who takes the swordsman — the assignment falls out of who each of them is. Each crew member has a narrow, well-understood capability and takes the sub-problem that matches it, and there is no ambiguity to resolve. That is the supervisor pattern with a perfect router: a specialist per task, scoped tightly, chosen without deliberation. When your problem decomposes that cleanly, multi-agent is genuinely the right architecture, and the reason it helps is the reason from the last slide — each of them is doing one narrow thing they are suited for, not because the group is smarter than its members. Now watch where it nearly falls apart, because that is the more useful half. Almost nobody knows what anyone else has found. Robin learns something crucial and there is no way to tell the others. Decisions get made on information that was true twenty minutes ago. People fight battles that are already unnecessary because the situation changed elsewhere. Every one of those is a handoff failure, and they are not caused by anyone being wrong — they are caused by there being no channel. And the thing that actually holds the operation together is one piece of shared state that everybody can see from wherever they are: the flag burning above the building. It is a single signal, globally visible, that tells every one of them the objective is still live and everyone else is still committed. It is not communication. It is shared state. So the lesson to take is not that splitting up is powerful, which is the lesson the demo version of this teaches. It is narrower and more useful: splitting up works when the split is obvious enough that nobody has to negotiate it, and when there is one piece of shared state that every participant can read. Take away the clean division and you get people duplicating each other's work. Take away the shared signal and you get nine agents improvising against a picture of the world that stopped being true.

Here is the default I would defend, and it is deliberately conservative because the failure mode in this area is enthusiasm. Start with one agent and a good tool set. One model, a well-chosen handful of tools with careful descriptions, a step cap, and good tracing. That configuration handles far more than people expect, and it is cheap, debuggable and explainable. Add a second agent only when you can point at a specific failure it fixes — the prompt has grown so long that instructions are being ignored, or two domains need genuinely incompatible system prompts, or one part of the task needs a much more expensive model than the rest. Those are real reasons. Wanting the architecture to look sophisticated is not, and the resulting system will be worse in every measurable way. Second, prefer a workflow wherever the sequence is knowable, which is the same advice as two lessons ago and it applies with more force here. If you know the steps — research, then draft, then edit — then write that as three function calls with a model in each, and you get something testable, cheap, reproducible and easy to reason about. Calling it a multi-agent system does not change what it is, and structuring it as one adds coordination machinery you do not need. Genuine multi-agent is for the case where the decomposition itself is dynamic: you do not know in advance how many specialists will be needed or which, because that depends on what the first one finds. That case is real and it is rarer than the literature suggests. Third, if you do split, split cleanly and give everyone one shared state object. Ambiguity about which agent owns a decision is the source of most multi-agent pathology — two agents doing the same work, or each assuming the other handled something. Make the routing unambiguous, the way Enies Lobby's was, and make sure there is one thing every participant can read to know the current situation. Passing summaries between agents is lossy; a shared state that each agent updates is not. Fourth, and last: instrument before you scale out, not after. Per-agent tracing, token cost attributed per agent, step counts per run. Without those, a bad final answer is unattributable — you cannot tell which specialist produced it or on what basis — and the instinct when you cannot diagnose a problem is to add another agent to compensate, which makes the next diagnosis harder still. That is how these systems become unmaintainable, and it happens gradually and reasonably at every step. Measure first, then grow.
neural-networks: Let's build the whole of deep learning out of one part, because there really is only one part. A neuron holds a weight for each of its inputs, plus one extra number called the bias. It multiplies each input by its weight, adds them all up, adds the bias, and gets a single number z. Written out, that is z equals w dot x plus b — and if that dot product looks familiar it should, because it is exactly the sum you learned on the Compass Rock in Part One. Then it does one more thing, and this is the thing that matters: it passes z through a non-linear function to get the output a. Multiply, add, bend. That is the entire unit, and everything in this part of the course is that unit repeated. It is worth being clear about what the two kinds of number mean, because they are not interchangeable. The weights say how much each input matters and in which direction — a large positive weight means this input pushes strongly toward firing, a large negative weight means it pushes strongly against. The bias says something different: how easily this neuron fires at all, regardless of input. Geometrically, the weights turn the decision boundary and the bias slides it. Take the bias away and the boundary is nailed to the origin, which cripples the neuron for no good reason. Now, history, because it explains why the field looks the way it does. One neuron with a hard step at the end is a perceptron, from 1958, and it was genuinely exciting: it learns, from examples, to draw one straight line and tell you which side of it you are on. It is a linear classifier with a more romantic name. And in 1969 Minsky and Papert pointed out that a single perceptron cannot learn XOR — the function that is true when exactly one of two inputs is true. Draw the four points and try to separate the two diagonal pairs with one straight line; you cannot. That observation was correct, it was taken as an indictment of the whole idea, funding dried up, and the field lost roughly fifteen years to a problem that two layers solve without effort. Keep that in mind as we stack.

Now the sentence that most people skip and then spend a year confused by. The bend is not a detail. The bend is the whole reason any of this works, and here is the proof, which takes one line. Suppose you stack two linear layers with nothing between them. The first computes W-one times x, the second computes W-two times that. Compose them and you get W-two W-one x. But W-two W-one is just another matrix — multiply them together once, in advance, and you have a single layer that does exactly the same thing. Which means a hundred stacked linear layers is still one straight line. Depth with no non-linearity buys you nothing at all, no matter how much compute you throw at it. Put a bend between the layers and the collapse cannot happen, and now the stack can bend space repeatedly and represent shapes that no single matrix could. So which bend? The default, and it is almost insultingly simple, is ReLU: max of zero and z. Negative becomes zero, positive passes through untouched. That is one kink at the origin and it is enough. Two things make it the standard. Its gradient is exactly one for positive inputs, so it does not shrink the signal as backpropagation travels through many layers — and that is the reason deep networks became trainable at all. And it costs one comparison, which matters when you are computing it a trillion times. The older choices were sigmoid, which squashes everything into zero-to-one, and tanh, which squashes into minus-one-to-one. Both are smooth and both have the same fatal habit: they saturate. Once the input is far from zero in either direction, the curve is flat, the gradient is nearly zero, and learning through that unit essentially stops. Stack a few of those and the gradient reaching the early layers is vanishingly small. So the rule is: keep sigmoid for a binary output, where you actually want a probability, and do not build hidden layers out of it. The modern variants — GELU, which transformers use, SiLU or Swish, and Leaky ReLU for the case where units get stuck at zero forever — are all small refinements of the same idea. Pass the positive part, suppress the negative, and put a kink somewhere near the origin.

One neuron is not much. Put n of them side by side, all reading the same inputs but each with its own weights and its own bias, and you have a layer — and here is the piece of bookkeeping that makes everything efficient. Stack those n weight vectors as the rows of a matrix W, and the whole layer is one matrix multiply: a equals sigma of W x plus b. Every neuron is one row of W. So a layer is a matrix, and a network is a chain of matrices with a bend after each one. Nothing in this is more exotic than the graph paper you stretched in Part One, and that is why a graphics card can run it: matrix multiplication is the one thing those chips do superlatively well. Feed one layer into the next and you have a multilayer perceptron — the plainest neural network there is. Input layer, one or more hidden layers, output layer. They are called hidden for a mundane reason: nothing outside the network ever looks at their values. You hand in an input, you read an output, and everything in between is the network's own business. Now the famous theorem, and the honest reading of it. The universal approximation theorem says that a network with a single hidden layer, made wide enough, can approximate any continuous function to any accuracy you like. People quote this as if it settles something. It does not. It is an existence result: it says a good setting of the weights exists, and it says nothing whatsoever about how wide that layer would have to be — the answer can be absurd — and nothing about whether gradient descent will ever find those weights. It is a reassurance that you are not attempting the impossible. It is not a recipe. And in practice the recipe runs the other way: depth beats width, decisively. A deep stack composes its features. The first layers learn cheap, general parts, and later layers build on those parts rather than rediscovering them, so a deep network reaches the same accuracy with far fewer parameters than one enormous flat layer. That compositional reuse is the entire reason the field is called deep learning and not wide learning.

Here is the picture to hang all of that on. In Water Seven, the Galley-La yards build a ship as a chain of crews, and it is worth watching how the work is divided. One crew does nothing but shape timber: take a rough log, produce a shaped plank to spec. The next crew never touches a log — they take shaped planks and join them into frames. The crew after that takes frames and assembles them into a section of hull. And so on, up to the rigging. Each crew's output is the next crew's raw material, and each crew's job is narrow, repetitive and unglamorous. Now notice two things about that arrangement. First, no single shipwright is holding the whole ship in their head. Iceburg draws the intent, but the man cutting the fourteenth plank of the morning is not reasoning about seaworthiness; he is producing a plank to a tolerance. Second, none of the individual jobs is clever. The ship is not the product of one genius step; the ship is the product of the arrangement. That is exactly the claim about neural networks. The neuron is trivial — multiply, add, bend. The behaviour comes from the arrangement. And this is not a metaphor that falls apart when you look closely; it is what actually happens inside a trained network, and you can go and look at it. In a vision network trained on photographs, the first layers converge on edge detectors and colour blobs — the timber-shaping crew. The middle layers combine those edges into corners, textures, repeated patterns, wheel-shaped things. The late layers combine those into car, or dog, or face. Nobody labelled an edge. Nobody told the network that wheels exist or that they are relevant to cars.
