The only instruction the network ever received was a loss on the final answer, and this entire vocabulary of intermediate parts appeared underneath it because the arrangement made it the cheapest way to be right. That is called representation learning, and it is the real prize of this whole part of the course. In classical machine learning you designed the features by hand — you sat down and decided that word counts, or edge histograms, were what mattered, and the model was only as good as your imagination. A deep network learns the intermediate vocabulary itself. And because those learned parts are general, you can take a network trained on one enormous task and reuse its lower layers on a task with almost no data, which is the idea that the last two parts of this course are built on.

Let's finish with the practical part — the things that actually stop a network training, and the settings you have to choose. First, initialization, which sounds like a formality and is not. Never initialize all the weights to zero. If every neuron in a layer starts identical, then every neuron computes the same output, and — this is the fatal part — every neuron receives exactly the same gradient, so they update identically and stay identical forever. Your layer of five hundred neurons is one neuron wearing five hundred hats, and no amount of training breaks the symmetry. So we initialize randomly. But not with any random numbers: the scale matters, because if the variance of the activations grows or shrinks layer by layer, then by layer twenty the signal has either exploded or faded to nothing. The standard answers are He initialization when you are using ReLU, and Xavier or Glorot when you are using tanh. Both simply set the random scale from the number of inputs so the variance stays roughly constant as the signal moves up the stack. Every framework does this for you by default; you should know why. Second, the failure that puzzles people: dead ReLUs. If a unit's input gets pushed far negative, its output is zero, and because ReLU's gradient is zero on that side, the unit receives no gradient — so it can never come back. It is dead for the rest of training. The usual cause is a learning rate high enough to knock units off the cliff in one step, and the usual fixes are lowering the learning rate or switching to Leaky ReLU, which lets a small negative slope through so there is always some gradient. Third, the output layer, which is chosen by the task and not by taste. Predicting a number? No activation at all on the last layer, plain linear output, and mean squared error. Two classes? One unit with a sigmoid, and binary cross-entropy. More than two classes? One unit per class, a softmax across them so they sum to one, and cross-entropy. Those three pairings are fixed, and if you find yourself inventing a fourth, check the task again. And finally, sizing, which is far less mysterious than it looks. Start with two or three hidden layers a few hundred units wide. Then before you tune anything at all, take a tiny subset of your data — a few dozen examples — and check that your network can overfit it completely, driving the training loss to nearly zero. That is not a good model; it is a test of your plumbing. If a network cannot memorize forty examples, something is wrong with your data pipeline or your loss, and no amount of architecture tuning will save you. Once it passes that test, add the regularization and the real data, and only then start caring about size.
probability: A probability is nothing more than a number between zero and one that tracks how strongly you believe something, with one hard constraint: the beliefs over all mutually exclusive outcomes must sum to one. Everything else is bookkeeping rules. The joint probability of A and B is P of A-given-B times P of B. The marginal probability of A is the sum over all values b of the joint of A and B-equals-b — you sum out the variable you do not care about. The bar symbol reads given: P of A-given-B is the probability of A in the world where B is known to be true. And conditional probability is the single load-bearing idea for all of AI, because P of rain given dark clouds is not P of rain — conditioning is updating on information. This is not an analogy for language models; it is literally what they are. A language model is precisely a machine for one conditional distribution: P of the next token given all the previous tokens. When people say LLMs just predict the next word, the technically exact statement is that they compute this conditional distribution over the vocabulary, and we sample from it. Hold onto that, because it reframes the entire second half of this course. One more idea: independence. A and B are independent when knowing B changes nothing about A — P of A-given-B equals P of A, or equivalently the joint of A and B equals P of A times P of B, the probabilities simply multiply. Most naive-but-useful models, like Naive Bayes in Part Two, work by pretending the features are independent even when they are not, precisely because that pretense makes the math collapse into a clean product of per-feature terms. Probability, then, is just disciplined bookkeeping of uncertainty, and conditioning is the verb that does all the work.

Bayes' rule flips the conditioning direction, and it is derived in one line from the two equal ways of writing the joint of H and E. The result: P of H-given-E equals P of E-given-H, times P of H, divided by P of E. Say it in named pieces: the posterior equals the likelihood times the prior, divided by the evidence. In words, your belief in hypothesis H after seeing evidence E equals how well H explains E, times how plausible H was beforehand, all renormalized. Those three names — prior for P of H, likelihood for P of E-given-H, and posterior for P of H-given-E — are permanent vocabulary; you will hear the word prior in every ML conversation you ever have. And Bayes guards against a famous trap, the base-rate fallacy, which deserves a full worked example. A disease affects one percent of patients. A test catches ninety percent of true cases, its sensitivity, but also false-alarms on nine percent of healthy patients. You test positive. What is the chance you are actually sick? Run Bayes: nine-tenths times one-hundredth, on top, divided by nine-tenths times one-hundredth plus nine-hundredths times ninety-nine-hundredths — that is nought-point-zero-zero-nine over nought-point-zero-nine-eight-one, which is about nine-point-two percent. Not ninety percent — nine. Picture ten thousand patients: ninety of them are truly sick and test positive, but eight hundred ninety-one healthy ones also test positive, so your ninety true positives drown under the false alarms. Most people, including doctors in published studies, guess eighty to ninety percent, and they are wrong because the prior is doing the work: rare things stay improbable even after moderately strong evidence. This is exactly why fraud-detection and medical-AI systems produce mostly false positives on rare classes unless the model is extremely precise, and it connects directly to precision and recall in Part Two. Bayes is the arithmetic of not fooling yourself when the base rate is low.

Three distributions cover most of what you will meet, plus one distinction that trips people constantly. The Bernoulli of p is the simplest: one yes-or-no event with success probability p. The output of a binary classifier — spam or not spam — is a Bernoulli p, and logistic regression in Part Two is exactly a machine that maps input features to that single p. Next, the categorical distribution: one draw among k options with probabilities p-one through p-k that sum to one. This one matters enormously, because the output of every large language model at every single step is one categorical distribution over roughly a hundred thousand tokens — and temperature and top-p, which you will meet in Part Six, are simply ways of reshaping and then sampling from that distribution. Third, the Gaussian, or normal, written N of mu and sigma-squared: the bell curve, pinned down entirely by its mean mu and its variance sigma-squared. It is everywhere for three real reasons. The Central Limit Theorem says that sums or averages of many small independent effects come out bell-shaped no matter what the individual pieces looked like. It is the maximum-entropy distribution for a given variance, meaning the least-opinionated choice consistent with that spread. And it is analytically convenient. Weight initialization, measurement-noise models, variational autoencoders, diffusion models — all of it is Gaussian country. Finally the distinction that trips everyone: distributions come as a PMF or a PDF. A probability mass function gives the actual probability of each discrete outcome — a bar chart, and the bars sum to one. A probability density function is for continuous values, and it is a density, not a probability: the area under the curve over an interval is the probability, while the height alone is not a probability at all and can happily exceed one. A narrow Gaussian peaks well above one in height, and that is fine, because only its integrated area is ever a probability. Mixing up density with probability is a classic interview filter, so keep it straight: bars are probabilities, curve-heights are densities, and only areas under a density are probabilities.

Two summary numbers compress a whole distribution. The expectation, E of X, is the sum over x of x times the probability of X equals x — the probability-weighted average. The variance, Var of X, is the expected value of the squared deviation from the mean, E of the quantity X-minus-E-of-X, squared, and its square root sigma is the standard deviation. Expectation is the long-run average per trial: a fair die has expectation one-plus-two-up-to-six over six, which is three-point-five — a value never actually rolled, but always approached as you average more and more rolls. Variance just measures how spread out the outcomes are around that average. The lottery makes expectation concrete as a decision tool. The Friends gang pools money for Powerball, and Phoebe insists the vibes are right, but run the numbers: a ticket costs one dollar, the jackpot is three hundred million, and the odds are about one in two hundred ninety-two million, so the expected winnings are three hundred million times one-over-two-hundred-ninety-two-million, about one dollar three cents before taxes and shared jackpots drag the realistic return to roughly fifty cents per dollar ticket. Expectation does not say you will not win — someone does — it says the probability-weighted average outcome is a loss, every ticket turning a dollar into fifty cents on average, forever. Now why machine learning cares, concretely and deeply: every loss you minimize is an expectation — the average wrongness over the data distribution — which you estimate by averaging over a batch of examples. And here is the statistical license for the whole training procedure: stochastic gradient descent works because a random mini-batch's average gradient is an unbiased estimate of the true full-data gradient, meaning its expectation equals the true gradient, with a variance that shrinks as the batch grows. That is the entire justification for training on batches of thirty-two examples instead of the whole internet at every step — the batch gradient is noisy but centered on the right answer, and bigger batches just reduce the noise. Casinos, insurance, loss functions, and the expected-reward objective of RLHF in Part Six all live on this one formula: the probability-weighted average, computed before the dice roll.

Usopp gives you Bayes as a permanent instinct. He bursts onto deck — a Sea King the size of an island is behind us — and the question is whether to man the cannons. Nami runs the numbers. The prior: island-sized Sea Kings are rare, say one voyage in a hundred, one percent. The likelihood if one were truly there: Usopp would certainly yell, near one hundred percent. But the crucial second likelihood: Usopp yells about imaginary monsters constantly, so even on a monster-free day there is a thirty percent chance of exactly this performance. Bayes gives a posterior of about three-point-three percent — after the famous alarm, belief rose from one percent to just three-point-three, because evidence from a noisy channel barely moves the needle against a strong prior, and Zoro goes back to sleep. But Bayes cuts both ways: moments later Nami herself sees the shadow, and her false-alarm rate is about one percent, so her identical report pushes the posterior to about fifty percent, and two independent reports together push it near certainty. Same prior, different likelihood ratios — the reliability of the sensor determines how much a positive report is worth. That is the instinct to carry: the posterior is the prior reshaped by the reliability of the channel, weak channels barely move beliefs, reliable ones move them a lot, and it is exactly why one weak signal should not flip your fraud model's decision. The lottery pins the other half: expectation is the probability-weighted average, computed before the dice roll, the arithmetic behind casinos, insurance, and every loss function you will minimize. Three things to retire before you go. First, probability versus likelihood: it is the same formula with a different variable held fixed — P of data given theta, read as a function of the data, is a probability distribution, but read as a function of theta with the data already observed, it is the likelihood, and that reading is the entire basis of maximum likelihood estimation in the next lesson. Second, never invert the conditional carelessly: P of A given B is not P of B given A — most drug users drank milk does not make milk drinkers drug users — and correcting that inversion is precisely what Bayes' rule exists to do, at the cost of a prior. Third, do not read PDF heights as probabilities, and do not trust a neural network's softmax output as a calibrated real-world probability, because modern nets are systematically overconfident unless you explicitly calibrate them. Prior reshaped by the channel, expectation computed before the roll — that is probability as a working instinct for the rest of the course.
pytorch-fundamentals: You have now done, by hand, everything this library does. You built a neuron, you derived the chain rule through two layers, you wrote the four-step loop, and you tuned an optimizer. So it is worth being precise about what a framework actually buys you, because the honest answer is narrower than the marketing and much more useful to know. In the backprop lab you derived gradients for a two-layer scalar network. That was six lines of careful algebra and it was tractable. Now picture a network of forty layers with attention and normalization and residual connections, and picture re-deriving all of it every time you move a layer or change an activation. It is not hard mathematics — it is the same chain rule — it is just thousands of terms, and every one is a chance to make a sign error you will not find for a week. That specific labour is what a framework removes. It removes the bookkeeping. It does not remove the thinking. PyTorch is three ideas, and once you see them the rest of the library is vocabulary. The first is the tensor: an n-dimensional array, very much like numpy, with two extra abilities we will come to. The second is autograd: while your forward pass runs, PyTorch quietly records every operation it performs, and that recording is enough to replay the whole thing backwards and hand you every gradient. The third is nn dot Module: a container that holds layers and, crucially, knows which of its own numbers are parameters, so you never have to keep a list of them yourself. Tensors, autograd, Modules. Everything in the last five parts of this course is those three things arranged differently. Now the part people skip. The framework does not automate the mathematics, the training loop, or the debugging. When you call loss dot backward, PyTorch computes the correct gradients of whatever you actually wrote — and it will do that perfectly for a loss function that is wrong, for data you forgot to shuffle, for a learning rate ten times too high, and for a model that is quietly training on its own labels. It has no opinion about any of that. Everything you learned in the last three lessons is what tells you the numbers coming out are sensible, and that judgement is the part that stays yours. One last idea, and it explains why this library rather than the others. PyTorch is define-by-run: the computation graph is built by executing your Python code, line by line, as it runs. There is no separate compile step and no session to submit work to. Which means an if statement inside your forward pass is legal, a Python for loop over a sequence is legal, and both are differentiable, because the graph simply records what actually happened this time. And it means you debug a model the way you debug any other Python: put a print in the middle and look. That single design decision is why the research world moved here, and it is why the code in the rest of this course is readable.

Start with the tensor, because everything else is built on it and because most of the time you lose in your first month is lost here. A tensor is an n-dimensional array. If you know numpy you already know ninety percent of the interface: indexing, slicing, sums along an axis, matrix multiply. The two additions are the point. A tensor can live on a graphics card instead of in main memory, and the same line of code runs on either. And a tensor can carry a gradient, which is what lets the next slide work at all. Four attributes will resolve most of the confusion you are going to have, so learn to check all four by reflex. Shape, which is the size along each dimension. Dtype, the numeric type. Device, whether it is on the CPU or a GPU. And requires-grad, whether autograd is watching it. When something is behaving strangely, print those four before you print anything else. Now, shape errors, which I want to be honest about: they are the tax you pay for the rest of this course. Everybody hits them, experts included, and the cure is not cleverness, it is the habit of reading shapes constantly and writing them in comments. The conventions are worth memorizing because they are near-universal. Batch comes first, always. Tabular data is batch by features. Images are batch, channels, height, width. Sequences are batch, time, and the model dimension. Four operations reshape almost everything you will ever need: view or reshape, which reinterpret the same numbers in a different arrangement; permute, which swaps the order of the axes; and squeeze and unsqueeze, which remove and insert dimensions of size one. Next, broadcasting, which is the single most useful and most dangerous rule in the library. When you combine two tensors of different shapes, PyTorch lines the shapes up from the right-hand end and stretches any dimension of size one to match. That is why a batch of thirty-two by ten can be added to a bias of length ten with no ceremony at all. And it is why a column of shape thirty-two by one, added to a row of shape one by thirty-two, quietly gives you a thirty-two by thirty-two matrix instead of the error you were hoping for. It will not warn you. It will produce a number, your loss will look plausible, and your model will never learn. When a result has more dimensions than you expected, suspect broadcasting first. Finally, dtypes, briefly. Float thirty-two is the default and is almost always the right answer. Float sixty-four doubles your memory and your bandwidth to buy you precision that no neural network can make use of. Half precision is the opposite trade and belongs in a later conversation about speed. And integer tensors cannot carry gradients at all — if your loss sits at exactly the same value forever, the very first thing to check is whether something in the chain became an integer.

This is the idea that made the library, and having derived backprop by hand you are in the rare position of being able to see exactly what it is doing. When you create a tensor with requires-grad set to true, PyTorch starts watching it. Every operation you then perform on it — a multiply, an addition, a ReLU, a matrix product — is recorded onto what is usually called a tape: a record of which operation happened and what its inputs were. The forward pass builds this tape as a side effect of simply running. Then you call backward on your loss, and PyTorch walks that tape from the end to the beginning, applying at each step exactly the local derivative rule you worked out in the Baratie lesson, multiplying as it goes, and depositing the final gradient for each parameter into that parameter's dot-grad attribute. That is the whole mechanism. It is your lab, automated, and it is not doing anything you have not already done on paper. Now the behaviour that catches everybody, and it catches them silently. Gradients accumulate. When backward runs, it adds to dot-grad rather than overwriting it. That is a deliberate design decision and it is genuinely useful: it is how you train on a batch too large to fit in memory, by running several small forward and backward passes and letting their gradients pile up before you step. But it means that if you forget to clear them, step number ten is being taken using the sum of the gradients from all ten steps, your effective learning rate grows without limit, and your loss goes to infinity in a way that looks like an exploding gradient and is not. This is why optimizer dot zero-grad sits at the top of every training loop you will ever read. It is not boilerplate. It is load-bearing. Next, the two ways to switch autograd off, because you do not always want the tape. Wrap a block in with torch dot no-grad, and nothing inside it is recorded. Use that for validation and for inference, where you have no intention of calling backward and the tape is pure wasted memory — on a large model it is most of your memory. And use dot detach when you want to cut one particular tensor loose from the graph while everything else keeps recording; the classic case is taking a value out to log it, or stopping a gradient from flowing back into part of a model you have decided to freeze. Finally, the error message you will meet within your first week. The tape is freed as soon as backward has used it, because keeping it would leak memory on every iteration. So if you call backward twice on the same graph, you get: tried to backward through the graph a second time. Ninety percent of the time this does not mean what it says. It means a tensor from the previous iteration is still being held in a Python variable — you appended the loss itself to a list instead of loss dot item, say — and so the old graph is still alive and got dragged into this iteration's backward pass. Look for the tensor you forgot to let go of.

Here is the picture for the whole lesson. Think about how Usopp makes a part. He cuts it by eye and by feel, checks it against the gap, shaves a little more off, checks again. It works. He learns the wood while he does it, and he knows exactly why the finished part is the shape it is, because he made every decision on the way. And it takes him a morning. Now walk into Franky's dock. There is a jig for that cut. You clamp the stock in, you run the lathe, and the part comes out to the same tolerance every time, in minutes rather than hours, all day, without the drift that creeps into a tired hand. Nobody in that dock would go back to cutting by eye. But notice what the jig is and is not. The jig does not know what ship is being built. It does not know whether this part belongs to a keel or a railing. It holds an angle, and that is the entirety of its contribution. Which means if you set it to the wrong angle, with complete confidence, it will reproduce your mistake perfectly — a hundred identical wrong parts, produced faster than Usopp could have made one right one, all of them looking beautifully finished. The tool has removed the possibility of a random error and has done nothing whatsoever about a systematic one. So the shipwright's job does not disappear. It moves. It moves from cutting accurately to deciding what to cut, and to the thing Franky actually does all day, which is walking the dock and noticing that a run of parts is coming out subtly wrong before four hundred of them exist. That is exactly the trade you are making with PyTorch, and I want you to hold it clearly, because it is the difference between the people who get good at this and the people who stay stuck. Autograd holds the tolerance on the arithmetic. It will not make a sign error, ever, and that alone is worth the whole library. But it has no opinion about your loss function, your data, your evaluation split, or whether the number going down means the thing you care about is going up. And the speed cuts both ways: a wrong decision now costs you a thousand wrong parts instead of one, and it costs them in twenty minutes on a machine you are paying for by the hour. Everything you learned by hand in the last three lessons is what lets you walk the dock. The library is the jig. You are still the shipwright.

The last piece is the plumbing, and then you can read any model in the rest of this course. An nn dot Module is a class with two methods that matter. In init you build your layers; in forward you write the mathematics. And there is one piece of magic worth understanding rather than memorizing: anything you assign to self that is itself a Module or a Parameter gets registered automatically. Which means model dot parameters already contains every weight in the whole tree of submodules, in the right order, with no list for you to maintain — so handing it to an optimizer is one line and it cannot go out of date when you add a layer. The same registration is what lets model dot to device move the entire model onto a GPU in one call, and what lets state-dict save the whole thing. Note also that you call the model, not the forward method — model of x, not model dot forward of x. They look identical and are not: calling the object runs the hooks that several important features are built on. Then the feeding machinery, which is two objects with a clean division. A Dataset answers exactly two questions: how many examples are there, and give me example number i. That is all you implement. A DataLoader wraps a Dataset and handles everything tedious around it — collecting examples into batches, shuffling between epochs, and fetching in parallel worker processes so the GPU is not sitting idle waiting for your disk. Shuffle the training set, because a network trained on sorted labels learns the order. Never shuffle validation, because you want the same comparison every time. Now three mistakes that will genuinely cost you afternoons. First: model dot train and model dot eval. These are not decoration. They flip a switch that dropout and batch normalization read — dropout turns off in eval, and batch norm stops using this batch's statistics and starts using the running averages it accumulated during training. If you forget eval before validating, your validation numbers are worse than your training numbers for no reason at all, and people lose days chasing that. If you forget train afterwards, your model quietly stops regularizing. Second: save the state-dict, which is just a dictionary of tensors, rather than pickling the model object. Pickling stores a reference to your class, so the saved file breaks the moment you rename a file or move a directory, and it will break on someone else's machine. Save state-dict, rebuild the architecture in code, load the weights into it. Third, and this is the one to keep: the sanity check from the last lesson has not gone away just because you have a framework now. Before you train on anything real, take ten examples and check that your model can overfit them to a loss of nearly zero. It costs thirty seconds and it catches a wrong loss, a broken label, a frozen layer and a learning rate of zero — all of which look exactly like a model that is simply learning slowly.
rlhf-alignment: Last lesson ended on a sentence worth repeating: what comes out of pretraining is a base model, and a base model is not an assistant. Let me make that concrete, because until you have seen a base model's output the claim sounds like a technicality. Type what is the capital of Nepal into a raw base model and a very plausible continuation is: what is the capital of Bhutan? What is the capital of Sri Lanka? What is the largest city in Asia? It has produced a list of quiz questions, and it has done so because on the open web, a line that looks like a question is very often followed by more questions — worksheets, FAQs, forum threads, trivia pages. The model is not confused and it is not being difficult. It is doing precisely the thing it was trained to do, which is predict what text follows, and it is doing it well. The fault is in our expectation, not in the model. Notice carefully what is and is not missing. The knowledge is there — the model knows the answer, in the sense that the information is represented in its weights and the right prompt will extract it. The reasoning is there. The fluency is there. What is missing is the whole frame of being addressed by somebody who wants something: that a question is a request rather than a text pattern, that a response should answer rather than continue, that when several answers are all true one of them is more useful than the others, and that some requests should be declined. None of that is capability. All of it is behaviour. Which is good news, because behaviour turns out to be much cheaper to install than capability. Pretraining costs months and millions; the alignment stages cost a rounding error by comparison — thousands of examples rather than trillions of tokens, days rather than months. The whole difference between the raw artifact and something you can talk to is bought in that last, small step. There are two stages and they do different jobs. The first is supervised instruction tuning, which teaches the format: this is what a request looks like, this is what a response looks like, and the response comes after the request. The second is preference alignment, which teaches the choice: given two responses that are both well-formatted and both true, this is the one a person would rather have. The first stage makes the model usable. The second is what makes the difference between usable and good, and it is the more interesting half.

The first stage is the less glamorous one and it does most of the visible work. You assemble a dataset of pairs: an instruction, and a good response to that instruction. Summarize this article, and a good summary. Write a function that does this, and the function. Explain this concept to a beginner, and the explanation. Translate this, refuse this, reformat this. You want many task types, because you are teaching a general shape rather than a specific skill. Then you wrap each pair in the model's chat template — the role markers we met in the tokenization lesson — and train with exactly the same next-token loss that pretraining used. One important detail: mask the loss so that it is only computed on the response tokens. You do not want the model learning to generate plausible instructions; you want it learning to produce a response given one. That is the whole method. It is plain supervised fine-tuning, it uses machinery you have had since Part Three, and there is nothing clever in the algorithm. Everything difficult about this stage is in the data. And the most useful empirical result here is one that surprised people. The LIMA paper took a thousand examples — one thousand, written and curated carefully by hand, spread across a wide range of task types — and fine-tuned on those alone. The result was a better assistant than models trained on fifty thousand automatically collected examples. A fiftieth of the data, better outcome. Think about what that implies, because it is the theme of this whole part of the course. If a thousand examples suffice, then this stage is not teaching the model how to summarize or how to write code — a thousand examples is nowhere near enough to teach either. The ability was already in there from pretraining. What the thousand examples do is show the model which of its abilities to bring forward, and in what shape. Instruction tuning is a surfacing operation, not a teaching one, and that is why quality and diversity of examples matter so much more than quantity. After this stage you have something recognizably useful. It answers questions instead of continuing them, it respects formats, it holds a multi-turn conversation, it stops when it is done. And it has one characteristic flaw that motivates the next stage: it is uniformly confident. Every example it was trained on was a good answer, confidently given. Nothing in the dataset showed it what to do when it does not know, when the request is ambiguous, when the honest answer is a hedge, or when the right response is to decline. It has learned the shape of a good answer and applies that shape everywhere, including where a good answer does not exist. Fixing that needs a signal about which of two answers is better, and that is a different kind of data.

The second stage exists because of a problem that has no direct solution. We want the model to be helpful, honest and harmless. None of those can be written as a loss function — you cannot differentiate helpfulness, and nobody can specify it precisely enough to code. But here is the observation the whole field is built on: while people cannot define quality, people are quite reliable at comparing. Show someone two answers to the same question and ask which is better, and you get a consistent signal, from annotators who could never have written a specification. So you collect comparisons rather than scores. Absolute ratings drift — one person's seven is another's five, and the same person's seven drifts over an afternoon. Pairwise preferences are stable. Classic RLHF then has three steps. You already have the instruction-tuned model from stage one. Step one: sample several responses per prompt and have humans rank them, giving you a dataset of preferred and rejected pairs. Step two: train a reward model — usually the same architecture with a scalar head — to predict which of two responses a human would pick. That reward model is a learned stand-in for a person, and it is what lets you get a score for a response nobody has ever looked at. Step three: optimize the language model to produce responses the reward model scores highly, using PPO, a reinforcement learning algorithm. And there is a term in that optimization doing essential work: a KL divergence penalty that pulls the model back toward the instruction-tuned model it started from. Without it, the policy discovers that the reward model is a model, with quirks and blind spots, and drifts into whatever maximizes it — which in practice is degenerate text that scores beautifully and reads like nothing a person would write. The KL term says: get a higher reward, but do not become a different model to do it. Now, this pipeline works and it produced ChatGPT, and it is also genuinely painful. Three models in memory at once, a reinforcement learning loop that is famously unstable, and a pile of hyperparameters that interact. So the practical story has a second act. Direct Preference Optimization observed that the reward model and the RL step can be collapsed algebraically. If you write down what the optimal policy under a KL-constrained reward objective looks like, you can rearrange it into a simple loss over the preference pairs themselves — one that raises the likelihood of the preferred response and lowers the likelihood of the rejected one, relative to the reference model. No reward model. No sampling loop. No PPO. It is a supervised loss you can train with the same code as stage one, it is stable, and on most benchmarks it performs comparably. That is why nearly every open-weight model released recently is DPO-tuned or one of its variants. The insight to keep is not the algebra: it is that the expensive part was never the algorithm. It is the preference data, and both methods need exactly the same data.

Luffy is the clearest illustration of this distinction I know, and once you see it the whole lesson holds together. He arrives on the ship with more raw capability than anyone on it. That is not in question and it never becomes the problem. What he also arrives with is a set of defaults that would get everybody killed: charge in first, take every fight offered, ignore what the sky is doing, announce the plan to the person you are about to fight, eat before checking whether the food is trapped. Enormous power, and no judgement whatsoever about when to deploy it. That is a base model after pretraining. Now watch what the crew actually does over the next several hundred episodes, because the negative is as important as the positive. They never train his strength. There is no arc where Nami makes Luffy punch harder — she could not, and it would not help. What they do is correct choices, one at a time, in the moment. Not now. Not that one. Go around. Wait for Zoro. And notice the form the correction takes, because it is exactly the shape of the data we just described. It is almost never an abstract rule, because nobody can write down the rule for when Luffy should charge in — the crew certainly cannot, and they have tried. It is comparative and situated: this option, not that one, here. That is a preference pair, and it is collected the same way, by someone who knows a better answer when they see it and could not have specified it in advance. Then the part of the analogy I like most, because it maps onto the piece of RLHF that seems most abstract. Nami cannot be standing next to Luffy at every decision. So what he actually ends up carrying is not her corrections — it is an internalized model of what Nami would say. He pauses, briefly, and something in him scores the option the way she would have. That is the reward model exactly: a learned stand-in for a human judge, trained on their past comparisons, available to evaluate situations the human has never seen. And the crew's judgement generalizes to islands Nami has never visited, which is precisely what you need a reward model for. Finally, the constraint, and it is the most important part. Through all of that correction, Luffy stays Luffy. If the crew succeeded in making him cautious, they would have destroyed the thing that makes them survive anything at all — the willingness to attack a problem that a sensible person would walk away from. The corrections are meant to shape when he charges, not to stop him charging. That is the KL penalty, and it is not a technical footnote. Over-optimize a model against a preference signal and you get something that is agreeable, hedging, refuses reasonable requests, and has quietly lost the capability you were paying for. An aligned Luffy who never charges in is not an improvement. He is a different and much less useful crew member.

Let us finish with the failures, because they are predictable, they are visible in models you use every day, and recognizing them is most of what this lesson is for. The central one is reward hacking, and it follows directly from Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Your reward model is a proxy for human preference, and it is imperfect, so optimizing hard against it optimizes the gaps. The examples are concrete and familiar. Human annotators mildly prefer longer, more thorough-looking answers, so the reward model learns that length correlates with quality, so the policy learns to pad — and you get four paragraphs where one sentence would do. Annotators prefer confident phrasing, so hedging is trained out, including in exactly the cases where a hedge was the honest answer. Formatted output with headings and bullet points scores better, so everything arrives with headings and bullet points, whether or not the content has structure. None of these were intended by anyone; all of them are the optimizer finding the cheapest route to a higher score. Sycophancy is the same failure wearing a human face, and it deserves naming separately because it is the one that damages trust. People giving feedback prefer being agreed with. So the model learns to agree — to soften a correct answer when the user pushes back, to adopt the premise of a leading question, to praise a bad idea. A model that folds under mild disagreement is in some ways worse than one that was simply wrong, because you cannot use its confidence as a signal about anything. Then the alignment tax. Aligned models frequently score slightly lower on raw capability benchmarks than the base models they were built from. Some of that is real — the KL constraint and the preference data genuinely narrow the distribution. Usually it is a trade worth making, because a slightly less capable model you can actually direct is more useful than a more capable one you cannot. But you should know you are paying it, and it is why serious evaluations report base and aligned numbers side by side. Two closing notes. Constitutional AI addresses the fact that human feedback is the bottleneck — it is slow, expensive, and inconsistent across annotators. Instead, write down a set of principles, and have a model critique and revise its own outputs against them, generating the preference data automatically. That is RLAIF, and it scales, and it moves the hard question rather than removing it: from who is annotating to who wrote the principles. Which brings me to the last thing, and it is the thing to carry. Alignment is not the same as safety, and it is not a solved problem with a technical answer. It is a procedure for fitting a model to a set of preferences, and every deployed model embeds a specific set, chosen by a specific organization, reflecting specific judgements about what is helpful and what should be refused. Those choices are frequently reasonable and they are never neutral. Knowing that a model's manners were fitted, by someone, to something, is the correct way to hold every aligned model you will use.
self-attention: The last lesson ended with attention as a repair bolted onto a recurrent encoder-decoder, and with the question of what happens if you remove the recurrence and keep only the attention. This lesson is the answer, and the whole thing turns on one word. In the seq2seq setting, attention was cross-attention: two different sequences, with the decoder looking across at the encoder. The source sentence was one thing and the translation was another, and attention was the bridge between them. Self-attention points exactly the same machinery at a single sequence. Every token in a sentence looks at every token in that same sentence — including itself — and rebuilds its own representation out of what it finds there. No second sequence. No bridge. The sentence attending to itself. That sounds like a small change and it is the whole architecture, so let me say what it buys, because it is precisely the thing we said was missing at the end of the embeddings lesson. A static embedding gave the word bank one vector, forever, a compromise between the river and the money. Self-attention fixes this in the most direct way possible. The token bank arrives at the layer carrying its static embedding, it looks at the other tokens in the sentence, it finds river sitting three positions away with a high relevance score, and the vector that leaves the layer is a blend that includes river. In a different sentence it finds account instead, and a different vector leaves. Same input embedding, different output, because the output is computed from the company. That is a contextual embedding, and it is produced not by storing more vectors but by computing one on the spot. Here is the example everybody uses, and it is worth walking through because it shows the mechanism doing something no earlier architecture could. Take the sentence: the animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired. What does it refer to? A human reads that instantly — the animal, because streets do not get tired. Now change one word: the animal didn't cross the street because it was too wide. Now it is the street. Nothing about the position of the word changed; the referent flipped because of a single adjective at the far end of the sentence. A bag-of-words model cannot represent the question. An RNN would have to carry the answer forward through every intervening word. Self-attention does it directly: the token it computes relevance against every other token, finds a high score on animal, and the vector for it is literally assembled partly out of the vector for animal. The resolution is not inferred afterwards by some separate module. It happens inside the representation, in one step, because that is what the layer does.

Now the machinery, and it rests on one idea that is worth getting exactly right, because everything else is arithmetic around it. Every token, before anything else happens, projects its vector three separate ways using three separate learned matrices. The three results are called the query, the key and the value, and they are three different roles the same token plays at the same time. The query is what this token is looking for. If the token is the word it, its query is something like: I am a pronoun and I need a noun that could be tired. The key is what this token offers to anyone looking. If the token is animal, its key advertises: I am a living thing, singular, could be a subject. And the value is what this token actually contributes if it does get chosen — the content that will be mixed into somebody else's representation. Now, why three and not one? Because relevance and content are different questions, and collapsing them costs you. The decision about who should attend to whom is made by comparing queries against keys. The material that then flows is the values. Keeping them separate means a token can be highly relevant for one reason and contribute something quite different — the key can say I am the subject of this clause while the value carries what the subject actually is. If you used the same vector for both, every token would have to advertise itself using exactly the content it plans to hand over, and the model would lose the ability to be found for one reason and useful for another. The cleanest way to hold this is as a soft dictionary lookup, and the terminology is borrowed directly from that. In an ordinary hash table you have a query, you compare it against the keys, exactly one matches, and you get back that one value. Attention is the same shape with the hardness removed: you compare the query against every key, you get a score against each of them rather than a single match, you turn those scores into weights, and you return a blend of all the values in proportion. Nothing is selected and nothing is discarded — everything contributes a little, and the relevant things contribute a lot. That softness is exactly what makes it differentiable, which is what makes it trainable at all. One last piece of bookkeeping that ties this back to the previous lesson. In self-attention, all three projections are computed from the same input sequence, which is what the word self is doing in the name. In the cross-attention we met in seq2seq, the query comes from the decoder and the keys and values come from the encoder — the decoder asks and the source answers. It is the identical computation with different inputs, which is why one implementation serves both, and why the encoder-decoder transformer in the next lesson does not need any new machinery to connect its two halves.

Here is the whole thing in one line, and then we will take it apart. Attention of Q, K and V equals softmax of Q times K transpose over the square root of d-k, all multiplied by V. Four steps. Step one: Q times K transpose. Q holds one query per token as its rows, K holds one key per token, so this product computes the dot product of every query with every key at once, producing an n-by-n matrix of raw scores where entry i, j says how much token i cares about token j. Step two: divide by the square root of d-k. Step three: softmax each row, so every token's scores become weights that are positive and sum to one. Step four: multiply by V, which for each token takes the weighted average of all the value vectors. Four matrix operations, and every one of them is a GPU's favourite instruction. Now the scaling factor, because it is the one part that looks arbitrary and is not. The dot product of two d-dimensional vectors is a sum of d terms, so its typical magnitude grows with d — for a five-hundred-dimensional key, dot products are large numbers. Feed large numbers into a softmax and it saturates: it becomes almost one-hot, putting essentially all the weight on a single position. And a saturated softmax has almost no gradient, so learning through it stops. Dividing by the square root of d-k rescales the scores so their variance stays around one regardless of dimension. It is one symbol in the formula and it is the difference between the architecture training and not training. Next, multi-head attention, which is what actually gets used. Instead of computing one attention over the full dimension, split the dimension into h pieces — eight or twelve or ninety-six, depending on the model — run a separate, independent attention on each piece with its own Q, K and V matrices, then concatenate the results and pass them through one more learned projection. The total compute is roughly the same, because each head works in a smaller space. What you gain is specialization. A single attention has to commit to one notion of relevance and average everything through it. Eight heads can hold eight different notions at once, and when people examined trained models they found exactly that: heads that follow syntactic dependencies, heads that link pronouns to their referents, heads that attend to the previous token, heads that seem to do nothing at all and can be pruned. It is an ensemble of readings computed in parallel, and it is cheap. Finally, masking, which is a small implementation detail that does something enormous. Before the softmax, you can add a matrix of negative infinities to the scores, and any position you mark that way gets a weight of exactly zero. Two uses. A padding mask hides the filler tokens added to make a batch rectangular. And a causal mask hides the future: for token i, everything at position greater than i is masked out, so a token can only attend to itself and what came before it. That one triangular matrix is the entire difference between a model that reads a whole sentence at once and a model that can generate the next word — it is why BERT and GPT can share an architecture and behave completely differently.

Picture the crew before they go ashore somewhere new. Everyone is on deck, and the striking thing about that scene, if you look at it as a computation, is that every single person is doing three things simultaneously. Each of them is holding a question they need answered — Zoro wants to know what he will be fighting, Sanji wants to know what food is on the island, Nami wants to know what the weather is going to do. Each of them is also, in effect, wearing a badge that says what they are expert in: navigator, doctor, archaeologist, cook. And each of them is carrying actual knowledge they would hand over if asked. Question, badge, knowledge. Query, key, value. Same three roles, held at the same time, by everybody. Now watch how an answer actually gets formed, because this is the part people expect to work differently. Luffy asks whether it is safe to go in. He does not turn to exactly one person and take their answer whole. He reads the room — he weighs Nami's badge heavily because weather is most of the question, Robin's somewhat because she knows what the ruins mean, Chopper's a little because there was a rumour about a fever, and Usopp's not at all on this particular question. And what he ends up believing is a blend, in those proportions. That is the weighted sum, and notice that nothing was selected and nothing was thrown away. Usopp contributed a very small amount rather than zero. That softness is the difference between attention and a lookup table, and it is what makes the whole thing trainable. Now the detail that justifies having three roles instead of two, because it is easy to miss and it is the real content of the slide. Chopper's badge says doctor. That is what gets him consulted. But the thing he actually says is not the word doctor — it is a specific fact about the fever, the incubation period, whether it is airborne. The badge is how you get found; the knowledge is what you contribute. They are different objects, deliberately. If the crew could only advertise themselves using the exact content they were about to say, nobody could be consulted for a reason and then supply something unexpected, and half the value of a council would be gone. Keys and values are separate for the same reason. And one last observation about that deck. It is not one conversation. Down at one end Nami and Franky are talking about the approach and the current; in the middle Zoro and Sanji are arguing about who takes the left flank; over there Chopper is asking Robin about the writing on the rock. Several independent conversations, running in parallel, over the same group of people, each one weighting the crew differently — and then all of it is pulled together into one decision about what the crew does. That is multi-head attention exactly: the same tokens, read several different ways at once, concatenated and projected into a single output. Not a bigger conversation. Several conversations, and then a decision.

Every architecture buys something and pays for something, and it is worth being just as precise about the bill as about the benefit. Look again at what the first step computes: Q times K transpose, every query against every key. For a sequence of n tokens, that is n squared scores. Not n. n squared. And you need the whole matrix in memory to run the softmax over it. So both compute and memory grow with the square of the sequence length, and doubling your context does not double the cost, it quadruples it. Put numbers on that, because the numbers are what make it real. A thousand tokens gives you a million scores, per head, per layer — with twelve heads and twelve layers that is a hundred and forty-four million numbers just for the attention matrices, and it is fine. Ten thousand tokens gives you a hundred million per head per layer. A hundred thousand tokens gives you ten billion. That is why the context window is a headline feature that companies advertise and compete on rather than a parameter you set to whatever you like, and it is why the recurrent model's linear cost in length was not nothing — we gave up a genuinely good property to get parallelism and short paths. Now, what is actually done about it, and there are two different families with different philosophies. The first attacks the memory, and it is the more important one. FlashAttention observes that the real bottleneck is not the arithmetic — GPUs have arithmetic to spare — it is writing that enormous n-by-n matrix out to slow high-bandwidth memory and reading it back. So it restructures the computation into tiles that fit in the small, extremely fast SRAM on the chip, computes the softmax incrementally as it goes, and never materializes the full matrix at all. The mathematics is unchanged — bit for bit the same result — and it is several times faster and uses a fraction of the memory. That is why it went from a paper to being in everything within about a year, and it is a good lesson in its own right: sometimes the win is in how you move the data, not in the algorithm. The second family changes the mathematics to avoid the square. Sparse attention lets each token attend only to a chosen subset. Sliding-window attention restricts it to a local neighbourhood, sometimes with a few global tokens that everyone can see. Linear attention rewrites the operation so it never forms the n-by-n matrix in the first place. All of these are approximations — they give up some exactness — and at very long context that is obviously the right trade, because exact attention over a million tokens is not a thing you can afford. But I want to end on the balance, because it is favourable. In exchange for a quadratic bill you get both of the things the recurrent network could not give you. Every position is computed in parallel, so the hardware is finally saturated and training on enormous corpora becomes practical. And the path between any two positions is exactly one step, no matter how far apart they are, so nothing fades. Quadratic cost is a problem you can throw engineering at, and the field has. Sequential dependency and fading memory are problems you cannot.
seq2seq-attention: Everything we have built so far turns a sequence into one thing: a label, a number, a class. Translation does not have that shape. You read a sentence in Nepali and you write a sentence in English, and crucially the output length is not determined by the input length — a five word source can be a nine word target, and you do not know which until you are most of the way through writing it. Summarization has the same shape, so does question answering, so does code generation. Sequence in, different sequence out, lengths unrelated. That needs a new architecture, and the one the field settled on in twenty fourteen is the encoder-decoder, and it is exactly what the name says. Take one recurrent network — the encoder — and feed it the source sentence, one token at a time, with no output at all. You are not asking it to produce anything; you are just letting it read. When it reaches the end, its final hidden state is a vector that summarizes, in some learned way, everything it just read. That vector is called the context vector, and it is handed to a second network — the decoder — as its starting state. The decoder's job is to generate. And generation works differently from anything you have written so far, because it is a loop rather than a single forward pass. You start it with a special start-of-sequence token. It produces a distribution over the vocabulary, you pick a word, and then — this is the important part — you feed that word back in as the next input, along with the updated hidden state. It produces the next word. And so on, until it produces a special end-of-sequence token, at which point you stop. Notice what that gives you for free: the model chooses its own output length, by deciding when to emit the end token. Nothing in the architecture had to be told how long the answer is. Now, training, and there is a genuine problem here worth understanding. At the start of training the decoder is terrible. If you let it feed its own outputs back in, then it produces a wrong first word, and the second word is now conditioned on a wrong first word, and the whole sequence derails, and the gradient signal is mostly noise about a sentence that has nothing to do with the target. Learning is glacial. The standard fix is called teacher forcing: during training, ignore what the model actually predicted and feed in the true previous token from the target sentence instead. Now every step is conditioned on a correct history, the model learns the local mapping quickly, and training converges. It is a good trick and it is what everyone uses. But it introduces a mismatch you should be able to name: during training the model only ever sees perfect history, and at inference it only ever sees its own history, mistakes included. That gap is called exposure bias, and it is why a generated sequence can start well and then wander off — the model is in a state it never encountered while learning. There are fixes, they are partial, and it remains a real property of every autoregressive generator, including the very large ones.

Now the flaw, and I want to state it precisely because the fix follows directly from the statement. In the encoder-decoder as described, everything the decoder will ever know about the source sentence arrives through one vector of fixed size. Five hundred and twelve numbers, say. The encoder reads the whole source, compresses it into those five hundred and twelve numbers, and then the source is gone — the decoder never sees it again. It generates the entire translation from that summary alone. For a short sentence this is fine. Five hundred and twelve numbers is plenty of room for six words. But the size does not grow with the input. A fifty-word paragraph with three clauses, two names and a negation gets exactly the same five hundred and twelve numbers, and it does not fit. Something has to be discarded, and the network has no way to know in advance which parts the decoder is going to need. This is the information bottleneck, and it is not a subtle theoretical worry — it was measured, immediately, and the shape of the result is dramatic. Translation quality holds up well to about twenty tokens and then falls off a cliff. Not a gentle decline as sentences get longer, which is what you would expect from a task simply getting harder. A collapse. That shape is the signature of a hard capacity limit being hit, and it told everybody that the problem was structural rather than a matter of more training or more data. There is a second, related symptom worth naming, because it explains what the failures actually look like. The encoder's final hidden state was, by construction, most recently updated by the last few tokens it read. Everything earlier has been passed through the recurrence dozens of times and partially overwritten. So the context vector is systematically biased toward the end of the source sentence, and in a long input, the beginning is faint. Translations lose their opening clauses. Summaries forget the first paragraph. This is the fading-memory problem from the RNN lesson, showing up in a new place. Now, the obvious question, and it is worth walking through because the answer is instructive: why not just make the vector bigger? Because it does not solve anything. Whatever size you choose is fixed, and there is always a longer input that overflows it — you have moved the cliff, not removed it. And a very large context vector is wasteful and harder to train on short sentences, where most of it is empty. You cannot buy your way out of a structural constraint with more numbers. The fix has to change the structure. And the change, when it came in twenty fifteen, is almost embarrassingly simple to state: stop forcing everything through one vector. Keep all of the encoder's hidden states — one per source token — and let the decoder look back at whichever ones it needs, at each step of generation. That is attention.

Here is the mechanism, and it is worth going slowly because you will meet this exact computation in every model for the rest of the course. Change one thing about the encoder: instead of throwing its intermediate states away, keep all of them. One hidden state per source token, so a twenty-word sentence leaves twenty vectors on the table. The source is no longer summarized; it is still there, laid out. Now the decoder. At each step of generation, before it produces the next word, it does three small things. First, scoring: take the decoder's current hidden state — which represents roughly what am I about to write — and compare it against every one of the encoder states, producing one number per source position that says how relevant this source word is to what I am doing right now. Second, softmax: push those scores through a softmax so they become positive and sum to one. You now have a set of weights across the source sentence — a distribution of attention. Third, the weighted sum: multiply each encoder state by its weight and add them all up. The result is a single vector, the same shape as before, and the decoder uses it exactly as it used the old context vector. So what has actually changed? The context vector is no longer computed once. It is recomputed at every single output step, and each time it is a different blend of the source. When the decoder is writing the subject of the sentence, the weights concentrate on the source subject; when it moves to the verb, the weights move too. The decoder gets a fresh, task-specific view of the source for each word it writes. That is the entire idea, and it dissolves both problems at once: nothing has to be compressed into a fixed budget because the whole source is available, and the beginning of a long sentence is exactly as reachable as the end because it is one weighted sum away rather than three hundred recurrence steps away. Two things are worth emphasizing before we move on. The first is that none of this is hand-designed. Nobody writes rules about which source words matter for which target words. The scoring function is a small learned network, trained by the same translation loss as everything else, and the alignment behaviour appears because it is useful for getting the translation right. The second is a gift nobody planned. Because the attention weights are just numbers, you can plot them: source words along one axis, generated words along the other, brightness for weight. And when people did that in twenty fifteen, they saw a word alignment — a visible diagonal, with clean off-diagonal jumps exactly where the two languages reorder. You could see the model looking at la maison while it wrote the house. After years of neural networks being opaque, here was a model that showed its work, and that legibility is a large part of why attention was adopted so fast.

Ohara is the right place to end this, because Robin is a translator and translation is exactly the task, and the two designs we have just compared are two different scholars. Imagine the first one. She stands in front of the Poneglyph and reads the entire inscription carefully, top to bottom. Then she closes her eyes, turns away from the stone, and recites the translation from memory. For a short inscription this is genuinely impressive and it works. For a wall of glyphs it does not, and notice what specifically fails: not the whole thing, but the beginning. By the time she is reciting the ending, the opening lines have been crowded out by everything that came after them. That is the fixed context vector, and that is the recency bias, and if you have ever tried to summarize a long document from memory you know the feeling exactly. Now watch what Robin actually does, because it is completely ordinary and it is the entire mechanism. She keeps the stone in front of her. She writes one line of translation, and while writing it, her eyes go back to the particular glyphs that line came from. Then she writes the next line, and her eyes move to a different part of the stone. She is not holding the inscription in her head at all — she is holding a place in her work, and looking up whatever the current place requires. She might glance at one glyph three separate times, for three different lines, because it matters to all three. And that is attention, with nothing lost in the translation of the metaphor. The stone still standing there is the encoder states, kept rather than discarded. The glance is the scoring step, asking which part of this do I need for what I am writing now. What she is looking at in this moment is the context vector for this word — recomputed, every line, from the same unchanged source. And the fading problem simply does not arise, because the beginning of the inscription is as available at the end of the work as it was at the start. It never had to survive being carried; it never moved. There is one more thing in the picture, and it is the gift I mentioned. Suppose you sat beside Robin and could not read either the glyphs or her handwriting. You could still watch her eyes. You would see that when she wrote this line she looked there, and when she wrote the next she looked somewhere else, and from her eyes alone you could build a map between the stone and the page. You would learn something real about the structure of the translation without understanding a single word of it. That is what an attention map is, and it is why this family of models is the most inspectable thing in deep learning. Everything before it kept its reasoning inside its weights. This one looks at things, and you can see where.

Let us finish by placing this properly in the story, because the twenty fifteen paper is not the famous one and it is important to understand why. Attention, as Bahdanau and colleagues introduced it, was a repair. The architecture was still an encoder-decoder made of recurrent networks; attention was bolted onto the side to fix the bottleneck. And it worked — long-sentence translation stopped collapsing, quality jumped, and within a couple of years every serious sequence-to-sequence system had it. But look at what it did not fix. Underneath the attention, the encoder and the decoder were still RNNs, and an RNN still processes one token at a time, each step waiting for the last. So the second complaint from the CNN and RNN lesson — the one about hardware, about a GPU with thousands of cores sitting almost idle — was completely untouched. You had a model that could now remember a long sentence and still could not be trained quickly on a long corpus. So the question that produced the next architecture is, in hindsight, the obvious one, and it is worth sitting with for a moment because this is what good research often looks like. Attention is doing the real work of connecting positions. The recurrence is expensive, it is the thing forcing everything to be sequential, and now that attention exists, what exactly is it still contributing? And the answer, tested in twenty seventeen, was: not enough to keep. Take the recurrence out. Keep only attention. That is the transformer, and the title of the paper — Attention Is All You Need — is a literal description of the experiment. Two things fall out of that removal immediately, and they are the two complaints answered at once. First, with no step-to-step dependency, every position in the sequence can be computed simultaneously. The whole sentence goes through the model in parallel, the graphics card is finally doing what it was built for, and training on enormous corpora becomes practical — which is the door to every large model that followed. Second, the path length between any two positions is now one. Not three hundred, not ten. Position one and position five hundred are a single attention step apart, so distance stops mattering at all. There is a cost, and it is worth naming so the picture is honest. Recurrence was doing one useful thing quietly: it knew what order the words came in, because it read them in order. Remove it and attention, which is just a weighted sum, has no idea whether a word was first or last — shuffle the input and the output is unchanged. So order has to be added back deliberately, as positional encodings, and that is one of the first things the next lesson deals with. But that is a detail to be engineered, not a wall. Everything from here to the end of this course — BERT, GPT, the model you will build in the code lab, and the largest systems running in the world today — is this slide, scaled up.
statistics-mle: The crew has captured three Marine patrol ships, and stamped on each hull is a serial number: No. forty-two, No. one-seventeen, No. one-eighty-nine. Nami wants to know how big the whole Marine fleet in this sea is — but nobody can sail out and count the population, so Robin must reason from the sample. That gap between the sample you can see and the population you care about is the whole subject of statistics. The population is the entire world you care about — all emails ever, all future users, the whole Marine fleet — and the sample is the finite dataset you actually have, the three captured hulls. Every dataset in machine learning is a sample, which means every model you ever train is a statistical inference across that gap, whether you admit it or not. An estimator is a formula that turns a sample into a guess about the population: the sample mean x-bar estimates the true mean mu, and a trained model's weights estimate the true input-to-output relationship. Estimators have quality properties you must name. Bias asks does it aim at the right target on average — the expected value of the estimator minus the truth. Variance asks how much does it wobble from sample to sample. You met this pair informally with mini-batches, and Part Two makes it the master trade-off of all of machine learning. Here is one concrete classic so that bias is never abstract: the naive variance estimator, one-over-n times the sum of x-i-minus-x-bar squared, is biased — it is systematically too small, because x-bar was itself fit to the very same sample and therefore sits closer to the data than the true mu does. Dividing by n-minus-one instead of n fixes it, and that is Bessel's correction, the mysterious ddof-equals-one you see in NumPy. But do not memorize the fix; remember the mechanism, because it is the most important sentence in this lesson: anything fit to a sample looks better on that sample than on the world. That single sentence, scaled up from variance to a billion-parameter model, is overfitting.

Suppose the fleet had a thousand ships, Robin says. Then three random captures would probably include some high numbers — the odds that all three fall below one-ninety are one-ninety-over-a-thousand, cubed, about zero-point-seven percent, so our observations would be a bizarre coincidence. Now suppose the fleet has exactly one-eighty-nine ships — then numbers like ours are perfectly typical. Under which fleet size is what we actually saw most probable? That question — rank all the hypotheses by how well they explain the observed sample — is maximum likelihood estimation. You have data, and a family of models with a knob theta, and MLE says pick the theta under which your observed data would have been most probable. Formally, theta-hat is the argmax over theta of the probability of the data given theta, which we rewrite as the argmax of the sum of log-probabilities of each data point. We maximize the log rather than the raw likelihood for two reasons: it does not change the argmax, since log is increasing, but it turns products of tiny numbers into sums, which is kind both to the algebra and to floating point. Here is the coin example, fully worked. You flip ten times and see seven heads. The model: heads with probability p. The likelihood is p-to-the-seven times one-minus-p-to-the-three, and its log is seven log-p plus three log-one-minus-p. Differentiate using last lesson's tool and set it to zero: seven-over-p minus three-over-one-minus-p equals zero, which gives p-hat equals zero-point-seven. The intuitive answer, now derived rather than assumed — and the exact same calculus works when theta is a billion weights instead of one number. Now the payoff that reorganizes everything you will learn after this. Assume regression with Gaussian noise on the errors, and the log-likelihood of each point becomes minus the residual squared over two-sigma-squared, plus a constant — so maximizing it is exactly minimizing the mean squared error. MSE is not a convention handed down from nowhere; it is maximum likelihood wearing a work uniform. For classification, the model outputs a probability per class, and maximizing the log-probability of the true labels is exactly minimizing cross-entropy — same story. And LLM pretraining in Part Six maximizes the sum of log-probability of each next token given its context, over trillions of tokens. GPT's training objective is literally Robin's coin derivation at cosmic scale.

Maximum likelihood has a known and dangerous failure mode: with little data, it chases noise. Flip a coin just twice and see two heads, and MLE says p-hat equals one-point-zero — the coin can never land tails, which is absurd on the evidence of two flips. The Bayesian fix is to bring a prior, a belief about the parameter before you saw any data. Instead of maximizing the probability of the data given theta, maximize the probability of the data given theta times the prior probability of theta — that is MAP estimation, maximum a posteriori. Take the log and it reads: argmax over theta of log-likelihood plus log-prior, which is identically argmin over theta of loss plus penalty. Now watch which priors give which penalties, because this is the whole secret. A zero-mean Gaussian prior on the weights contributes a penalty of lambda times the norm of w squared — that is L2 regularization, also called weight decay. A Laplace prior contributes lambda times the L1 norm of w, which pushes weights to exactly zero and gives you sparsity. Robin adds the same footnote to her fleet estimate: if the fleet were truly one-eighty-nine ships, capturing exactly the maximum serial would be a little lucky, so a wise estimator nudges above the largest serial seen — that upward nudge is a prior doing its work, the same shape as adding one imaginary head and one imaginary tail to the coin to keep p away from the absurd boundary. So when Part Two adds plus-lambda-norm-w-squared to a loss and calls it regularization, you will know exactly what it secretly is: a prior belief that weights should be small, keeping the fit from chasing noise in a small sample. One equation, two philosophies — the frequentist calls it a penalty, the Bayesian calls it a prior — and the same line of code.

Two statistical ideas close this lesson, and both are interview staples. First, correlation versus causation. The Pearson correlation coefficient r, ranging from minus one to plus one, measures the linear co-movement of two variables, and it is genuinely useful — but it is famously not causation. Ice-cream sales correlate with drownings, not because ice cream drowns people, but because summer causes both. Models trained on observational data learn correlations, full stop; a model will happily learn that hospital visits predict death, and other confounded patterns, because it only sees what moves together. Knowing when a correlation actually supports an intervention — if we change X, will Y move — requires either a real experiment, an A-B test, or careful causal reasoning. Sheldon shows the difference: he does not merely observe that Penny is quieter on chocolate days and declare victory, because that correlation could mean anything, maybe she buys chocolate on already-calm days. Instead he runs an intervention, handing her a chocolate every time she behaves correctly, and her behavior shifts measurably — by controlling the variable rather than passively recording it, he isolates the causal arrow, to Leonard's horror. The one-sentence answer interviewers respect: my model predicts well under the data distribution it saw, but acting on it changes that distribution. Second, the train-test split, restated as statistics rather than convention. Evaluating on training data measures only how well you fit this particular sample, and by Bessel's lesson it always does so optimistically. Evaluating on held-out data estimates performance on the population, which is the thing you actually care about.
