And here is the trap: if you touch the test set repeatedly while making decisions — choosing hyperparameters, architectures, when to stop — it silently becomes training data, and your estimate inflates. That is why serious work uses three splits, train, validation, and test, and touches the test set exactly once, at the very end. This is not ritual or Kaggle superstition; it is unbiased estimation, the same principle as Bessel's correction operating at the scale of your whole pipeline.

Step back and Robin's hull numbers have made maximum likelihood a scene you can replay forever: line up the candidate worlds, ask which one makes the observed sample least surprising, and pick the winner — that is MLE, and it is not a toy. The exact same reasoning famously ran the German tank problem in the Second World War, where Allied statisticians estimated German tank production from captured serial numbers at about two hundred seventy a month while intelligence guessed fourteen hundred, and the statisticians were right. Three things to carry forward. First, the master correspondence that reorganizes the rest of the course: every loss function is secretly a likelihood. MSE is Gaussian-noise MLE, cross-entropy is categorical MLE, and mean absolute error is Laplace-noise MLE — which is precisely why MAE is robust to outliers, because the Laplace distribution has heavy tails and does not panic about them. So when you pick a loss, you are silently assuming a noise model, and the question should I use MSE or MAE becomes an answerable one about your data: how heavy are my outliers? Second, always work in log-space. The probability of a thousand specific coin flips is about ten-to-the-minus-three-hundred, which underflows to exactly zero-point-zero in float64 and destroys all information, whereas the log keeps it as a tame minus six-ninety. That is why PyTorch gives you log-softmax and negative-log-likelihood loss — compute in log-space, always. Third, report uncertainty, not bare point estimates. Ninety percent accuracy on a hundred test examples is really a range, roughly eighty-four to ninety-six percent, from the binomial standard error, and that is worth saying out loud before you ship a conclusion. The general workhorse is the bootstrap: resample your test set with replacement a thousand times, recompute the metric each time, and take the two-point-five to ninety-seven-point-five percentiles — no formula needed, works for F-one, AUC, anything. Telling an interviewer you would bootstrap the evaluation is an instant seniority signal, because it shows you know a single accuracy number is itself a sample statistic with its own wobble.
text-as-numbers: Every model we have built so far eats vectors of numbers. Text is not that. So before any of it can touch a document, we need an honest way to turn words into numbers, and the first one is called bag-of-words. Here is the recipe. Go through your whole collection and build a vocabulary of every distinct word — say fifty thousand of them. Now each document becomes a vector fifty thousand long, where each position holds how many times that word appeared in that document. That is the entire idea, and the name is precise: you have tipped the document into a bag and shaken it. All order is gone. 'Zoro fought Mihawk' and 'Mihawk fought Zoro' produce byte-for-byte identical vectors, even though one of them is a rather different story. That is an enormous loss of information, and here is the uncomfortable fact that made this technique dominate for thirty years: it is very often enough. If your question is what a document is about, which words appear matters far more than the order they appear in. A document containing 'sword', 'duel' and 'wound' is about a fight, and you did not need the grammar to know it. Where it fails is anything where order carries the meaning — sentiment, negation, sarcasm. In bag-of-words, 'not good' and 'good' are near neighbours, which is a catastrophe for review classification. Two practical notes. First, these vectors are enormous and almost entirely zero: fifty thousand columns, of which perhaps eighty are non-zero for any given document. Never store them densely. Store the positions and values only — a sparse representation — and both your memory use and your dot products drop by three orders of magnitude. Every serious text library does this by default. Second, you can buy back a little of the lost order cheaply. Index adjacent pairs of words as well as single words, so that 'not good' becomes a feature in its own right. These are called n-grams, and they genuinely help — but the vocabulary explodes combinatorially, so cap it at the most frequent few hundred thousand. It is a dial you trade against, not a free win.

Raw counts have an obvious problem, and fixing it gives us the workhorse of classical text retrieval. The most common words in any document are 'the', 'of', 'and', 'is'. They will dominate every vector, and they distinguish absolutely nothing, because they are present in every document ever written. What you actually want to weight heavily is the opposite: words that are rare across the corpus but frequent in this particular document. That is TF-IDF, term frequency times inverse document frequency. The formula is: the count of the word in this document, multiplied by the log of N over df, where N is the total number of documents and df is how many of them contain the word at all. Look at what that log term does. A word appearing in every document has df equal to N, so N over df is one, and log of one is zero — the word is annihilated. It contributes nothing, automatically, with no stopword list needed. A word appearing in three documents out of a million gets log of about three hundred thousand, a large multiplier. So 'Poneglyph' outweighs 'the' by an enormous factor, exactly as it should. Now here is my favourite part of this lesson, because it connects two islands you already visited. That inverse document frequency term is essentially the self-information from the information theory lesson. Log of one over probability. A rare word is a surprising word, and a surprising word is an informative word. The very same quantity that defined entropy is now ranking your search results. This is not a coincidence or an analogy — Shannon's measure of surprise turns out to be the correct measure of what a word tells you about a document. One final step that people skip and then wonder why their search is broken: L2-normalize every document vector, dividing it by its own length. Without this, a five-thousand-word chapter has a vector far longer than a two-hundred-word note, and the long one wins every similarity comparison purely for being long. After normalization, every document sits on the unit sphere and only its direction — its mix of topics — matters.

Now we cash all of this in, and the payoff is that you can build a real search engine this afternoon. Take the user's query — 'ancient weapon location' — and treat it as a very short document. Vectorize it with exactly the same vocabulary and exactly the same idf weights you computed over the corpus; this must be the same transformation, not a fresh one, or the dimensions do not correspond. Now score every document by the cosine similarity between the query vector and the document vector, and sort. That is it. That is a search engine, and the ranking function is the dot product from the very first lesson of this course. Why cosine rather than plain Euclidean distance? Because cosine ignores magnitude entirely and compares only direction. Two documents about navigation point the same way whether one is a paragraph or a book. Euclidean distance would call the long one and the short one dissimilar simply because one vector is longer, which is precisely the wrong invariance for text. And note the small elegance: once you have L2-normalized everything, the cosine and the dot product are literally the same number, and the division disappears from your code. Then there is the trick that makes it fast enough to be real. Your query has maybe five non-zero terms. Any document that shares none of those five words scores exactly zero, and there is no point computing that. So you precompute an inverted index — a map from each word to the list of documents containing it — look up only the five posting lists, and score only the union of those candidates. That is how a query returns in milliseconds across millions of documents, and it is the same structure that has powered search since the seventies. Finally, notice that vectorizing the text was the entire job. Those same TF-IDF vectors feed straight into logistic regression from the last lesson, and you have a spam classifier. Feed them into the clustering we do next lesson, and you have automatic topic discovery. The models did not change at all. Once text is vectors, every tool you already own applies to it.

Let us finish by being precise about where this breaks, because each wall we hit is the motivation for a later lesson, and seeing that now makes the rest of the course feel inevitable rather than arbitrary. Wall one: no concept of synonyms. In bag-of-words, 'ship' and 'vessel' are two entirely separate columns with no relationship whatsoever. A document that talks exclusively about vessels scores a perfect zero against a query about ships. The model has no idea they mean the same thing, because it has no notion of meaning at all — only of column identity. That wall is what embeddings tear down in lesson twenty-one, where words that appear in similar contexts end up as nearby vectors. Wall two: no order and no syntax. We said this at the start and it remains true. 'Dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' are identical. N-grams patch it locally, over two or three words, and fail completely at any longer range. That wall is what attention tears down in lesson twenty-three, where every word gets to look at every other word regardless of distance. Wall three: nothing to say about unseen words. If a word was not in the vocabulary when you fitted the vectorizer, it is silently dropped at query time. Typos vanish. New names vanish. Newly coined slang vanishes. That wall is what subword tokenization tears down in lesson twenty, where an unknown word is broken into known pieces rather than discarded. So three walls, three later lessons. But — and this genuinely matters for your work — do not conclude that TF-IDF is obsolete. It has one property that embeddings do not: it is exact. If a user searches for a product code, an error number, a surname, or any rare token, TF-IDF matches it precisely, while an embedding blurs it into a neighbourhood of vaguely similar things and may rank the exact match below a semantic cousin. This is why serious retrieval systems in production do not choose. They run both, keyword and vector, and merge the two ranked lists. That is hybrid search, we will build it in lesson thirty-four, and half of it is what you learned today.

Let me close with the decisions that actually change your numbers, because textbooks list ten preprocessing steps and in practice about four of them matter. Lowercasing. It merges 'Ship' at the start of a sentence with 'ship' in the middle, which is almost always what you want, and it halves your vocabulary. But be aware of what it destroys: 'US' the country becomes 'us' the pronoun, 'IT' the department becomes 'it'. For topic classification, lowercase freely. For named-entity extraction, do not. Stemming and lemmatization. Both try to collapse 'running', 'runs' and 'ran' into one feature. Stemming does it by chopping suffixes with crude rules, which is fast and sometimes produces non-words — 'universe' becomes 'univers'. Lemmatization uses an actual dictionary and grammatical analysis, which is slower and correct. My honest advice: try without either first. On a large corpus, the different forms of a word each get enough examples that the model handles them fine, and you may find the whole step changes your score by nothing at all. Now the two dials that give the biggest return for the least thought: minimum and maximum document frequency. Drop every word that appears in fewer than about three documents — those are overwhelmingly typos, scanning errors and one-off noise, and they are pure variance. Drop every word appearing in more than about ninety percent of documents — those are stopwords by measurement rather than by list, and they carry no signal. These two settings routinely cut the vocabulary in half with no loss of accuracy, and a smaller vocabulary means faster training and less overfitting. And finally, the rule that outranks all of the above. Fit the vectorizer on the training set only. Building the vocabulary and computing the idf weights over your whole dataset before you split it means the training features were chosen with knowledge of the test documents. Your reported score goes up, your real performance does not, and nothing anywhere raises an error. This is the single most common bug in applied text machine learning, and it is invisible unless you look for it deliberately.
tokenization: Every model in the rest of this course eats numbers. Not text — numbers. So before you can do anything at all with language, you have to make one decision: how do you chop a piece of text into units, and what integer does each unit get? It sounds like plumbing. It is not. This decision is made once, before training, it is baked into the shape of the embedding table, and every layer above it inherits it forever. You cannot change your mind about tokenization later without throwing the model away and starting again. So it is worth understanding properly, and there are exactly three answers people have tried. The obvious one is words. Split on spaces and punctuation, give every distinct word an integer, and you are done. It fails in two ways, and both are serious. The first is the size of the tail: English has hundreds of thousands of word forms once you count plurals, tenses, compounds, names and misspellings, and every single one needs its own row in the embedding table, most of which will be seen a handful of times and learned badly. The second is worse. At inference time you will meet a word you never saw in training — a name, a typo, a product released last month — and a word-level model has no way to represent it. It becomes the unknown token, and everything that word meant is gone. There is no partial credit. So people tried the opposite: characters. Now the vocabulary is about a hundred symbols, the table is tiny, and nothing is ever unknown, because any string is just a sequence of characters. But you have traded one problem for two others. Sequences become enormous — a short sentence is hundreds of steps, and the cost of most architectures grows badly with length. And each unit carries almost no meaning: the letter t on its own tells the model nearly nothing, so the network has to spend capacity reassembling words from letters before it can start on the actual task. The answer that every modern language model uses is the middle: subwords. Keep common words whole, because they are common and deserve their own vector, and split rare words into pieces that get reused across many rare words. Unhappiness becomes un, happi, ness. You get a fixed vocabulary of a manageable size — typically thirty to a hundred thousand — nothing is ever unrepresentable, sequences stay a reasonable length, and the pieces themselves carry real meaning, because a prefix like un genuinely does something predictable to whatever follows it. The only remaining question is where the pieces come from, and the beautiful part is that nobody writes them down. They are learned.

Byte-Pair Encoding is one of those algorithms that is so simple you suspect you have misunderstood it. You have not. Here it is in full. Start by treating every single character as its own token, so your vocabulary is just the alphabet. Now go through your entire training corpus and count every adjacent pair of tokens — how many times does t followed by h appear, how many times does h followed by e appear, and so on for every pair. Find the most frequent pair. Merge it: create one new token that means that pair, add it to the vocabulary, and replace every occurrence in the corpus. Then count all the pairs again, in the corpus you have just rewritten, and merge the new most frequent pair. Repeat until your vocabulary has as many entries as you asked for. That is it. That is the whole algorithm, and you will implement it in the lab in about thirty lines. Watch what happens as it runs. The first merges are the most common letter pairs — t h, e r, i n. Then those merged tokens start appearing in pairs themselves, so t-h merges with e to give the whole word the. A few thousand merges in, every common English word is a single token, and the pieces left over are exactly the productive fragments: ing, ed, un, tion, pre. Nobody taught it morphology. It has never heard of a suffix. It simply merged what was frequent, and frequency in real language happens to track meaning, because the pieces people reuse are the pieces that mean something. Now the part that trips people up. The output of training is not really a vocabulary; it is an ordered list of merge rules. To tokenize a new piece of text, you split it into characters and then replay those merges in exactly the order they were learned. Order matters — apply them in a different order and you get different tokens. Which is why the tokenizer is a real artifact that ships alongside the weights, and why using the wrong tokenizer with a model produces fluent nonsense rather than an error. Two consequences worth naming. First, the vocabulary reflects your corpus, warts and all. Train it on English web text and English gets efficient tokens while Nepali or Thai gets chopped into bytes, so the same sentence costs three or four times as many tokens in one language as another — which is a real cost difference and a real quality difference. Second, the modern refinement: byte-level BPE, which GPT-2 introduced and almost everything since has used. Instead of starting from characters, start from the two hundred and fifty-six possible bytes. Now literally any input is representable — any script, any emoji, any corrupted encoding, any binary blob — and the unknown token stops existing altogether. It is a small change and it removed an entire category of bug.

So you have a tokenizer. What does it actually hand the model? A list of integers, called input-ids, one per token, each one a row index into a big table. That is genuinely all. And I want to be blunt about what those integers are not: they are not meaningful. Token four thousand and seventy-four is not more similar to four thousand and seventy-five than it is to nine. The numbers are addresses, assigned in merge order, and any arithmetic on them is nonsense. All the meaning arrives in the next lesson, when each address is used to look up a learned vector. Three practical things come with the ids. First, padding and the attention mask. Models process batches, batches need rectangular tensors, and your sentences have different lengths — so the short ones get filled out with a padding token to match the longest in the batch. But padding is not text and the model must not read it, so alongside the ids you get an attention mask: a parallel list of ones and zeros saying which positions are real. Pass the ids without the mask and the model will happily attend to your padding as though it were content, and your results will be quietly, mildly wrong in a way that is very hard to notice. Second, special tokens. These are added by the tokenizer, not by you, and they are structural. BERT-style models wrap the input in a classification token at the front and a separator between segments. GPT-style models have an end-of-text token that marks a document boundary. And instruction-tuned chat models have a template that wraps each turn in role markers — a system block, a user block, an assistant block — which the model was explicitly trained to expect. If you build the prompt string by hand and get that template wrong, the model still answers, and answers noticeably worse, and there is no error message anywhere. Use the tokenizer's apply-chat-template function and let it do this. Third, a couple of numbers worth carrying in your head, because they turn into money and into failures. For ordinary English prose, one token is about three quarters of a word — so a thousand tokens is roughly seven hundred and fifty words, or a page and a half. That ratio gets much worse for anything unusual: source code fragments into punctuation, long numbers split digit by digit, and any non-Latin script — Nepali, Arabic, Chinese, Thai — costs several times more tokens for the same content, because the tokenizer's merges were learned mostly on English. This is not a small effect. It means the same document can consume three times the context window and three times the API cost depending on what language it is written in. Every context limit you will ever hit and every bill you will ever pay is counted in tokens, never in words, and the conversion rate depends on your text.

The Baratie is the right kitchen for this, because Sanji's first decision on any ingredient is not the heat and it is not the seasoning. It is the cut. Whole, halved, sliced, julienned, diced, minced. And that decision constrains everything after it: a stock wants big rough pieces that give up flavour slowly, a stir-fry wants thin even slices that cook in seconds, a sauce wants it fine enough to disappear. Get the cut wrong and no amount of skill at the stove recovers it. The prep board decides what the dish can be. Now run our three options through that kitchen. Suppose you insist on serving every ingredient whole. Whole onion, whole fish, whole potato. You can make a few dishes that way, and they will be good ones, but your menu is small, and the first time a delivery arrives with something you have never handled before, you are stuck — you have no procedure for it and it does not go in the pot. That is word-level tokenization, and the unknown token is the ingredient the kitchen refuses. Now the opposite. Mince absolutely everything, down to a paste. Nothing is ever impossible now, because anything can be minced. But nothing is recognisable either — you have destroyed the texture that made the ingredient worth having, and you need an enormous pot and a very long time to build a dish back up out of paste. That is character-level, and the enormous pot is your sequence length. What a real kitchen does is cut to size, and the size depends on the ingredient. Things the kitchen handles constantly stay whole or nearly so, because everyone knows what to do with them. Things it rarely sees get broken down into pieces it already knows: this unfamiliar root behaves like a carrot once it is batonned, so baton it. And here is the part that is exactly BPE. In a busy kitchen, the cuts you call for most often get their own name. Brunoise, chiffonade, julienne. Nobody sat down and designed those words from first principles — they exist because those particular cuts came up constantly, and something you say a hundred times a night earns a short name. Frequency earns a name. That is the merge loop, in a kitchen. One last thing this picture explains, and it is the most useful part. Ask Sanji how many cells are in that onion and he cannot tell you, and it is not ignorance — it is that once the onion is diced, the dice are the unit. He works in dice. The cellular structure underneath is real but it is no longer something he handles or counts. That is precisely why a language model that can write a sonnet will confidently miscount the letters in a word. It never saw the letters. It saw tokens, and the letters are inside them, below the level at which the model works at all.

I want to finish with a list, because once you have this lesson a whole category of famous language-model failures stops being mysterious and starts being obvious. Start with the one everybody has seen: ask a model how many r's are in strawberry and watch it get it wrong. People take this as evidence that the model cannot reason, and that is the wrong conclusion. The model never saw the letters. Strawberry arrives as two or three tokens, and the information about which characters are inside them was discarded before the first layer ran. Asking it to count letters is like asking Sanji to count cells. The same cause explains the whole family: reversing a string, finding words that rhyme, writing an acrostic, counting syllables. Every one of those needs sub-token information the model was never given. Next, arithmetic. Language models are strangely inconsistent at maths in a way that does not look like a reasoning failure, and often it is not. Long numbers get tokenized inconsistently — one four-digit number might be a single token because it appeared often in the training data as a year, while the number next to it splits into two pieces. So the model is not looking at digits in fixed positions; it is looking at chunks that shift depending on the value. The evidence for this is direct: models that tokenize numbers digit by digit, or group them from the right, measurably improve at arithmetic without any change to the reasoning machinery. That tells you where the problem was. Third, and this one will bite you personally: trailing whitespace. The string the capital is, with a trailing space, tokenizes differently from the same string without it, because the space usually belongs to the front of the next token. When you leave a trailing space at the end of your prompt, you have handed the model a token boundary that essentially never occurred in its training data, and it now has to complete from an unnatural position. The output gets worse for no reason you can see in the text. Do not put a trailing space at the end of a prompt. Fourth, and it is the strangest: glitch tokens. The tokenizer is trained on one corpus and the model on another, slightly different one. Occasionally a string is frequent enough in the tokenizer's corpus to earn its own token, but essentially absent from the model's training data — usernames scraped from forums are the classic case. So that token exists, it has a row in the embedding table, and that row was initialized randomly and then almost never updated. Feed it to the model and you get bizarre, repeatable, completely non-obvious behaviour: refusals, unrelated words, evasion. These are real and documented, and they are pure tokenizer archaeology. So the summary is this. Tokenization is not preprocessing you can ignore. It is the interface between language and the model, it is decided before training and frozen forever, and a surprising share of what looks like a failure of intelligence is really the model doing perfectly sensible work on units that are not the units you had in mind.
training-neural-nets: Everything in the last two lessons converges here, and it converges into something almost disappointingly small. Training a neural network is four operations in a loop. You take a batch of examples and run them forward through the network to get predictions. You compare those predictions to the true answers and reduce the whole comparison to a single number, the loss. You run backpropagation, which turns that one number into a gradient for every single weight in the network. And then you take a step, nudging each weight a small distance in the direction that would have made the loss smaller. Then you do it again with the next batch. That is it. In PyTorch it is four lines you will type ten thousand times, plus one more that everybody forgets the first week: zero grad. PyTorch accumulates gradients rather than replacing them, which is deliberate and occasionally useful, and which means that if you do not clear them you are stepping on the sum of every batch you have ever seen. Learn the vocabulary properly now, because people use it loosely and it causes real confusion. An epoch is one pass over the whole dataset. An iteration, or a step, is one update, and it happens once per batch. Fifty thousand examples with a batch size of sixty-four is seven hundred and eighty-two steps in a single epoch, and it is the steps that move the weights.

The loss function is where your intention enters the machine, and it deserves more thought than it usually gets. If you are predicting a number, the loss measures distance, and the choice is mostly about outliers. Mean squared error squares every error, so one prediction that is ten away contributes a hundred while ten predictions that are one away contribute ten in total — squared error chases the worst case, which is right when the worst case matters and wrong when your data has a few bad rows in it. Mean absolute error treats them evenly and is the calmer choice. If you are predicting a class, the loss measures surprise. Cross-entropy takes the probability your model assigned to the correct answer and charges you minus its logarithm. Say ninety-nine per cent and be right, and you pay almost nothing. Say one per cent and be right, and you pay a great deal. That asymmetry is the whole reason cross-entropy produces models whose confidence means something. One practical warning that costs people days: PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss applies the softmax internally, so you hand it raw logits. If you apply softmax yourself and pass the result, nothing crashes — the model simply learns worse, and you will spend a week blaming your architecture. And the last idea is the one to keep. The loss has to be differentiable, and the thing you actually care about almost never is. Accuracy has no useful gradient. So you optimise a stand-in and you watch the real number beside it, and when the two disagree, the real number is the one that is right.

Backprop hands you a gradient. The optimizer decides what to do with it, and there are three you need. Plain stochastic gradient descent is the honest one: subtract the learning rate times the gradient, and that is the whole algorithm. Its entire personality is that learning rate. Set it too small and the model creeps; set it too large and the loss climbs and then becomes NaN, usually within a few hundred steps, and the first thing to try when that happens is always to divide the learning rate by ten. Momentum is the first improvement, and the physical picture is exact. Instead of stepping along the current gradient, you step along a running average of recent gradients. In a long narrow valley — which is what almost every loss surface actually looks like — plain descent bounces from wall to wall and creeps forward slowly, while momentum cancels the bouncing, because the sideways components alternate in sign and average out, while the forward component does not. Adam adds a second idea on top: every parameter gets its own learning rate, scaled by how large that parameter's gradients have recently been. A weight that rarely gets a gradient takes large steps when it finally does; a weight being shouted at from every batch takes small careful ones. The practical upshot is that Adam trains almost anything at three times ten to the minus four without you tuning a thing, which is why it is the default. Two exceptions worth carrying: well-tuned SGD with momentum still generalises a shade better on vision models, and if you are using weight decay, use AdamW rather than Adam, because Adam's decay interacts with the per-parameter scaling in a way that is not what the name promises.

Rayleigh spends two years training Luffy on Rusukaina, and the striking thing, if you watch what he actually does, is how little of it is teaching. He does not hand over a new technique each week. He puts Luffy on an island that hits back, and lets a small set of moves he already knew run against real feedback, thousands of times. That is a training loop, and the moves are the architecture, and the loop is where the learning lives. Notice how carefully the island is chosen. Rusukaina has weather that changes every hour and animals that can beat him, which means that every single day produces a signal. An island where nothing could hurt him would be a training set the model already fits — the loss would be zero, the gradient would be zero, and two years would change nothing at all. The difficulty is not an obstacle to the training; the difficulty is the training. And look at the feedback itself. Nobody tells Luffy that his left shoulder was four degrees out. He gets one outcome, thrown across a clearing, and has to work backwards to what in his own movement produced it. That is credit assignment, which is the exact problem backpropagation solves, and it is why a single scalar loss is enough. But the part people skip is the ending. He stopped. Two years and he left, at the point where the island had stopped producing new information. Keep training past that point and the network is no longer learning to fight; it is memorising one island, in enormous detail, including the parts that will never appear anywhere else.

The failure mode you will meet most often is overfitting, and the good news is that it is easy to see if you have set yourself up to look. Split your data three ways before you do anything else. The training set fits the weights. The validation set chooses everything you choose by hand — the learning rate, the architecture, the epoch to stop at. The test set is opened once, at the end, to report a number. The moment you make any decision based on the test set, it has become a validation set, and you no longer have an honest estimate of anything. The diagnosis is a single plot with two curves. If the training loss keeps falling while the validation loss turns around and starts climbing, the model has begun memorising, and the epoch where validation bottomed out is the model you should have kept. If both are stuck high, you are underfitting instead, and the answer is a bigger model, less regularisation, or a learning rate that is wrong. As for what to turn: the learning rate matters more than everything else combined, so tune it first and tune it on a logarithmic scale. Batch size comes next and is a trade — bigger batches give smoother gradients and better hardware use, smaller batches give noise that acts as a mild regulariser. Then dropout, which switches off a random fraction of units during training and must be off at evaluation time, which is what model dot eval does. Then weight decay. And then early stopping, which costs nothing, needs no tuning and is the one people forget. Underneath all of it sits a simpler truth: every regulariser is a way of pretending you have more data. If you can actually get more data, do that first.
transformer-architecture: We ended the last lesson with a gap, and it has to be closed before anything else, because it is not a small one. Look hard at what attention computes: a weighted sum of value vectors. Addition is commutative. So if you take a sentence, shuffle the tokens into a completely different order, and run self-attention over it, every token attends to the same set of other tokens with the same scores, and you get back the same output vectors — just sitting in different places. The layer is what mathematicians call permutation-equivariant, and in plain terms it means the mechanism has no concept of order whatsoever. Dog bites man and man bites dog are, to raw self-attention, the same input. That is catastrophic for language, where order carries a large part of the meaning. And notice where the problem came from, because it is instructive. The recurrent network never had this problem, and it never had to solve it either — it read the tokens one after another, so order was implicit in the act of reading. When we deleted the recurrence to buy parallelism, we deleted that for free property along with it. This is a very common shape in engineering: you remove something for a good reason and discover it was quietly doing a second job. So order has to be put back deliberately, by adding position information to the token embeddings before they ever reach the first layer. The original transformer did this with sinusoids. For each position you build a vector out of sines and cosines at many different frequencies — fast-oscillating components that distinguish neighbouring positions, slow ones that distinguish distant regions — and you add it to the token's embedding. Three things recommend it: it has no learned parameters, it produces a distinct pattern for every position, and because of the trigonometric identities, the encoding for position p plus k is a fixed linear function of the encoding for position p. That last one matters: it means a constant offset is the same transformation everywhere in the sequence, so the model can learn about relative distance rather than memorizing absolute slots. The alternative, used by BERT and GPT-2, is simply to learn a position embedding table like any other embedding — which works well and has one hard limit: it cannot represent a position longer than the table you trained. What most current models actually use is rotary position embedding, RoPE, and the idea is elegant enough to state. Instead of adding anything to the input, rotate the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to their position, in two-dimensional slices. Because rotating both vectors by their own angle makes their dot product depend only on the difference of the angles, the attention score between two tokens ends up depending on the distance between them and not on where the pair sits in the sequence. Relative position, injected at exactly the place where position is used, with no extra parameters, and it extrapolates. That is why it won.

Now we can assemble the thing, and the pleasant surprise is how little there is. A transformer block has exactly two sublayers. The first is the multi-head self-attention you learned last lesson. The second is a small feedforward network. Each of the two is wrapped in the same pair of helpers — a residual connection around it and a layer normalization — and that is the entire block. Stack N of them and you have a transformer. Let us look at the second sublayer, because it gets much less attention than it deserves and it is where most of the parameters live. The feedforward network is two linear layers with a non-linearity in between, usually GELU. It expands the representation to about four times the model dimension, applies the bend, and projects it back down. And the crucial word is position-wise: the same small network is applied independently to every position, with no interaction between positions at all. Token five's feedforward output depends only on token five's vector. If you know one thing about the parameter budget of a transformer, know this: that feedforward block is roughly two thirds of all the weights in the model. The attention everyone talks about is the minority. Now, why both sublayers? Because they do genuinely different jobs and neither can substitute for the other. Attention moves information between positions — it is the only part of the architecture that lets one token see another, and it is essentially a weighted average, which is a fairly limited kind of computation. The feedforward does the computing, within a position, on whatever the attention just gathered. One mixes, the other thinks. A stack of pure attention layers would just be repeated averaging with very little capacity to transform anything; a stack of pure feedforwards would be an MLP that never lets tokens communicate. Alternating them, over and over, is how the model builds up: gather relevant context, process it, gather again with a better representation, process again. There is a useful way to read this that has become standard, and it is worth carrying. Think of each token as having a residual stream running through the whole depth of the model — a vector that starts as the embedding and gets progressively refined. Each block reads from that stream, computes something, and writes an update back into it. Attention writes in information gathered from other positions; the feedforward writes in the result of processing. Nothing is ever replaced wholesale; everything is accumulated. And finally, the point that surprises people who expect large models to be complicated: you just repeat this block. There is no different architecture further up, no special layers near the output, no clever hierarchy. BERT base is this block twelve times. GPT-3 is this block ninety-six times, with a wider model dimension. The recipe does not change with scale; only the numbers do, and that uniformity is precisely why the architecture scaled the way it did.

These two wrappers look like housekeeping in the diagram and they are the reason the architecture can be a hundred layers deep, so let us take them seriously. The residual connection is written x plus Sublayer of x. You compute the sublayer as normal, and then you add the original input back on. Two things follow from that plus sign, and both are important. The first is about gradients. When backpropagation comes through an addition, the gradient splits and flows down both branches unchanged, because the derivative of x with respect to x is one. So there is a path from the loss all the way back to layer one that consists entirely of additions, and multiplying by one, however many times, is still one. Compare that with the vanishing-gradient story from Part Three: without residuals, the gradient reaching the early layers of a deep stack has been multiplied by dozens of Jacobians and is essentially noise. With them, every layer has a direct line to the loss. This is the single trick that made networks of a hundred layers trainable, it came from ResNet in computer vision, and the transformer inherited it. The second consequence is about what a block has to learn, and it is subtler and just as useful. Without a residual, a block that wants to leave its input mostly alone must learn to reproduce that input exactly through a matrix multiply and a non-linearity — which is hard, and wasteful. With a residual, doing nothing is the default: if the sublayer outputs zeros, the block is the identity. So each block only has to learn the difference it wants to make, the update rather than the whole representation. That is why you can stack ninety-six of them and the ones that turn out to have nothing useful to contribute simply learn to contribute nearly nothing, instead of actively damaging the signal. Now layer normalization. The mechanic is simple: for each token, take its vector, subtract the mean of its features, divide by their standard deviation, and then scale and shift by two learned parameters. The point is to keep the inputs to each sublayer in a well-behaved range as the residual stream accumulates update after update — without it, activations drift in scale as you go up the stack and training becomes unstable. The word to underline is layer. This normalizes across the features of one token, independently of every other token and of the batch. Contrast batch normalization, which normalizes each feature across the examples in the batch: that makes the result depend on which other examples happen to be alongside yours, it needs different behaviour at training and inference time, and it degrades badly with small batches and variable-length sequences. All three problems are fatal for language, which is why every transformer uses LayerNorm and none use BatchNorm. And one final detail that looks cosmetic and is not: where you put the norm. The original paper did post-norm — apply the sublayer, add the residual, then normalize. It works, but it is fragile, and training it at depth requires a learning-rate warmup period to stop it diverging in the first few hundred steps. Pre-norm — normalize first, then the sublayer, then add — leaves the residual path completely clean, trains stably without the warmup, and is what essentially every modern model does. It is a one-line change in the code and it decides whether large models train reliably.

Franky built the Sunny as a stack of decks, and the detail worth noticing is not the decks — it is the corridor. There is one main passage that runs straight down through all of them, and every room opens off it: the galley, the workshop, the infirmary, the aquarium, the cabins. None of those rooms sits in the corridor. You walk past their doors. Now think about what that arrangement makes possible. If Chopper needs something from the storeroom at the bottom of the ship, it comes straight up the corridor. It does not have to be handed through the galley, and then handled by whoever is in the workshop, and then passed through the infirmary, arriving changed by each of them. It travels the whole height of the ship untouched. That is the residual stream, and it is exactly the property the plus sign gives you. Information — and, running the other way, gradient — has a clean route from one end of the model to the other, because the path does not go through the sublayers, it goes past them. A ship where every deck had to be walked through to reach the next one would be the pre-residual network, and the thing at the bottom would arrive unrecognizable. Notice the second property, because it is the one people underrate. A room can be shut. If the workshop is closed for the day, nothing about the ship breaks — the corridor still runs, and everything that was going past continues to go past. Compare a design where the corridor ran through each workshop: closing one would sever the ship in half. That is exactly the difference the residual makes to a block that has nothing useful to contribute. Without it, a bad layer actively corrupts what passes through, and adding depth can make a model worse. With it, a useless block learns to output nearly zero and simply gets walked past. Doing nothing is free, so extra depth is never actively harmful, so you can afford to build ninety-six decks and let training work out which ones matter. There is one more fitting in this picture. Along the bulkhead at every deck are gauges keeping the pressure and the flow in a sensible range, and they are there for a mundane and important reason: it means the same fittings, the same pipe diameters, the same doors work on every deck. Franky did not have to design deck forty differently from deck three. That is layer normalization. By keeping the scale of what enters each sublayer well-behaved, it lets one block design be repeated identically all the way up, instead of every layer needing its own hand-tuned settings. Corridor, rooms, gauges. A residual stream, sublayers hanging off it, and normalization keeping the whole stack in range. That is a transformer, and there is genuinely nothing else in the building.

Let us finish by walking one token all the way through, and then naming the three ways this architecture gets configured, because after this everything in the course is a variation on what you are about to hear. The journey. Your text is tokenized into integers. Each integer indexes the embedding table and comes out as a vector — that is the word-embeddings lesson, and it is still layer zero. Position information is added or, with RoPE, applied inside the attention. Now the vector enters the stack. In block one, layer norm tidies it, self-attention lets it gather from every other token in the sentence, and the result is added back into its residual stream. Then layer norm again, the feedforward processes what it now holds, and that result is added in too. That is one block, and the vector that comes out is the same shape as the one that went in — which is exactly why you can repeat the block. So it does, twelve times, or ninety-six. Deep in the stack, that vector is no longer really about the token it started as; it is a representation of that position in the context of the whole sentence. At the top, a final layer norm, and then one last linear projection from the model dimension out to the size of the vocabulary — producing one score per possible token — and a softmax turns those scores into a probability distribution. That distribution is the model's output. Every large language model you will use is that path. Now the three configurations, which differ only in which parts you keep and what mask you use. Encoder-only is BERT: no causal mask, so every token attends to every other token in both directions, and the representation of each position is informed by the entire sentence. That bidirectionality makes it excellent at understanding — classification, named entity recognition, retrieval, anything where you have the whole input in hand. It cannot generate, and the reason is worth stating precisely: if every position can see every other position, then during training a position can see the answer it is meant to predict. There is nothing to generate. Decoder-only is GPT, and it is what almost everything is today. Apply the causal mask, so position i sees only positions up to i, and train the whole thing to predict the next token. Generation is then immediate — feed what you have, take the distribution at the last position, sample, append, repeat. It sacrifices bidirectional context and, as the field discovered somewhat to its own surprise, that turned out to matter far less than being able to train on any text at all and generate. Encoder-decoder keeps both stacks, and is what the original paper described, because the original task was translation. The encoder reads the source with no mask. The decoder generates the target with a causal mask, and each of its blocks has a third sublayer between the two you know: cross-attention, where the queries come from the decoder and the keys and values come from the encoder. That is the attention from the seq2seq lesson, unchanged, and it needs no new machinery — it is the same function with different arguments, which is the tidiest thing about the whole design.
using-models-apis: You have built a model, so now the honest question: in a real project, where does the model actually come from? There are three answers, and the choice is mostly an economics and constraints decision rather than a technical one. First, a hosted API. You send text to OpenAI or Anthropic or Google, you get text back, you pay per token. The advantages are real and worth stating plainly: these are the strongest models available, you operate no infrastructure, you get improvements without doing anything, and you can be running in an afternoon. The costs are equally real. You pay per call forever, your data goes to a third party, you have a hard dependency on a company whose pricing, availability and model behaviour can all change without your involvement, and a model you built a careful prompt against can be deprecated on a schedule you do not set. Second, open weights that you host yourself. Download Llama or Mistral or Qwen or Gemma, put it behind vLLM or Text Generation Inference on a GPU you rent or own, and serve it. Now the data never leaves your infrastructure, which for health, legal and financial work is often not a preference but a requirement. Your cost is per hour of GPU rather than per token, which changes the shape of the bill completely. Nothing is deprecated underneath you — the weights on your disk are the weights on your disk. And in exchange you are now operating a GPU service, with all that implies about capacity planning, monitoring, upgrades and someone being on call. Third, local. Ollama or llama.cpp running a quantized model on your own machine — a laptop, a workstation, a single card. It is free, it is completely private, it works with no network, and the models available are roughly a generation behind the frontier. That gap is smaller every year and it is currently real. This tier is excellent for development, for iterating on prompts without paying per attempt, for anything that must run offline, and for data that genuinely cannot leave the building. Now the economics, because this is the part that decides real projects. Per-token pricing is unbeatable at low volume: a thousand calls a day costs a few dollars and needs no infrastructure, and self-hosting would be strictly worse in every dimension. But per-token pricing scales linearly forever, while a rented GPU costs the same whether you send it one request an hour or a thousand a minute. So there is a crossover, and it arrives sooner than people expect — often in the low millions of tokens per day. The mistake teams make is not picking wrong at the start; the API is almost always right at the start. The mistake is not noticing when they have crossed over, and continuing to pay per token for a workload that has become steady and predictable.

This slide is short and it will save somebody a legal conversation. The phrase open source has a specific, long-established meaning, and most of the models described as open in this field do not meet it. Open weights means one thing: the parameters are downloadable and you can run them on your own hardware. That is genuinely valuable, and it is not the same as open source. What you typically do not get with open weights is the training data — nobody publishes the corpus, partly for competitive reasons and partly because its provenance would not survive scrutiny. You do not get the training code, or the exact data mixture, or the hyperparameter schedule. Which means you cannot reproduce the model, you cannot audit what went into it, and you cannot answer the question of why it behaves a particular way by looking at what it read. You have the artifact and not the recipe. And the licences are frequently not open-source licences at all. Llama's licence is a custom document with a monthly-active-user threshold above which you need a separate agreement, plus a list of prohibited uses. Several other model licences forbid using the model's outputs to train a competing model, which matters a great deal if distillation was part of your plan. None of these terms are unreasonable, and all of them will surprise a team that assumed open meant Apache or MIT. Read the licence before the model is load-bearing in a product, not after. There is a genuinely open-source category, and it is worth knowing it exists. Projects like OLMo from AI2 and Pythia from EleutherAI publish everything: the data, the training code, the intermediate checkpoints across the whole run. Those models are less capable than the frontier and vastly more useful if your question is scientific rather than commercial, because you can trace a behaviour back to the data that produced it and watch it emerge across checkpoints. If you are doing research on how these systems work rather than building a product with them, that is where to look. So the practical summary. Open weights buy you three specific things: reproducibility, in the sense that the model on your disk today is the model on your disk next year; privacy, because inference happens on your infrastructure; and freedom from deprecation, which is not a small thing when a hosted model you tuned prompts against gets retired with three months notice. They do not buy you the general freedom the word open suggests. Both of those facts should be in your head at the same time when you choose.

There is a default that costs teams a great deal of money, and it is: use the best model for everything. It feels safe. It is expensive and often slower for no benefit, and here is the reasoning. Frontier models cost somewhere between ten and fifty times per token what small models cost, and they are several times slower to respond. That premium is entirely justified on hard tasks — multi-step reasoning, subtle judgement, long-context synthesis, difficult code. It is entirely wasted on easy ones. And here is the uncomfortable observation about real systems: most of the traffic in a production LLM application is not hard. It is classifying a support ticket into one of six categories. Extracting four fields from a form. Deciding which of three tools to call. Rewriting a sentence into a house style. Summarizing a short paragraph. On those, a small model with a well-written prompt produces the same answer as the frontier model, at a twentieth of the cost and a third of the latency. Paying the premium there buys you nothing measurable at all. So the technique is routing, and it is the largest single cost lever in most LLM products. Send the easy majority to a small, fast model. Escalate to the expensive one when the small model's confidence is low, when the input is long or unusual, when the task is explicitly flagged as hard, or when a cheap validation step fails. In a typical application eighty to ninety percent of calls can be served by the small model with no quality difference a user could detect, which turns a cost curve from steep to nearly flat. And the same logic applies to latency: users notice a two-second response and do not notice a three-hundred-millisecond one, so routing improves the product as well as the bill. Finally, how to choose, because this is where leaderboards mislead people. A benchmark average tells you how a model does on a distribution of tasks that is not your distribution. It is weakly correlated with performance on your actual workload, and the correlation is weakest exactly where you care most — on the specialized, narrow thing your product does. So do the measurement yourself, and it is genuinely a day of work. Write down fifty to a hundred real examples of your task, with the answers you want. Run every candidate model against them with the same prompt. Compare quality, latency and cost per call side by side, in one table. You will frequently find that a model costing a twentieth as much is within a point or two of the leader on your specific task, and occasionally you will find that it is better, because your task rewards something the benchmark does not measure. That table is worth more than every leaderboard you will read this year.

A Transponder Snail is a lovely piece of technology to think with, because everything true of it is true of an API call. When Luffy calls somebody on a Den Den Mushi, he gets access to knowledge that is not on the ship. He is talking to an expert who is somewhere else, who knows things no one aboard knows, and he did not have to feed that expert or find them a bunk. That is an enormous capability multiplier for a small crew, and it is exactly what a hosted API is: you are renting an ear and a mind that live on someone else's infrastructure. And notice the thing that is easy to miss and matters most: the capability is not the crew's, and it does not become the crew's. However many times Robin calls a scholar, the crew does not become scholars. Now the properties of the call, all of which the show is careful about. There is a delay — you wait for the connection and you wait for the answer, and in the middle of an emergency that delay is the whole problem. Someone can be listening; a line to the outside is a line the outside can listen to, and there are episodes that turn on exactly that. And the line can be cut, or the snail can be out of range, or the person on the other end can simply not pick up. Latency, privacy, availability. Those are not properties of the answer you get. They are properties of the fact that you asked somebody else. So the crew also carries a Baby Den Den Mushi, and it is the local model. Shorter range, less capability, no access to anyone outside — and it is on the ship, it works in the middle of the ocean, it costs nothing to use, and nobody else hears it. When you must have an answer and cannot rely on a line to the outside world, that is what you have, and that is exactly the argument for running a quantized model locally: it is not as good, and it is always there, and some of your requirements are about always-there rather than about best. Which brings me to the point of the picture. The skill Nami and Robin actually demonstrate is not owning the most powerful snail. It is judgement about which calls are worth making. Most questions on a ship are answered by asking the person standing next to you. You place a call when the question genuinely needs someone who is not aboard — and you place it knowing it will cost you time, and that you are telling somebody outside the crew what you are asking about. That is routing, and it is the same discipline. Ask the small model first. Reach for the line when the question actually needs it.

Let us finish with the architecture advice, which is short, boring, and the difference between a project that can adapt and one that cannot. Rule one: put every model call behind a single thin interface that you own. One function in your codebase that takes a list of messages and some parameters and returns text, with the actual provider selected by configuration. That is a small amount of work on day one and it is the difference between changing providers in an afternoon and rewriting a codebase. The failure mode is easy to picture: provider SDK calls sprinkled through forty files, each with its own retry logic and its own parameter names, and now a price change or an outage means a month of work. Rule two, and it follows immediately: that one boundary is where all the operational concerns belong. Retries with exponential backoff, because rate limits and transient failures are normal and not exceptional. Timeouts, because a hung call must not hang your request. Token counting, so you know your cost per user before the invoice tells you. Caching of identical calls, which on many workloads is a large and free saving. Structured logging of the prompt, the parameters and the output. And a fallback to a second provider, so a single vendor outage degrades your product instead of stopping it. Write each of these once, at the boundary, and every call site gets them. Rule three: assume the model will change, because it will. Hosted models are deprecated, new versions behave differently, and you will want to move for cost reasons. This has a direct consequence for how you write prompts: a prompt that has been tuned against one model's specific quirks is a liability, because those quirks are exactly what will not survive the switch. Keep prompts plain and explicit — say what you want rather than discovering an incantation that happens to work. And keep a regression set: twenty to a hundred inputs with expected outputs, that you run against any new model or new prompt before shipping. It takes an hour to build and it is how you find out a swap broke something, rather than learning it from a user three days later. Rule four, and it is the one people skip until it costs them: log the model name and version, the full prompt, the parameters and the output, together. The characteristic LLM incident is that behaviour changed overnight and nothing in your repository changed. Without those logs there is nothing to investigate — you cannot diff a black box against a memory. With them, you can point at exactly what moved. And that is Part Six. You know how these models are pretrained, how they are aligned, how they generate, how to adapt them and how to obtain them. Part Seven is about giving them access to information they were never trained on, which is where most real applications actually live.
vectors-cosine: A vector is just an ordered list of numbers — v equals bracket two, three — and that is the whole definition, but you should learn to see it three ways simultaneously, because each view unlocks a different part of the course. First, a vector is a list of measurements: a document described by word counts, a user described by age, income, and clicks, where each slot, each dimension, is one feature. Second, a vector is a point in space: bracket two three is the point two across and three up, and with seven hundred sixty-eight numbers it is a point in seven-hundred-sixty-eight-dimensional space — you cannot picture that, but here is the great trick of linear algebra: all of the two-dimensional formulas still work, completely unchanged, in any number of dimensions. Third, a vector is an arrow from the origin, with a direction and a length, and this is the view where similarity equals small angle comes from — the view this entire lesson is built on. Now the reason all three views matter: in modern AI, everything gets turned into a vector — a word, a sentence, a picture, a user, a song. The whole game of embeddings, which is Part Four, is to design the vector-making function so that similar things land near each other in the space. And once things are vectors, comparing meaning reduces to comparing arrows — which is exactly the math on this page. Word embeddings, attention scores, RAG retrieval, recommendation engines: all of them are literally vectors, dot products, and the angle between them. This is the single most reused idea in the entire course, so it is worth slowing down and building the three-views habit now.

Two quantities do all the work in this lesson: the length of a vector and the dot product of two vectors. The norm, the length, is just Pythagoras generalized to any number of dimensions: the norm of v is the square root of v-one squared plus v-two squared and so on. The length of bracket three, four is the square root of nine plus sixteen, which is five — the same three-four-five triangle you already know, now stated so it works in seven hundred dimensions. The dot product of two vectors multiplies matching slots and sums them: a-dot-b is a-one times b-one plus a-two times b-two, and so on. Bracket two three dotted with bracket four one is two times four plus three times one, which is eleven. Now, there are two ways to read that number, and you need both. The algebraic reading: the dot product is a matching score. The sum is large when the two vectors have big values in the same slots — they agree — near zero when their big values sit in different slots — unrelated — and negative when one is positive where the other is negative — they oppose. Sit with this one, because it is exactly how attention will decide which words should look at which words in Part Five. The geometric reading comes from a theorem worth memorizing: a-dot-b equals the norm of a, times the norm of b, times cosine theta, where theta is the angle between the arrows. So the dot product is the length of a, times the length of b, times how aligned they are. Cosine theta is plus one for the same direction, zero for perpendicular at ninety degrees, and minus one for opposite. Perpendicular vectors, called orthogonal, have a dot product of exactly zero — and in machine-learning language, that means they share no information. Hold both readings, because the algebraic one explains attention and the geometric one is about to give us cosine similarity.

Now rearrange that theorem and you get cosine similarity — the alignment score with the lengths divided out. Cosine theta equals a-dot-b divided by the norm of a times the norm of b. It always lands between minus one and plus one, and for non-negative data like word counts, between zero and one. Why divide out the lengths? Because in most machine-learning uses, magnitude is a nuisance and direction is the meaning. Picture a ten-thousand-word article about pirates and a hundred-word note about pirates. By raw length their word-count vectors are wildly different — but their direction is nearly the same, because they use the same words in the same proportions. Cosine says same topic; raw dot product or Euclidean distance would say totally different, purely because one document is longer. That is Nami's two-ships test: off Loguetown she watches a massive Marine galleon at full sail and a tiny fishing dinghy puttering slowly, and Usopp panics that they are nothing alike — but Nami draws each ship's velocity as an arrow and says, length is just speed, look at the angle. Both arrows point almost exactly the same way: both ships are heading for Reverse Mountain. The galleon being twenty times faster does not change where it is going. Then a luxury liner, fast and shiny, points ninety degrees away toward Loguetown port — big arrow, impressive speed, completely different destination, cosine zero. Let me make it concrete with three tiny word-count vectors over the vocabulary pirate, treasure, physics. Document one is bracket four, two, zero; document two is bracket two, one, zero; document three is bracket zero, one, three. Cosine of d-one and d-two is ten over ten, exactly one-point-zero, because d-two is simply d-one scaled by a half — identical direction, perfect similarity. Cosine of d-one and d-three is about zero-point-one-four — they barely overlap. This exact computation, with smarter vectors than raw word counts, is TF-IDF document search in Part Two, embedding and RAG retrieval in Part Seven, recommendation by similar-taste vectors, and the attention score inside every transformer in Part Five. Learn it once here and you have learned it for the whole course.

Cosine is not the only way to compare vectors, and a good engineer knows both and knows when. Euclidean distance is the straight-line gap between the two points — the norm of a minus b — and it cares about magnitude and direction together. Use it when the scale of the features is genuinely meaningful: physical measurements, or k-means clustering in Part Two, where how far apart two points are is exactly the thing you care about. Cosine similarity, by contrast, cares only about direction. Use it when the vectors represent content or meaning and the length reflects something irrelevant, like document size or how loud a feature happens to be. Now here is a bridge worth knowing, because it comes up in interviews. For vectors normalized to length one, which is very common for embeddings, the two measures actually agree: the squared distance between a and b equals two minus two times cosine theta. Read that carefully — as cosine goes up, distance goes down, monotonically, so ranking your results by cosine similarity and ranking them by Euclidean distance give the exact same order. That is precisely why vector databases let you pick either metric, and why embedding models often ship their vectors pre-normalized to length one. When the vectors are already unit length, cosine similarity is just the plain dot product — one multiply-and-add loop per comparison, with no square roots and no divisions at query time. At millions of comparisons per query, that arithmetic saving is the difference between a snappy search and a slow one. So the practical picture is: cosine for meaning, Euclidean for physical scale, and for normalized embeddings they are two spellings of the same ranking — which is why the vector database you use in Part Seven quietly pre-normalizes and then races through plain dot products.

Step back and fix the one idea you must be able to retrieve instantly for the rest of the course: angle, not length. Scaling a vector by a positive number never changes its meaning — two ships on the same heading, one recipe at two batch sizes, the same direction is the same content. Monica's palate makes the sitcom version: a giant stockpot and a tiny saucepan of the same sauce point the same way, four parts tomato, two garlic, one basil, just scaled — same recipe, same taste — while Rachel's trifle-with-beef points somewhere no real dessert points near, a huge angle no matter the serving size. Now where does this exact computation reappear? Everywhere, with smarter vectors than raw word counts. TF-IDF document search in Part Two. Embedding and RAG retrieval in Part Seven, when a vector database finds relevant documents by running Nami's two-ships test a million times a second. Recommendation, by finding users with similar taste vectors. And the attention score inside every transformer in Part Five, where the un-normalized dot product is used directly and scaled by one over the square root of d to keep the numbers in a friendly range — you will see exactly why. Two high-dimensional facts and two traps to carry forward. First, in high dimensions two random vectors are almost always nearly orthogonal, cosine near zero, so a cosine of zero-point-three between seven-hundred-sixty-eight-dimensional embeddings can already mean quite related — thresholds are calibrated on your own data, never imported from two-dimensional intuition. Second, the traps: do not compare raw dot products between vectors of different lengths and read them as similarity, because a long document beats a short one just by being long — divide by the norms or normalize first. And watch the zero-vector edge case: cosine similarity is undefined, zero over zero, for an all-zeros vector, which genuinely happens with the word-count vector of a stopword-only string. Learn angle-not-length cold, and the flashiest machinery later in the course stops being mysterious — it is Nami's two ships, all the way down.
word-embeddings: At the end of the last lesson we had a list of integers and I said, fairly bluntly, that the integers mean nothing. Let me make that concrete, because it is the whole motivation for this lesson. If the tokenizer assigns cat the id four thousand and seventy-four and dog the id nine thousand two hundred, those numbers came from the order in which merges happened. They are addresses. There is no sense in which four thousand and seventy-four is closer to four thousand and seventy-five than it is to nine. So if you feed raw ids into a network, the very first thing it does is arithmetic on them — multiply by a weight, add — and that arithmetic is meaningless. You have handed the model a number line that has nothing to do with language. The traditional fix is one-hot encoding. Give every word a vector as long as the vocabulary, all zeros except a single one at that word's position. That does fix the arithmetic: there is no false ordering any more, no implication that one word is bigger than another. But look at what it costs. Every pair of distinct words is now exactly the same distance apart. The angle between any two one-hot vectors is ninety degrees, always. So cat and dog are precisely as unrelated as cat and bureaucracy, and there is no way for the representation to say otherwise. Similarity is not merely absent, it is structurally impossible. And the vectors are enormous and almost entirely zeros. The answer is the embedding, and it is one of those ideas that is much simpler than its reputation. An embedding is a lookup table: a matrix with one row per vocabulary entry and, say, three hundred columns. To represent a token, you take its row. That row is a short, dense vector of real numbers — three hundred of them, all non-zero, all meaningful. There is a nice piece of bookkeeping worth noticing here: multiplying a one-hot vector by that matrix selects exactly one row, so a lookup is not an approximation of the matrix multiply, it is the same operation with the wasted work removed. That is literally how it is implemented. Now the crucial point, and it is the one that makes the rest of this lesson possible. Those numbers are not designed by anybody. The table starts filled with small random values, it is part of the model, and it is trained by gradient descent exactly like every other weight in the network. Nobody decides that cat should sit near dog. The position of every word emerges as a by-product of being useful for whatever task the network is being trained on. Which raises the obvious question: what task, exactly, makes a network place words in a way that matches meaning? The answer turns out to be startlingly cheap, and it is the next slide.

The question we left hanging was: what task would force a network to place words meaningfully? And the answer comes from a linguist, not a computer scientist. In nineteen fifty-seven, J. R. Firth wrote the sentence this entire field rests on: you shall know a word by the company it keeps. The claim is that if two words tend to appear surrounded by the same other words, they tend to mean similar things. Test it on yourself. If I say a word you have never heard — suppose I write, we drank a glass of chilled blurn with dinner, and later, he ordered a bottle of blurn — you now have a fairly confident idea of what blurn is. Nobody defined it. You inferred it entirely from the company it kept. Now, why this matters so much computationally: context is countable. A dictionary definition requires a human being to sit down and write it. Context does not. You can measure, from raw unlabelled text, exactly which words appear near which other words, at any scale you have text for. There is no annotation, no expert, no cost beyond compute. That turns meaning into something you can learn from the internet. So the training task writes itself, and it is what we now call self-supervised learning. You take a sentence from the corpus. You hide one word and ask the model to predict it from its neighbours — that is the continuous bag of words setup. Or you do the reverse: take a word and ask the model to predict which words are likely to surround it — that is skip-gram. Either way the corpus provides both the question and the correct answer, for free, for every position in every sentence you own. This is what makes it scale, and it is the same trick, at a vastly larger size, that trains modern language models. And here is the crucial move, the one worth remembering when the details fade. Nobody actually wants the prediction. The prediction task is a pretext. What we want is the by-product: in order to predict context well, the network is forced to represent words in a way that groups together words with similar behaviour, because that is the only way it can reuse anything it has learned. If cat and dog appear in the same kinds of sentences, the cheapest way for the network to do well on both is to give them similar vectors. The geometry falls out of the pressure to generalize. Throw away the prediction head when training finishes, keep the embedding table, and you have a map of the language. And finally, the honest caveat, because it explains a real limitation you will meet. This procedure can only ever capture distributional similarity — which words keep the same company. Usually that tracks meaning very well. But consider hot and cold: they appear in almost identical contexts, in the same sentence positions, with the same neighbours. So they end up close together, despite being opposites. The vectors know that hot and cold are the same kind of thing. They do not know that they are on opposite ends of it.

Let us make that concrete with the model that started it, word2vec, published by Mikolov and colleagues in twenty thirteen. There are two variants and I will focus on the one that won, skip-gram. Here is the setup. Slide a window over your corpus — say five words either side of a centre word. For the sentence the cat sat on the mat, with cat as the centre, the words the, sat, on and so forth are its context. Every centre-and-context pair you can extract is a training example, and the model's job is: given the centre word, make its real context words likely. Structurally there are two embedding tables, not one — a word gets one vector when it is being the centre and a different vector when it is being context, which turns out to train better. At the end you keep the centre table and throw the other away. Now the problem that makes the naive version impossible. To say make the real context words likely, you have to compare against everything else, which means a softmax over the entire vocabulary — a million words — computed at every single training example, of which there are billions. That is not slow, it is impossible. Negative sampling is the fix, and it is a genuinely clever reframing.
