Instead of asking which of the million words comes next, ask a much cheaper question: here is a pair of words — did this pair actually occur together in the corpus, yes or no? Now take your real pair, cat and sat, and label it yes. Then draw five or ten random words from the vocabulary — cat and bureaucracy, cat and helicopter — and label those no. Train a plain binary classifier with a sigmoid. You have replaced one million-way decision with about ten yes-or-no decisions, and the gradient still pushes real pairs together and random pairs apart, which is all you wanted. Two details make the difference between this working and not, and they are worth knowing because they recur. First, you do not draw the negatives uniformly, and you do not draw them by raw frequency either. Raw frequency means almost every negative is the, of or and, which teaches the model nothing. word2vec raises each word's frequency to the power zero point seven five before sampling, which flattens the distribution — common words still appear more often, but not overwhelmingly. Second, subsampling: very frequent words are randomly dropped from the corpus entirely, with a probability that rises with their frequency. This speeds training up and, more importantly, lets the windows reach further past the filler to the words that actually carry content. And I want to end on the thing that surprises people most about word2vec. There is no hidden layer. There is no depth. The entire model is two lookup tables, a dot product between them, and a sigmoid. That is it — a shallower model than the perceptron you met in Part Three. Its power comes from nowhere except the sheer volume of context it has seen: billions of windows, each one nudging the geometry very slightly. It is a strong argument that in language, data and objective can matter far more than architecture.

Nami's charts are the cleanest picture of this I know, and they make the analogy-arithmetic result feel inevitable instead of magical. Think about how she actually maps a new sea. She does not fly above it and measure. She records relationships: this current runs from here to there and takes two days; this wind holds from the south in this season; from this island you can reach those three, and the sea between them behaves like this. Every entry in the log is about a relationship to something else. And then the chart — the actual position of each island on the paper — is whatever arrangement makes all of those recorded relationships consistent at once. The position is not measured. It is inferred, from company. That is the distributional hypothesis with a compass on it. Now notice the consequence, because it is exactly the property we want. Two islands that have the same currents running past them, the same seasonal winds, the same neighbours a day's sail away, will end up drawn near each other on the chart — even if no ship has ever sailed directly between the two. They are close because they behave the same way, not because anyone measured the distance. That is why cat and dog end up near each other in embedding space. Not because the model was told they are both animals, but because the sentences they live in are shaped alike. Now the part that makes the famous result obvious. On a chart, direction means something on its own, independently of where you are. North-east is north-east from every island in the sea. So if you know that a particular bearing and distance takes you from a spring island to its paired summer island, you can apply that same bearing from a different spring island and arrive somewhere sensible. The offset is a fact about the sea, not about the starting point. That is precisely what people found in word2vec's space: take the vector for king, subtract man, add woman, and the nearest word to where you land is queen. The male-to-female offset is a direction in the space, and it is roughly the same direction everywhere, because the same relationship recurs throughout the language and the geometry had to accommodate all of it at once. Capital-of is a direction. Plural-of is a direction. Past-tense-of is a direction. Nobody built any of them in. And finally, the honest limit, which is where the next lesson begins. A chart gives each island exactly one dot. That works beautifully for a place that is always the same place. But Alabasta in a sandstorm and Alabasta on a calm night are not the same thing to sail into, and one dot on the paper cannot hold both. A word embedding has the same shape of problem: bank gets one vector, and it must serve the river and the money at once. The compromise is a position somewhere between the two, which is a poor description of either.

So where does this end, and what survives? Start with the ceiling, because it is a single sentence: a static embedding gives one vector per word, permanently, with no knowledge of the sentence it is currently in. Bank has one row in the table. That row has to serve I sat on the bank of the river and I transferred it to my bank account, and it cannot. What training produces is a compromise position somewhere between the two senses, which describes neither of them well. And this is not a rare edge case — polysemy is everywhere in language, and every word with more than one sense is blurred in exactly this way. The model cannot even represent the question, because there is nowhere for context to enter. The other limitation is one you have a professional responsibility to know about. The geometry is learned from a corpus, so it encodes whatever is in that corpus, including things nobody intended to teach it. If the text of the internet places doctor near he and nurse near she, then the vectors place them that way too, and because the analogy machinery works, you can ask the model for man is to doctor as woman is to what, and it will answer nurse. That is not a bug in word2vec; it is word2vec working correctly on the statistics it was given. Debiasing methods exist, they help, and they do not solve it — the associations are distributed throughout the geometry rather than sitting in one place. The practical rule is: if embeddings are feeding a decision that affects people, audit what the geometry has learned before you ship it, not afterwards. Now, the fix for the main problem, which is the whole arc of the rest of this course. If one vector per word cannot handle context, stop storing a vector per word. Compute a vector per occurrence instead — read the entire sentence, and produce a representation of this word, here, in this company. Then bank in the river sentence and bank in the money sentence get genuinely different vectors, because they were computed from different neighbours. That is what contextual embeddings are, that is what ELMo and BERT and every model since actually do, and the mechanism that makes it possible is attention, which is two lessons away. But I want to end by being clear about what did not get replaced, because it matters. The embedding table is still there. Open any transformer, including the largest models running today, and the very first thing that happens to your token ids is a lookup in a matrix of exactly the kind you have just learned about. It is layer zero of everything. What changed is that it is no longer trained separately on a pretext task and then frozen — it is learned jointly with the two hundred layers above it, as part of one system. So word2vec is not a historical curiosity you can skip. It is the ground floor of the building, and everything from here on is storeys added on top of it.
